title: On Buddha-Recitation (Annotated Sayings of Master Chewu)
author: Compiled and annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: A single recitation of the Buddha’s name, free of all other conditions; when the ten recitations are perfected, one instantly transcends many kalpas.

inline.s: Course
Textbook
Master Chewu
Sayings
A single recitation of the Buddha’s name, free of all other conditions; when the ten recitations are perfected, one instantly transcends many kalpas.
But so long as thought succeeds thought without interruption, the subduing, the severing, the cultivating, and the realising that result cannot be conceived or spoken of.
Master Yinguang said:
“The Sayings of Chewu are indeed
(in truth)
the most essential instruction of the Pure Land school.”
(From the Preface to the Collected Works of Chan Master Mengdong)

This book is the standard and the guide for Buddha-recitation, a jewel among treatises, and so it is named “On Buddha-Recitation.” The words within it are the very practice of Master Chewu. Not only did the master speak them, he also accomplished them, and confirmed them through the many auspicious signs of his rebirth — which is the most rare and admirable aspect of all.

“To know the way through the mountain, one must ask one who has already travelled it.” Master Chewu knew the time of his passing ten months before he died, and the auspicious signs of his rebirth appeared in abundance; thus he is one who has already traversed the road to the Land of Bliss. His words are true and his meaning is real, and to act in accordance with them can never go wrong.

[gui nie] refers to the gnomon (gui biao), a metaphor for a standard or a rule. [Gnomon] an astronomical instrument of ancient China: a ruler (gui) is laid flat on a stone base with a pole (biao) set up at each of the north and south ends. From the length of the sun’s shadow one can determine the solar terms and the length of the year.

Although “On Buddha-Recitation” comprises only thirty-nine sections and few in words, yet concerning the principle, practice, conduct, and realisation of the Pure Land school it gives a penetrating and comprehensive exposition, and it instructs one to understand the First Principle and to work upon the mind-ground — truly a guide of study and practice for all who recite the Buddha’s name. Therefore one should earnestly embrace it with all one’s heart, set it before one’s seat, and read it, awaken to it, and practise it constantly, so that all may enter deeply into the realm of the Pure Land teaching and ascend directly to the highest lotus seat, in order not to be unworthy of the master’s great compassionate heart.
[The First Principle] the supreme and unsurpassed truth, which is the reality of all dharmas. The Buddha said:

“All dharmas are false and illusory; in the very place where they cease, that is called real, that is called reality, that is called the dharma-realm, that is called ultimate wisdom, that is called the truth of the First Principle, that is called the emptiness of the First Principle.”
(The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra,
Fascicle Forty,
the Kaundinya Chapter.) [The reality of all dharmas] what is called “reality” is the true state of things; “the reality of all dharmas” is the true state of all dharmas. In the Buddha-store Sutra,
the Buddha-Recitation Chapter, the second, the Buddha said:
“What is called the reality of all dharmas? That is, all dharmas are ultimately empty, without any existence.”
The Diamond Sutra says:
“Whatever has form is false and illusory.”
[quan quan fu ying] to hold fast earnestly and never forget. Quan quan: to grasp tightly and not let go, extended to mean earnest and sincere; fu ying: to keep deeply in the mind.

Of the thirty-nine sections in the whole work, the first thirty-eight are from the “Dharma Words” portion of the Collected Works of Master Chewu, while the last section is excerpted from the Collected Works of Master Chewu, “Reply to the Layman Xiangyan.” The numbering and titles of the sections were added by the annotator for ease of understanding and reference, and are not part of the original text.

blocks.text: A Brief Biography of the Master

inline.s: Master Chewu (
), an eminent monk of the Qing dynasty, a native of Fengrun in Hebei. His lay surname was Ma, his given name Jixing, and his style name Chewu,
his sobriquet Mengdong, and he lived in the Qianlong era. He was the

thirty-sixth patriarch of the Linji school and the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, and was thoroughly versed in the Chan lineage, the scriptural teaching, and the Pure Land teaching. Even as a child the master was exceptionally intelligent and especially fond of study; among the classics, histories, and the wide range of books there was none he did not examine and read. At the age of twenty-two, through a serious illness he awakened to the impermanence of this illusory body, and immediately resolved to leave the world. After leaving the home life he went about visiting teachers and sitting in their lectures. He went to Xiangjie Temple to hear Master Longyi lecture on the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, and from dawn to dusk he questioned and probed, seeking the profound meaning, until he awakened to the whole purport of that sutra. He then followed Master Hui’an of Zengshou Temple to hear lectures on the Dharma-characteristic school and gained its essential point. Later, sitting at the feet of Master Biankong of Xinhua Temple, he heard the Lotus, the Surangama, the Diamond, and other sutras, and suddenly opened to the perfect understanding, so that the doctrines of the nature school and the appearance school, the one-mind three contemplations, and the meaning of the ten contemplations were entirely free of obstruction. Afterwards he visited Chan Master Cuiruchun of Guangtong Temple to investigate the matter of the supreme vehicle (seeing one’s own nature and realising the mind). Master and disciple answered each other and were wholly in accord, and Master Chun thereupon confirmed him, making him the thirty-sixth patriarch of the Linji school. The master broadly opened his lecture halls, led the assembly in meditation, and exhorted younger students with tireless enthusiasm. For fourteen years, as constant as a single day, his fame spread across the land and the style of his teaching flourished greatly.

But afterwards, whenever Master Chewu recalled Master Yongming — who, though a master of the Chan school, still turned his heart to the Pure Land, reciting the Buddha’s name a hundred thousand times a day and longing for rebirth in the Land of Bliss — he reflected that in the present Dharma-ending age he should all the more follow the legacy of Chan Master Yongming. So he set his mind upon the Pure Land and advocated the Lotus school. Each day he allowed only the time it takes to burn one measure of incense for receiving guests; the rest he devoted entirely to bowing to the Buddha and reciting the Buddha’s name.

The master attained the profound meaning of both the Chan school and the Pure Land school. He was extremely strict with himself and deeply earnest toward others; in his exposition and teaching his words poured forth like water from a vase and gathered like rising clouds, and in his day he was the foremost person of the Dharma-gate. Whenever he set forth the Tathagata’s grace in rescuing beings from suffering and granting them joy, the master would shed tears as he spoke, and none who heard him could keep from weeping until their robes were damp. Master Yongming said:
“One who has Chan and also the Pure Land is like a tiger wearing horns: in this present life he is a teacher of men, and in the life to come he becomes a Buddha and a Patriarch.”
From this one can see the truth of it.

Ten months before his passing, the master already knew the time of his departure. In the second month of the fifteenth year of the Jiaqing era he went to Wanshou Temple to sweep the ancestral pagoda and took leave of the patrons of the mountains. In the third month he returned to the mountain and ordered preparations for his cremation. On the seventeenth day of the tenth month he gathered the assembly, entrusted the affairs of the monastery, and ordered his disciple Songquan to lead the congregation and preside.

[Patrons (wai hu)] the lay people apart from the monks and nuns — such as kinsmen and dana-patrons (almsgivers) — who practise various good deeds for the sake of Buddhism, such as supplying the clergy with clothing and food to support their peaceful cultivation, or doing all they can to protect and advance the spread of the Dharma. [tu pi] cremation.

Half a month before he revealed his passing, he saw in the empty sky countless banners and canopies, coming from the west. He then told the assembly: “The signs of the Pure Land have appeared; I am about to return to the West.” When the assembly urged him to remain in the world by way of exhortation, the master said: “A hundred years are but a sojourn, and in the end there is a place of return.
I have attained the holy state,
and you should rejoice for the master’s sake; why trouble to keep me here?”
[A hundred years are but a sojourn] in living a hundred years, it is nothing more than a temporary lodging. [zhen] to reach; to attain. Example: perfecting it day by day.
On the sixteenth day of the twelfth month he ordered the setting up of the nirvāṇa feast. On the seventeenth day, in the shen period (three in the afternoon), he told the assembly:
“Yesterday I already saw the three great beings Manjusri, Avalokitesvara, and Mahasthamaprapta (Shizhi); now I have again received the Buddha’s personal welcome, and I am now departing.”

The assembly recited the Buddha’s name with ever greater vigour. The master sat upright facing the west, palms joined, and said: “Recite one line of the sacred name and behold one portion of the marks of excellence.” Then he formed the Amitābha mudra with his hands and passed away serenely, and all present smelled a rare fragrance floating in the air. After seven days of offerings his face was as in life, kindly and full, his white hair had turned black, and his complexion was extraordinarily smooth and radiant. After the second seven-day period he was placed in the coffin, and after the third he was cremated, yielding more than a hundred relics.

The master was born in the sixth year of the Qianlong era, on the fourteenth day of the tenth month, in the wei period (one to three in the afternoon), and passed away in the fifteenth year of the Jiaqing era, on the seventeenth day of the twelfth month, in the shen period (three to five in the afternoon). His worldly age was seventy, his monastic age forty-nine, and his Dharma age forty-three. The Collected Works of Master Chewu is widely circulated in the world.
[Monastic age (seng la)] the number of years since a monk or nun received the precepts. [Dharma age (fa la)] the number of years since a bhiksu received the precepts.

The essential way: a single recitation of the Buddha’s name encompasses faith, understanding, cultivation, and realisation; therefore the essentials of the Greater Vehicle, the Lesser Vehicle, and all the sutras are all contained within it. Hence the practice of reciting the name is the essential way.
[Of all gateways of understanding, the essential is to illuminate the mind; of all gateways of practice, the essential is to purify the mind.]
Of all gateways of understanding, the essential is to illumine and realise the true mind; of all gateways of practice, the essential is to remove the defilements of the mind.

[Gateway of understanding (fa men)] the “gateway of the teaching” meant here is the gateway of understanding, that is, what is commonly called the gateway of insight, which chiefly consists in studying and comprehending the doctrine. [Gateway of practice (xing men)] the gateway of practice is to set out upon practice in accordance with the teaching, chiefly devoted to actual cultivation. [Defilements of the mind (xin gou)] another name for the afflictions.

[Since the essential of illuminating the mind is none other than Buddha-recitation. To recollect the Buddha and to recite the Buddha, whether in the present or in the future, one will surely see the Buddha; without relying on any expedient means, the mind naturally opens. Thus — is not Buddha-recitation the essential of illuminating the mind?]

Then, for illuminating and realising the true mind there is nothing more excellent than Buddha-recitation. For in recollecting the Buddha and reciting the Buddha, whether in the present or in the future, one will certainly see the Buddha; without borrowing any other expedient means (without reliance on expedient means) the true mind is fully revealed (the mind naturally opens — this is the state of great and complete awakening). This being so, is not Buddha-recitation the essential of illuminating the mind?

[Moreover, the essential of purifying the mind is likewise none other than Buddha-recitation. When a single thought accords, that thought is Buddha; when every thought accords, every thought is Buddha. When a clear jewel is cast into murky water, the murky water cannot but become clear; when the Buddha’s name is cast into a confused mind, the confused mind cannot but become Buddha. Thus — is not Buddha-recitation the essential of purifying the mind?]

Furthermore, for purifying the defilements of the mind there is nothing more excellent than Buddha-recitation. When a single thought accords, that thought is Buddha (and that thought, of course, is free of affliction); when every thought accords, every thought is Buddha. When a clear jewel is cast into murky water, the murky water cannot but grow clear; when the Buddha’s name is cast into a vexed and scattered mind, that vexed and scattered mind cannot but turn into the serene, bright, and still Buddha-mind. This being so, is not Buddha-recitation the essential of purifying the mind?

[When a single thought accords, that thought is Buddha; when every thought accords, every thought is Buddha] when the pure and unmixed thought of Buddha-recitation is present (no deluded thought being mingled within this single line of the name), it is called “a single thought of accord.” “Accord” bears the meaning “this very mind is making the Buddha; this very mind is the Buddha.” (See the section on
“a Single Thought of Accord”
below.) [Clear jewel] a precious jewel that can purify murky water. The “Three Periods of Recollection” of Zhongfeng says:

“In the Western region there is a precious thing called the clear jewel. It is said that when this jewel is thrown into murky water, if it enters an inch of the water, that inch of murky water becomes clear immediately. As the jewel enters the water, from an inch to a foot and even to the bottom, the murky water likewise follows it and becomes clear and still. Know then that the clear jewel is a metaphor for the pure thought of Buddha-recitation; the murky water is a metaphor for the confused and scattered deluded mind.”

[A single recitation of the Buddha’s name encompasses the essentials of both the gateway of awakening and the gateway of cultivation. When awakening is raised, faith is within it; when cultivation is raised, realisation is within it. Faith, understanding, cultivation, and realisation are all encompassed, and the essentials of the greater and lesser vehicles and of all the sutras are exhausted without remainder. Then — is not this single Amitābha the essential way?]

From the above one can see that a single recitation of the Buddha’s name encompasses the essentials of both the gateway of awakening and the gateway of cultivation. When awakening is spoken of, faith is within it; when cultivation is spoken of, realisation is within it. A single recitation of the Buddha’s name encompasses faith, understanding, cultivation, and realisation, so that the essentials of the Greater Vehicle, the Lesser Vehicle, and all the sutras are entirely contained within this single name. Then — is not this single Amitābha Buddha the essential way?
[qing wu bu jin] here means contained without omission. “Qing” means to use up, all of it.

The conditions of rebirth: each thought we give rise to becomes a condition for rebirth in a future life. Carefully examine the thoughts that arise in the course of daily life — with which of the ten dharma-realms they accord most, and with which they accord most intensely — and then, without asking anyone else, you will know clearly which realm you will be reborn into in the next life and what your circumstances will be.

[This present thought of ours is, in its entirety, the true turned into delusion, and, in its entirety, the delusion that is itself the true; through the day it is unchanging, and through the day it follows conditions. If one does not follow the conditions of the Buddha-realm to think of the Buddha-realm, then one thinks of the nine realms; if one does not think of the three vehicles, then one thinks of the six ordinary realms; if one does not think of humans and devas, then one thinks of the three evil paths; if one does not think of ghosts and animals, then one thinks of hell. For as long as there is a mind, there cannot be no thought. And the mind-substance of no-thought is realised by the Buddha alone. From the stage of equal enlightenment downward, all beings have thought. Whatever thought arises must fall within the ten realms; there is no thought that goes beyond the ten realms, because the ten dharma-realms have no outside.]

This present thought of ours is either the deluded mind or the true mind; the substance of the mind is unchanging through the day, yet its state of delusion or awakening changes through the day as it follows the objects and thoughts it relies upon. If one does not follow the conditions of the Buddha-dharma-realm to think of the Buddha-dharma-realm, then one conditions the other nine dharma-realms and thinks of them. Within these nine realms, if one does not condition the three vehicles (sravaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva), then one conditions the six ordinary realms (hell, hungry ghost, animal, asura, human, deva). Within the six ordinary realms, if one does not condition humans and devas, then one conditions the three evil paths (hell, hungry ghost, animal). Within the three evil paths, if one does not condition ghosts and animals, then one conditions hell. This is all because, so long as there is a mind, one cannot be without thought. For the mind-substance of complete no-thought is realised by the Buddha alone; from the bodhisattva at the stage of equal enlightenment downward, all beings have thought. Then, whatever thought arises must be a thought of one of the ten realms, because the ten dharma-realms already encompass everything.

[The whole true becomes delusion; the whole delusion is itself the true] this present thought of the mind has two states, the true and the deluded. When self-nature holds sway it is true; when habitual tendencies hold sway it is deluded. “The whole true becomes delusion, the whole delusion is itself the true” means that true and deluded do not stand side by side; either it is wholly true or wholly deluded. In a single thought of delusion, the whole true mind becomes a deluded mind (the whole true becomes delusion); in a single thought of awakening, the whole deluded mind becomes a true mind (the whole delusion is itself the true). The “true” here means the original — that is, the true mind is the original state of the mind; the “deluded” means deluded movement, that which is confused. Because the original state is muddied and confused by deluded movement, the true mind becomes the deluded mind. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “In the previous thought of delusion, one is an ordinary person; in the later thought of awakening, one is a Buddha.” [Unchanging through the day, following conditions through the day] although the mind has the distinction of delusion and awakening — in delusion the whole true becomes delusion, in awakening the whole delusion is itself the true — yet the substance of the mind (self-nature) is in no way altered (without arising, ceasing, increase, or decrease), as it is said: “Unchanging through the day, following conditions through the day; following conditions through the day, unchanging through the day.” [The ten dharma-realms] hell, hungry ghost, animal, asura, human, deva, sravaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, Buddha. The first six are the six ordinary realms; the last four are the four sages. [Bodhisattva of equal enlightenment] among the fifty-two stages of the Greater Vehicle, the fifty-first stage is called equal enlightenment; this is the bodhisattva about to realise Buddhahood, whose merit and wisdom are nearly equal to the Buddha’s, hence the name “equal enlightenment.” The fifty-second stage is Buddhahood.
[Each thought one gives rise to is a condition for rebirth. If one truly understands this principle and yet does not recite the Buddha’s name — there has never been such a one.]
Each thought we give rise to becomes a condition for rebirth in a future life. If one truly understands this principle and yet does not recite the Buddha’s name, such a person can never exist.

[If this mind can accord with equanimity, great compassion, the merits of the proper and dependent rewards, and the sublime name of myriad virtues, then it is thinking of the Buddha-realm. If it can accord with the bodhi-mind, the six perfections, and the myriad practices, then it is thinking of the bodhisattva-realm. With a mind of non-self, according with the twelve links of dependent origination, it is thinking of the pratyekabuddha-realm. With a mind of non-self, contemplating the four noble truths, it is thinking of the sravaka-realm.]

If this present thought accords with the Buddha’s equanimity, great compassion, the merits of the proper and dependent rewards, and the sublime name of myriad virtues, then it is thinking of the Buddha-realm; if it accords with the bodhi-mind, the six perfections, and the myriad practices, then it is thinking of the bodhisattva-realm; with a mind of non-self, according with the twelve links of dependent origination, it is thinking of the pratyekabuddha-realm; with a mind of non-self, contemplating the four noble truths, it is thinking of the sravaka-realm.

[Proper and dependent rewards (yi zheng)] the dependent reward and the proper reward. The lands, dwellings, houses, and implements of the world are that upon which the body relies, and are called the “dependent reward”; the body of a sentient being, formed by the temporary union of the five aggregates, is the result of karma created in past lives, and is called the “proper reward.”

[If it accords with the four dhyanas and the eight concentrations, as well as the highest grade of the ten wholesome deeds, then it is thinking of the deva-realm. If it accords with the five precepts, then it is thinking of the human realm. If one cultivates the precepts, wholesome deeds, and other such dharmas while harbouring a mind of hatred, pride, and victory, then one falls into the asura-realm.]

If this present thought accords with the four dhyanas and the eight concentrations, as well as the supreme ten wholesome deeds, then it is thinking of the deva-realm; if it accords with the five precepts, then it is thinking of the human realm; if one cultivates the precepts, the ten wholesome deeds, and other such dharmas while harbouring a mind of resentment, pride, and competition, then it is thinking of the asura-realm.

[The four dhyanas and eight concentrations] the four dhyanas are the four concentrations of the form realm; the eight concentrations are the four dhyanas of the form realm and the four formless concentrations of the formless realm. [The ten wholesome deeds] the ten kinds of wholesome karma: not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, not speaking divisively, not speaking harshly, not speaking idly, not being greedy, not being hateful, not being deluded. [The five precepts] not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, not drinking alcohol. Not killing is not taking the life of living creatures; not stealing is not taking the property of others; not committing sexual misconduct is not engaging in sexual acts outside the bond of marriage; not speaking falsely is not uttering deceitful and fraudulent words; not drinking alcohol is not consuming intoxicating drinks or drugs.
[If, with a gentle
(identical with “soft”)

mind, one thinks of the lower grade of the ten evil deeds, then one falls into the animal-realm. Or, with a mind at once relaxed and intense, according with the middle grade of the ten evil deeds, one falls into the hungry-ghost realm. If, with a fierce and blazing mind, one accords with the highest grade of the ten evil deeds, then one falls into the hell-realm. The ten evil deeds are killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, idle speech, harsh speech, divisive speech, greed, hatred, and wrong views; to do the opposite of these is the ten wholesome deeds.]

If, with a gentle (not intense) mind, one thinks of the milder ten evil deeds, then one is thinking of the animal-realm. If, with a somewhat intense mind, one accords with the middling ten evil deeds, then one is thinking of the hungry-ghost realm. If, with a very intense (fierce and blazing) mind, one accords with the worst of the ten evil deeds, then one is thinking of the hell-realm. The ten evil deeds are killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, idle speech, harsh speech, divisive speech, greed, hatred, and ignorance; to do the opposite of these is the ten wholesome deeds.

[One should closely examine the thoughts that arise in daily life — with which realm they accord most, and with which they accord most intensely — and then the place where one will settle one’s body and establish one’s destiny in a future life, without troubling to ask another.]

One should carefully examine the thoughts that arise in the course of daily life — with which of the ten dharma-realms they accord most, and with which they accord most intensely — and then, without asking anyone else, you will know clearly which realm you will be reborn into in the next life and what your circumstances (the place where you will settle) will be.
[mi] fine and detailed; minute.

Carefully examine the thoughts that arise in the course of daily life — with which of the ten dharma-realms they accord most, and with which they accord most intensely — this is the very place of self-examination! Therefore the effort of cultivation must be made where thoughts arise.

blocks.text: 3. Karmic Retribution Manifested in the Mind

inline.s: Karmic retribution manifested in the mind: all states are produced by karma and manifested by the mind. The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is produced by pure karma and manifested by a pure mind. Therefore a cultivator who with single-minded focus recites the Buddha’s name and diligently cultivates pure karma will surely, through karmic response, be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[All states are produced by karma and manifested by the mind. In the very place where they appear, their own substance is the mind. As long as there is a mind, there cannot be a state absent. If the Buddha-state does not appear, then the states of the nine realms appear. If the states of the three vehicles do not appear, then the states of the six ordinary realms appear. If the states of devas, humans, ghosts, and animals do not appear, then the states of hell appear.]

All states are produced by karma and manifested by the mind. And the state that appears is itself the self-mind. As long as there is a mind, there cannot be a state absent. If this mind does not manifest the Buddha-state, it manifests the states of the nine realms (hell, hungry ghost, animal, asura, human, deva, sravaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva). If it does not manifest the states of the three vehicles (the Sravaka Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, the Bodhisattva Vehicle), it manifests the states of the six ordinary realms (that is, the six paths, for the six paths are all ordinary beings, hence the name “six ordinary realms”). If it does not manifest the states of devas, humans, ghosts, and animals, it manifests the states of hell.

[The states manifested by the Buddha and the three vehicles, though differing in their degree of superiority, are all, in essentials, enjoyment of the bliss of Dharma. The states manifested by the devas of the three realms are solely the enjoyment of the bliss of concentration and of the five objects of desire. The state of the human path is mixed with suffering and joy, each following its own karma, in varying measure. The states of ghosts and animals have much suffering and little joy. As for hell, it is wholly and solely extreme suffering.]

The states manifested by the minds of the Buddha and the three vehicles, though differing in excellence and inferiority, are all, in the essential thing, the enjoyment of the bliss of Dharma. The states manifested by the minds of the devas of the three realms are all the enjoyment of the bliss of concentration and of the five objects of desire. The state manifested by the mind of the human path has both suffering and joy, each person following his own karmic retribution, the proportion of suffering and joy differing. The states manifested by the minds of hungry ghosts and animals have much suffering and little joy. As for the state manifested by the mind of hell, it is wholly and solely extreme suffering.

[The three realms] the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. [The five objects of desire] form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Form refers to beautiful appearances; sound to melodious tones; smell to fragrant scents; taste to delicious flavours; touch to agreeable sensations. Because these five can cause one to give rise to a mind of greed and desire, they are called the five objects of desire.

[As the mountains, rivers, people, and things seen in a dream are all manifested by the dream-mind. Without the dream-mind there would certainly be no dream-state. And if there were no dream-state, neither would there be a dream-mind. Therefore know: apart from the mind there is no state, and apart from the state there is no mind. The whole state is the mind, and the whole mind is the state. If one would investigate the fruit within the cause, one should contemplate the mind; if one would verify the cause at the place of the fruit, one should contemplate the state. Hence it is said there has never been a state without a mind, and never a mind without a state. The fruit must follow from the cause, and the cause must realise the fruit. If one truly knows this principle that mind and state, cause and fruit, are one and not two, and yet still does not recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Pure Land — I do not believe it.]

This is like the mountains, rivers, people, and things one sees in a dream, all manifested by the dream-mind. If there were no dream-mind, there would certainly be no dream-state. Suppose there were no dream-state; then there would also be no dream-mind. Therefore we know: apart from the mind there is no state, and apart from the state there is no mind. The state is the mind, and the mind is the state. If one would investigate (come to know) the fruit within the cause, one must contemplate the mind; if one would verify (examine) the cause at the place of the fruit, one must contemplate the state. Therefore it is said: there is no state without a mind, and no mind without a state. The fruit must come from the cause, and the cause must manifest the fruit. If one truly knows this principle of mind and state, cause and fruit, as one and not two, and yet still does not recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss — I cannot believe it!
[yi ru, one suchness] not two and not different — this is called one suchness.

blocks.text: 4. The Essential Doctrine of the Pure Land

inline.s: The essential doctrine of the Pure Land: to take birth and death as a matter of genuine concern, to awaken the bodhi-mind, and, with deep faith and vows, to hold fast to the Buddha’s name.
[gang zong, essential doctrine] the principal outline and central purport.

[The sixteen words — “to take birth and death as a matter of genuine concern, to awaken the bodhi-mind, and, with deep faith and vows, to hold fast to the Buddha’s name” — are the one great essential doctrine of the gateway of Buddha-recitation.]

To take birth and death as a matter of genuine concern, to awaken the bodhi-mind, and, with deep faith and vows, to hold fast to the Buddha’s name” — these sixteen words are the one great essential doctrine of the gateway of Buddha-recitation.

[If the mind of “taking birth and death as a matter of genuine concern” is not aroused, then all instruction is nothing but idle words. Of all the heavy suffering in the world, none exceeds birth and death. If birth and death is not ended, then there is death upon death, birth upon birth, there being death in birth and birth in death. Out of one womb, into another womb; casting off one skin-bag, taking up another skin-bag — the suffering is already unbearable. Moreover, since the round of rebirth is not yet escaped, falling is unavoidable. The womb of a pig, the womb of a dog — into which will one not bore? The skin-bag of a donkey, the skin-bag of a horse — which will one not take up?]

If a cultivator does not arouse the mind of genuinely seeking to escape birth and death, then all instruction is, for him, merely idle talk (frivolous words). Of all the greatest suffering in the world, none exceeds birth and death. If birth and death is not ended, then there is birth upon birth and death upon death, the wheel of rebirth turning without cease. Out of one womb (dying), into another womb (being reborn); casting off one foul skin-bag (dying), taking up another foul skin-bag (being reborn) — the suffering is beyond words. Moreover, since the round of rebirth is not yet escaped, falling into the three evil paths is unavoidable. The womb of a pig, the womb of a dog — into which will one not bore? The skin-bag of a donkey, the skin-bag of a horse — which will one not take up?
[xi lun, idle words] words that have a playful and unrealistic character.

[This human body is the most difficult to obtain and the most easily lost. Through a single thought’s error one falls into an evil realm. The three evil paths are easy to enter and difficult to leave; the duration in hell is long and its suffering heavy. Whereas the seven Buddhas came and went, it has still been an ant; after eighty thousand kalpas, it has not escaped the body of a dove. The duration in the animal path is already extreme, and the duration in the ghost and hell paths is many times longer. Long enduring through endless kalpas — when is there an end, when a resting place? Amid the agonies of ten thousand sufferings, there is no refuge and no rescue. At every utterance of this, the hairs of the body stand on end. Each time one thinks of it, the five viscera burn as with fire. Therefore, from this very moment, one should acutely grieve over birth and death, as in mourning one’s father and mother, with the urgency of putting out a fire blazing on one’s head
(an archaic form of “burn”)

This human body is the most difficult to obtain and yet the most easily lost. Through a single thought’s error one enters an evil path. The three evil paths are easy to enter and hard to leave; if one falls into the hell path, the time is long and the suffering heavy. If one falls into the animal path, being deluded and attached to its body, life after life it is still that same animal. For example, a nest of ants — since the time of the seven Buddhas they have always been ants; and the dove, after eighty thousand kalpas, is still a dove. The time in the animal path is already extremely long, while the time in the hungry-ghost and hell paths is several times longer still. Long enduring through endless kalpas — when is there an end? Amid the agonies of ten thousand sufferings, there is neither refuge nor rescue. These circumstances, at every word of them, make the hairs of the body stand on end. Each time one thinks of them, the five viscera burn as if on fire. Therefore from this very moment one must grieve acutely over birth and death, as one mourns the death of one’s father and mother, with the urgency of one putting out a fire blazing on his head.

[Since the seven Buddhas, it has still been an ant] animals are deluded and always attached to this very physical body, and so their time in the animal path is extremely long. When the Jetavana Vihara was being built and the wall was being dug, the Buddha saw a nest of ants and said to the elder Sudatta: these ants have, since the time of the seven Buddhas, always been ants. [The seven Buddhas] the seven Buddhas of the past, namely Vipasyin Buddha, Sikhin Buddha, Visvabhu Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kashyapa Buddha, and Śākyamuni Buddha. [After eighty thousand kalpas, it has not escaped the body of a dove] one day the Buddha saw a dove and at once said to his disciples: this dove, even after eighty thousand kalpas, will still be a dove. [As in mourning one’s father and mother] grief as when one’s parents have died. [kao, bi] (deceased) father and mother.

[And yet I have birth and death, and I seek to escape. And all sentient beings are in birth and death, and all of them should escape. They and I are originally of one body. They are all my parents from many lives past, and Buddhas of the future. If one does not think of saving them all but seeks only one’s own benefit, then there is a deficiency in principle and the heart is not at ease. Moreover, if the great mind is not aroused, then outwardly one cannot be in communion with the Buddhas, and inwardly one cannot accord with one’s own nature; above, one cannot perfectly accomplish the Buddha Way, and below, one cannot broadly benefit the multitude of beings. The beginningless bonds of love — how can they be released? The beginningless debts of grievance — how can they be resolved? The karmic offences accumulated over many kalpas are hard to repent of; the roots of goodness accumulated over many kalpas are hard to bring to maturity. Whatever one cultivates is beset by many obstacles. Even should there be some accomplishment, in the end it falls into the one-sided and small. Therefore one must, in accord with one’s nature, awaken the great bodhi-mind.]

And yet I have birth and death, and I seek to escape. And all sentient beings are in birth and death, and all of them should escape. They and I are originally of one body; they are all my parents from many lives past, and also Buddhas of the future. If I do not save them all but seek only my own liberation, then there is a deficiency in principle and my heart is not at ease. Moreover, if the great mind (the bodhi-mind) is not aroused, then outwardly one cannot be in communion with the Buddhas, and inwardly one cannot accord with one’s own nature; above, one cannot perfectly accomplish the Buddha Way, and below, one cannot broadly benefit the multitude of beings. This being so, the beginningless bonds of love — how can they be released? The beginningless debts of grievance — how can they be resolved? The karmic offences accumulated over countless kalpas are difficult to repent of; the roots of goodness accumulated over countless kalpas are difficult to bring to maturity. Cultivating in this way, one is confronted at all times and places with many obstacles serving as tigers in one’s path. Even should there be some accomplishment, in the end it is an incomplete (one-sided) small fruit. Therefore one must, in accord with one’s nature, awaken the great bodhi-mind!

[Awaken the bodhi-mind] to arouse the great mind of seeking the Buddha Way above (to attain Buddhahood) and saving sentient beings below. Master Xing’an, in his “Exhortation to Awaken the Bodhi-Mind,” says: “The essential gateway to entering the Way is to make the resolve foremost; the urgent task of cultivation is to establish the vow first. When the vow is established, sentient beings can be saved; when the resolve is aroused, the Buddha Way can be accomplished. If one does not arouse the vast mind and establish the firm vow, then even should one pass through kalpas of dust, one would still remain in the round of rebirth; though one may cultivate, it is all in vain and full of toil. Therefore the Avatamsaka Sutra says: ‘To forget the bodhi-mind while practising all good dharmas is called the work of Mara.’ Forgetting it is already thus; how much more so never having aroused it? Hence one knows that if one wishes to learn the Tathagata Vehicle, one must first fully arouse the bodhisattva’s vow; this cannot be delayed.” [The Tathagata Vehicle] the teaching that leads beings to Buddhahood. A vehicle is a conveyance, used as a metaphor for the Buddha’s teaching; the teaching can carry beings to the far shore of nirvāṇa, and so it is called a “vehicle.”

[Since the great mind has been aroused, one should cultivate the great practice. And among all the gateways of practice, to seek the one most easy to begin, most easy to accomplish, most perfectly stable, and most perfectly sudden and complete — there is none like “with deep faith and vows, to hold fast to the Buddha’s name.”]

Since the great mind has been aroused, one should cultivate the great practice. And among all the gateways of practice, seeking the one most easy to begin, most easy to accomplish, and again most perfectly stable and most perfectly sudden and complete — there is nothing surpassing “with deep faith and vows, to hold fast to the Buddha’s name.”

Master Xing’an, in a verse instructing a meditator on Buddha-recitation, said: “One line of Amitābha is a case in point. No further deliberation is needed; settle it on the spot at once. Like a great fire, touch it and it burns. Like the sword Tai’a, oppose it and it is destroyed. The eighty-four thousand treasure-hoards of Dharma are wholly gathered in six words. The seventeen hundred tangled vines (the seventeen hundred cases of the Chan tradition) are cut through with a single stroke (with one line of the Buddha’s name, the tangled vines are all severed). Let the Buddha not be fond of hearing them; I for my part recall and recite with mind and heart. Pray do not speak many words; only keep the single mind unconfused.” (From the Records of Pure Land Sages)

Tangled vines: a term of the Chan tradition. It means that words and language, like creeping vines that spread and intertwine, are meant to explain and clarify principle, yet in turn entangle and bind one. To waste time over idle chatter and to speak of nothing to the point is called “pulling the tangled vines.” [Even the Buddha's one word, he is not fond of hearing] Master Zhaozhou told the assembly: “The single word ‘Buddha’ — I am not fond of hearing it.” Master Chewu said: “Sayings such as ‘the single word Buddha, I am not fond of hearing’ and ‘a single blow killing it and giving it to the dog to eat’ all reveal the supremely wonderful skillful means of the dharma-kaya's ascent; they are true Buddha-recitation.” (See item twenty-four below, “Like the Sky that Covers All.”) [Ascent above the dharma-kaya] To transcend the dharma-kaya is called the “ascent above the dharma-kaya.” The Chan school calls breaking through the first barrier (seeing the nature) “a matter alongside the dharma-kaya,” breaking through the second barrier “the true seat of the dharma-kaya,” and breaking through the third barrier (the barrier fortress) “the ascent above the dharma-kaya”; only with the ascent above the dharma-kaya does one see that one is equal to the Buddha.

As for so-called deep faith: the Brahman-voice of Śākyamuni Tathagata never speaks falsely; the great compassionate heart of Amitābha Buddha never makes empty vows. Moreover, taking as cause the recitation of the Buddha's name in seeking rebirth, one must surely receive as fruit the seeing of the Buddha and rebirth in his land. It is like planting melons and getting melons, planting beans and getting beans; the echo must answer the sound, the shadow must follow the form. The cause is not cast away in vain, the fruit is not gained for nothing. This is what one can be confident of of oneself without even asking the Buddha. How much the more, then, is the present single thought of our own mind-nature: the wholly real becomes the false, and the wholly false is the real; all day long it follows conditions, yet all day long it is unchanging. It extends across the ten directions and reaches down through the three times; within its own body there is nothing outside it, and the Amitābha Pure Land is wholly within it. With a mind that possesses the Buddha, reciting the Buddha that my mind possesses — how could the Buddha that my mind possesses not respond to the mind that possesses the Buddha? The Record of Rebirths sets down the auspicious signs at the end of life in clear, unbroken, verifiable rows — how could it deceive us!

As for so-called deep faith: believe that the Brahman-voice of Śākyamuni Tathagata never speaks falsely; believe that the great compassionate heart of Amitābha Buddha never makes empty vows. Furthermore, deeply believe that taking as cause the recitation of the Buddha's name in seeking rebirth must surely produce the fruit of seeing the Buddha and rebirth in his land. It is like planting melons and getting melons, planting beans and getting beans; the echo must answer the sound, the shadow must follow the form. The cause is never cast away in vain, and the fruit is never gained for nothing. These are what one can believe of oneself without even asking the Buddha! How much the more is the present single thought of our own mind-nature — either it is the false (the wholly real becomes the false), or it is the true (the wholly false is the real); though the mind-nature all day follows conditions, in truth it is all day unchanging. The mind-nature extends across the ten directions and reaches through the three times (past, present and future), great with nothing outside it, and so the Amitābha Pure Land is wholly within it. With a mind that possesses the Buddha, recite the Buddha that my mind possesses — how could the Buddha that my mind possesses not respond to the mind that possesses the Buddha? The Record of Rebirths sets down the auspicious signs at the end of life, in case after case; how could it deceive us!
[Gained in vain] To obtain for nothing.

With such faith established, the vow and its joy become naturally keen. Looking back from the bliss of that land upon the suffering of Sahā, the mind of renunciation grows naturally deep — as one leaving a cesspit, as one emerging from prison. Looking from afar at the bliss of that land and comparing it with the suffering of Sahā, one's joy and longing become naturally keen — as one returning to one's home village, as one hastening to a place of treasure. In a word: as the thirsty long to drink, as the hungry long to eat, as the sick and suffering long for good medicine, as the infant longs for its loving mother, as one shuns an enemy pressing in with a drawn knife, as one fallen into water or fire urgently seeks rescue. If one can indeed be this earnest, then no realm or condition can lead the mind astray.

With such deep faith established, the mind that wills for rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and delights in that rebirth becomes naturally keen. Looking back from the bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss upon the suffering of the Sahā world, one's mind of renunciation of the Sahā world becomes naturally deep — as one leaving a cesspit, as one emerging from prison. Looking from afar at the bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss and comparing it with the suffering of the Sahā world, one's mind of joy and longing for the Land of Ultimate Bliss becomes naturally keen — as one returning to one's home village, as one hastening to a place of treasure. In a word: as the thirsty long to drink, as the hungry long to eat, as the sick and suffering long for good medicine, as the infant longs for its loving mother, as one flees an enemy pressing in with a drawn knife, as one fallen into water or fire urgently seeks rescue. If one can indeed be this earnest, then no realm or condition can lure the mind of Buddha-recitation away.

Then, with this mind of faith and vow, hold to the Name. One recitation is a seed of the ninth-grade lotus; one utterance is a right cause of rebirth. You must let mind after mind be continuous and thought after thought be undivided — only single-minded, only diligent, without admixture, without interruption. The longer it goes, the firmer it grows; the more one holds it, the more earnest it becomes. After a long, long time, it naturally forms itself into a single mass and enters the samādhi of one-mind undivided. If, truly having reached this point, one were not reborn, then Śākyamuni Tathagata would be speaking falsely and Amitābha Buddha would be making an empty vow — is there any such principle!

Then (after deep faith and an earnest vow have been established), with this mind of faith and vow, hold to the Name: then a single utterance of the Buddha-name is a seed of the ninth-grade lotus dais, and a single phrase is a right cause of rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Be sure that mind after mind keeps the Buddha-name continuous (uninterrupted) and thought after thought keeps it undivided (not mixed with other thoughts) — only single-minded, only diligent, without admixture, without interruption. The longer one recites, the firmer the mind of the Buddha becomes; the more one holds it, the more earnest the mind of the Buddha becomes. After a long, long time, the Buddha-thought naturally forms itself into a single mass (so that in reciting there is no idle thought), and one enters the samādhi of one-mind undivided. If one truly reaches this stage and is yet not reborn, then Śākyamuni Tathagata would be speaking falsely and Amitābha Buddha would be making an empty vow — is there such a principle as that!

blocks.text: 5. The Mind Making the Buddha and Being the Buddha

inline.s: The mind making and being: when the mind thinks of the Buddha and recites, the mind is making the Buddha; this mind making the Buddha, this mind is the Buddha.

The two phrases of the Contemplation Sutra, “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha,” are even more direct and thoroughgoing than the Chan school's “point directly to the human mind, see the nature, and become a Buddha.” Why? Because seeing the nature is hard while making the Buddha is easy. What is seeing the nature? To separate from mind, intention, and consciousness, when the spirit-light bursts forth — that is seeing the nature, and therefore it is hard. What is making the Buddha? To hold the Buddha's name and contemplate the Buddha's adornments — that is making the Buddha, and therefore it is easy. The sutra says: “When you, in thought, think upon the Buddha, that mind is at once the thirty-two marks and the eighty minor signs.” Is this not to say that thinking upon the Buddha is making the Buddha?

The two phrases “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha” in the Sutra of the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life are even more direct and thoroughgoing than the Chan school's “point directly to the human mind, see the nature, and become a Buddha.” Why? Because seeing the nature is hard while making the Buddha is easy. What is seeing the nature? To separate from the mind (alaya-vijnana), the intention (manas-vijnana), and the consciousness (the first six vijnanas), when the spirit-light bursts forth — that is seeing the nature, and therefore it is hard. What is making the Buddha? To hold the Buddha's name and contemplate the adorned majesty of the Buddha's retribution — that is making the Buddha, and therefore it is easy. The Sutra of the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life says: “When you, in thought, think upon the Buddha, that mind is at once the thirty-two marks and the eighty minor signs.” Is this not to say that thinking upon the Buddha is making the Buddha?

Now, as between becoming a Buddha and being the Buddha, the principle is not twofold; yet as between seeing the nature and making the Buddha, the difficulty and ease differ so widely — is this not to say that Buddha-recitation compared with Chan investigation is all the more direct and thoroughgoing! One is the word of the patriarchs, the other is the word of the Buddha. Which is weighty, which is light, which to take, which to leave? The student has only to leave behind his old habits entirely, empty the mind and even the breath, and try pondering it and examining it within himself, and he is sure to nod assent that this saying is not mistaken.

As between becoming a Buddha and being the Buddha, the principle is not twofold; yet between seeing the nature in order to become a Buddha and reciting the Buddha in order to make the Buddha, the difficulty and ease differ so enormously — is this not to say that Buddha-recitation compared with Chan investigation is all the more direct and thoroughgoing? “Seeing the nature in order to become a Buddha” is the word of the patriarchs; “reciting the Buddha in order to make the Buddha” is the word of the Buddha. Which is weighty, which is light, which to take, which to leave? The student has only to leave behind his old habits entirely, empty his mind and even his breath, personally test, experience, and compare these two methods — seeing the nature and reciting the Buddha — and he is sure to affirm that the assertion that “Buddha-recitation compared with Chan investigation is all the more direct and thoroughgoing” is entirely right and not in the least mistaken.

Master Chewu, having investigated Chan and attained clear mind and seeing of the nature, became the thirty-sixth patriarch of the Linji school. Later he awakened to the directness, completeness, and suddenness of the practice of reciting the Buddha's name, and turned to cultivate the Pure Land, becoming the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school; he was versed in the school, versed in the teachings, and versed in the Pure Land. Therefore this judgment of the Master is the truthful word of one who has walked both paths, Chan investigation and Buddha-recitation.

blocks.text: 6. The Difficulty of Chan and the Ease of the Pure Land

inline.s: The difficulty of Chan and the ease of the Pure Land: to distinguish, in terms of ending birth and death and leaving the three realms, the ease of Buddha-recitation and the difficulty of Chan investigation — even to use the wide difference between a day and a kalpa, or between heaven and earth, as a simile is far from sufficient!

When Shishuang passed away, the assembly recommended Elder Brother Tai to succeed him as abbot. At the time Jiufeng Qian was Shishuang's attendant, and said: “If you are to succeed as abbot, you must understand the late master's meaning.” Tai said: “What meaning does the late master have that I cannot grasp?” Qian said: “The late master always instructed people: ‘
Be still, be at rest, be cold and dreary, let a single thought last ten thousand years, be as cold ashes and withered wood, be as the incense burner of a temple, go as a single roll of white silk.

’ The rest I will not ask about — what is it to “go as a single roll of white silk”?’ Tai said: “This only clarifies the matter of form and emptiness.” Qian said: “It turns out you have not understood the late master's meaning.” Tai said: “Light the incense! When the incense burns out, if I cannot depart, then I have not understood the late master's meaning.” Those around lit incense at once, and before the incense was finished burning, Tai passed away
(left the world)
. Qian, patting him on the back, said: “To sit out and die standing up — this you have, but the late master's meaning you have not even seen in a dream.”

When Shishuang (the Master Qingzhu of the Tang) passed into nirvāṇa, the assembly recommended Elder Brother Tai to succeed him as abbot. At this time Jiufeng Qian (the Chan Master Daogian of Jiufeng), who was Shishuang's attendant, said: “If you are to succeed as abbot, you must clearly awaken to the late master's meaning.” Tai said: “What meaning does the late master have that I cannot grasp?” Jiufeng Qian said: “The late master always instructed people: ‘Be still, be at rest, be cold and dreary, let a single thought last ten thousand years, be as cold ashes and withered wood, be as the incense burner of a temple, go as a single roll of white silk.’ The rest I will not ask about — what is “go as a single roll of white silk”?’ Elder Brother Tai answered: “This only speaks of the matter of form and emptiness.” Jiufeng Qian said: “It turns out you have by no means understood the late master's meaning.” Elder Brother Tai said: “Light the incense! If by the time this stick of incense has burned out I have not yet departed, that will show I have not understood the late master's meaning.” Those at his side at once lit incense, and before the incense had burned out, Elder Brother Tai had already departed. Jiufeng Qian, stroking his back, said: “Though you can sit out and die standing up, as for the late master's meaning — you have not even seen it in a dream.”

[Let a single thought last ten thousand years] To take away even that single thought of the state in which the ten thousand thoughts are gathered into one, and to enter the state of no-thought. Ordinarily, “one thought ten thousand years, ten thousand years one thought” has two senses: first, one thought is ten thousand years and ten thousand years is one thought — this expresses the transcending of relative notions such as great and small, long and short, lasting and brief, the so-called “the ten worlds and the ancient and present are in this very thought.” Second, it describes the state in which the ten thousand thoughts are gathered into one: no matter when, it is only this one thought, and this one thought can be maintained no matter when. For example, the Chan patriarchs often said: “
keep on with one thought through ten thousand years

, what further Dharma is there?’ [The incense burner of a temple] The incense burner of a temple (with only a single point of incense burning in an old temple): a simile for a thought pure and unadulterated — this is the state in which the ten thousand thoughts are gathered into one. “Go as the incense burner of a temple” (taking away even that single point of incense remaining in the old temple): a simile for the one returning to nothing, and entering the state of no-thought. [Go as a single roll of white silk] White silk: a roll of white silk. Here white silk too is a simile for a thought pure and unadulterated — the state in which the ten thousand thoughts are gathered into one. “Go as a single roll of white silk” means to take away even that single thought (the one returning to nothing), and enter the state of no-thought. [Sit out and die standing up] This is the accomplishment of being free in birth and death: able to leave when one says so, whether seated or standing, in both cases at ease.

The Chan Master Dahui said: “I have always delighted in the saying of the Monk Zhenjing: nowadays most people attain only a body and mind of extinction, where the before and after are cut off, and going still, going at rest, going with a single thought for ten thousand years, like the incense burner of an ancient temple, going cold and dreary — and they take this for the ultimate. They do not know that they are veiled and blocked by this exquisite realm, so that their own right knowledge and right understanding cannot appear, and their spiritual powers and light cannot burst forth.” (From the Recorded Sayings of the Chan Master Dahui Pujue)

Caoshan was seated in the hall, and the Paper-Robe Wayfarer passed below. Caoshan said: “Is this not the Paper-Robe Wayfarer?” The Wayfarer said: “I dare not presume.” Caoshan said: “What is the matter under the paper robe?” The Wayfarer said: “The moment this robe is hung upon the body, all things are as they are.” Caoshan said: “What is the function under the paper robe?” The Wayfarer said: “Yes,” and passed away. Caoshan said: “You know only how to go thus, and do not know how to come thus.” The Wayfarer opened his eyes again and asked: “When one spirit-true nature has entered without borrowing a womb, what then?” Caoshan said: “That is not yet the wonder.”

Caoshan (the Chan Master Benji, who was the Dharma-heir of Dongshan Liangjia, the founder of the Caodong school) was seated in the hall, and a cultivator of the Way named Paper-Robe passed below the hall. Caoshan asked: “Is this not the Paper-Robe Wayfarer?” The Paper-Robe Wayfarer answered: “I dare not presume.” Caoshan asked: “What is the matter within your body — the matter of your self-nature?” The Paper-Robe Wayfarer answered: “Though the self-nature has put on this foul bag of a form-body, the mind is unmoved and as it is with regard to all things.” Caoshan asked: “What is the function of the self-nature within your body?” The Paper-Robe Wayfarer answered: “Very well,” and closed his eyes and left the world. Caoshan said: “You know only how to go thus, and do not know how to come thus.” The Paper-Robe Wayfarer opened his eyes again and asked: “When the one spirit-true nature enters without borrowing a womb, what then?” Caoshan answered: “That is not yet the wonder.”

[Wayfarer] A term for one who cultivates the Buddha-Way. [I dare not] “I do not presume.” This is the humble acknowledgment of ancient times, an expression of modesty. [What is the matter under the paper robe] That is, what is the matter under the Paper-Robe man's body, that is, what is the matter of the self-nature within the Paper-Robe man's body. [Yes] A sound of assent, indicating agreement.
As for sitting out and dying standing up without having understood the great Dharma — this is indeed not settling the matter.

(In the two cases above, both had reached the accomplishment of sitting out and dying standing up, yet the great Dharma was not understood, and it still was not the ultimate; they could not attain complete liberation. This shows how hard is the practice of Chan.)

Yet the degree of their cultivation and attainment was by no means easy. If one could turn this same spirit toward single-minded recitation of the Buddha and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, one would surely and steadily attain the highest grade of the highest birth — how would one then be checked or faulted by others!

After citing the two cases of Elder Brother Tai and the Paper-Robe Wayfarer, both free in birth and death, Master Chewu commented with a sigh: sitting out and dying standing up — what an accomplishment! Yet the great Dharma was not understood, and they still could not attain complete liberation — this shows how very hard Chan investigation is! Yet the level of these two men's attainment was also very far from easy to reach. If one could turn back the energy and time it takes to reach such attainment and devote it to single-minded recitation of the Buddha and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, one would surely and steadily attain the highest grade of the highest birth — how would one then be criticized or questioned!
As when the Paper-Robe man pressed further and asked, “What is the wonder?” Caoshan answered, “Borrow yet do not borrow.” The Wayfarer bade him a respectful farewell
(taking leave)

and passed away. Alas! Rather than borrowing through the stench and filth of a womb, how much better to borrow the fragrant and pure lotus-flower! Even to set the stench and filth of a womb against the fragrance and purity of a lotus-flower, the superiority and inferiority already differ enormously. Moreover, once out of the womb one has the confusion of the intervening darkness, and it is very hard to be master of oneself; whereas as soon as the lotus-flower opens, the excellent conditions are wholly fulfilled. Here a day and a kalpa stand far apart, and heaven and earth are not enough to express the difference between their fortune and misfortune.

Again, for example, when the Paper-Robe Wayfarer pressed further and asked, “Then what is the wonder?” Caoshan answered, “Borrow yet do not borrow.” The Paper-Robe Wayfarer then bade Caoshan farewell, thanking him for his guidance, and passed away (left the world). Alas! Rather than borrowing through the stench and filth of the Sahā world's womb, how could it compare with borrowing the fragrant and pure lotus-flower of the Land of Ultimate Bliss? Even to set the stench and filth of the Sahā world's womb against the fragrance and purity of the Land of Ultimate Bliss's lotus, the superiority and inferiority already differ enormously. How much more so, since after emerging from the womb there is the confusion of the intervening darkness, and it is very hard to be master of oneself; whereas as soon as the lotus-bud opens, the excellent conditions are at once fulfilled — the flower opens, one sees the Buddha, and realizes the unborn. This shows that the difference between the ease of Buddha-recitation and the difficulty of Chan investigation is such that even using a day and a kalpa, or heaven and earth, as a simile is far from sufficient!
[Borrow yet do not borrow] Borrow but not really borrow: though one borrows a womb, one does not cling to the mark of a womb. [Alas] A classical exclamation, expressing emotion, grief, or a sigh.

In this koan, Caoshan was awakening and transforming the Paper-Robe Wayfarer, causing him, at the most critical juncture, not to take the wrong path — this too is the grandmotherly heart of a clear teacher!

No wonder Master Yongming said: “With Chan but without the Pure Land, of ten people nine take the wrong road; with no Chan but with the Pure Land, of ten thousand who cultivate, ten thousand go.” These are true words, real words, words wrung from the depths of a great compassionate heart; students should by no means overlook them!

No wonder Master Yongming said: “With Chan but without the Pure Land, of ten people nine take the wrong road; with no Chan but with the Pure Land, of ten thousand who cultivate, ten thousand go.” These are true words, real words, words laid bare from a great compassionate heart; students must by no means overlook this saying!

Master Yongming, like Master Chewu, both investigated Chan and awakened to the Way, and were counted among the Chan patriarchs; later they awakened to the directness, completeness, and suddenness of the practice of reciting the Buddha's name, and turned to cultivate the Pure Land, achieving distinguished success, and becoming the sixth patriarch of the Lotus school. Therefore Master Yongming's verse too is the truthful word of one who has walked both paths, Chan investigation and Buddha-recitation.
Please note that Master Chewu used the four words “tears wrung from the depths of the heart.”

blocks.text: 7. Delusion and Awakening in a Single Thought

inline.s: Delusion and awakening in a single thought: with a single deluded thought one is in the realm of sentient beings; with a single awakened thought one is in the realm of the Buddha.

At the very first, when self-nature is deluded as to the real and gives rise to the false, it is called “a single stirring thought.” At the very last, when it turns from the false back to the real, it is called “a single thought of correspondence.” Then, between the arising of the false and the returning to the real, is there any further dharma that can be outside this one thought? Therefore, with a single awakened thought and following the pure conditions, one is in the realm of the Buddha; with a deluded thought and following the defiled conditions, one is in the nine realms. The ten directions' space is this one thought's delusion and darkness; all lands are this one thought's clear stillness; the retribution-body of the four modes of birth is this one thought's union and separation of feeling and thinking; the dependent-body of the four great elements is this one thought's movement and stillness, its opposing and harmonizing. It is solely depending on this thought that all things are transformed and manifested; apart from this thought nothing whatever is obtainable.

At the very first, when self-nature is deluded as to the real and gives rise to the false, it is called “a single stirring thought.” At the very last, when self-nature turns from the false back to the real, it is called “a single thought of correspondence.” Then, between the arising of the false and the returning to the real, is there any further dharma that can be outside this one thought? Therefore, with a single awakened thought and following the pure conditions, one is in the realm of the Buddha; with a single deluded thought and following the defiled conditions, one is in the nine realms. The ten directions' space is this one thought's delusion and darkness; all lands are this one thought's clear stillness; the retribution-body of the four modes of birth (viviparous, oviparous, moisture-born, and metamorphic) is this one thought's union and separation of feeling and thinking; the dependent-body of the four great elements (earth, water, fire, and wind) is this one thought's movement and stillness, its opposing and harmonizing. It is solely depending on this thought that all things are transformed and manifested; apart from this thought nothing whatever is obtainable.

[A single thought of correspondence] When the initial enlightenment and the original enlightenment become one, it is called “a single thought of correspondence.” [Original enlightenment, initial enlightenment, final enlightenment] Original enlightenment is the pure mind of self-nature originally possessed by all sentient beings; initial enlightenment is when, after the original enlightenment has been veiled by ignorance, one begins gradually to remove ignorance and gradually to still the false mind, restoring its inherent original enlightenment; final enlightenment is the ultimate, complete awakening, that is, the Buddha's awakening.

The four lines “It is solely depending on this thought that all things are transformed and manifested; apart from this thought nothing whatever is obtainable” are extremely important. Once you understand this principle, you will know: take good care of the one Buddha-name at every moment, and when no false thought arises, you are already practicing the great practice.

For this single thought is originally the dharma-realm rising from conditions. Since conditions have no self-nature, the whole dharma-realm therefore extends across the ten directions and reaches down through the three times, transcending all error and beyond all determination, unthinkable; of itself it possesses this awesome spirit, and of itself it possesses this function.

So this single thought is originally the dharma-realm rising from conditions. Since conditions have no self-nature, the whole dharma-realm therefore extends across the ten directions (space) and reaches down through the three times (time), transcending the duality of opposites, unthinkable; of itself it possesses this awesome spirit, and of itself it possesses this function.

[Dharma-realm] That is, the dharma-nature, also called reality. [Dharma-nature] The inherent nature of all dharmas. [No self-nature] The meaning of “no self-nature” is that all dharmas have no substance, and are all illusions, like things in a dream. No self-nature is also called naturelessness. The Treatise on Consciousness-Only says: “All dharmas are without self-nature.” The Lotus Sutra says: “Know that all dharmas are ever without nature.” The Shurangama Sutra says: “All illusions become natureless.” [Three times] The past, present, and future. [Transcending error and beyond determination] Transcending the duality of opposites. [Of itself] Naturally, without dependence on contrivance. [Awesome spirit] Awesome virtue and spiritual powers. [Awesome virtue] What is to be awed is awesome; what is lovable is virtue.

Now, with this thought, one recites upon the Amitābha Buddha of the West, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. At the very moment of reciting, the dependent and proper retributions of the West are within my mind, and this mind of mine is already within the dependent and proper retributions of the West. It is like two mirrors exchanging light, containing and illuminating each other, image within image — this is the mark of extending across the ten directions. If we take it in terms of reaching down through the three times, then the moment of reciting the Buddha is the moment of seeing the Buddha, and also the moment of becoming the Buddha. The moment of seeking rebirth is the moment of being reborn, and also the moment of ferrying living beings across; the three times are simultaneous, with no before or after. The pearl-light of Indra's net is hard to equal in its whole; the dream-matters of Nanke can only compare a single spot.

Now, with this single thought, one recites upon the Amitābha Buddha of the West, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. At the very moment of reciting, the dependent and proper retributions of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss are within my mind, and this mind of mine is already within the dependent and proper retributions of the West. It is like two mirrors reflecting each other, mutually containing and illuminating, image after image appearing — this is spoken in terms of the mark of extending across the ten directions. If we take it in terms of reaching down through the three times, then the moment of reciting the Buddha is the moment of seeing the Buddha, and also the moment of becoming the Buddha. The moment of seeking rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is the moment of being reborn there, and also the moment of entering back into the Sahā world to ferry sentient beings across; past, present and future are simultaneous, with no before or after. This state of affairs is such that even the mutually reflecting, mutually taking-in of the pearl-light of Indra's net is hard to depict as a whole; the bizarre and strange dream-matter of Nanke can only compare to a single spot of the whole leopard.

[Indra's net] A net of jewels suspended in the palace of the heaven of Indra. [The pearl-light of Indra's net] The lights of these jewels on Indra's net shine on one another, each pearl reflecting the images of all pearls, and every pearl within those images again reflecting the images of all pearls, each in its turn, image after image appearing. [The dream of Nanke] “Nanke” is a south-facing branch of a tree. In the Tang dynasty Li Gongzuo wrote the Story of the Governor of Nanke, telling how Chunyu Fen dreamed he went to the kingdom of Huaian, married its princess, and was made Governor of Nanke, enjoying the height of glory and wealth for a time. Later he led an army on a campaign and was defeated; the princess too died, and falling under the king's suspicion, he was sent back home. On waking, he dug beneath the locust tree in front of the courtyard and found an ant-nest — that was the kingdom of Huaian of his dream. The commandery of Nanke was another ant-nest beneath the southern branch of the locust tree.

This principle is the hardest to awaken to, and yet the easiest to believe. If one can but take it up directly and without hesitation, in the end one is sure to enjoy it with one's whole being — so it may be said that the matter of study is finished and what should be done is done. If one is not yet able to take it up directly, then one should simply observe it as opportunity allows, and enjoy it in proportion to one's lot.

This principle of the single thought is the hardest to awaken to, and yet the easiest to believe. If one can but take it up directly, deeply believe without doubt, and recite only the Buddha, in the end one is sure to enjoy it with one's whole being — so it may be said that the matter of study is finished and what should be done is done. If one is not yet able to take it up directly, then one should conveniently observe it in detail, and receive the corresponding benefit according to the depth of one's understanding.

[The matter of study is finished] The matters of study and practice have come to an end. [What should be done is done] All that ought to be done has been done. Cultivation is originally for the sake of leaving the three realms, and so one practices the pure conduct. When one reflects that afflictions have been cut off and birth and death have come to an end, then it is said, “What should be done is done.”
The mind can turn karma: karma is created by the mind, and karma is turned by the mind.

The mind can create karma, and the mind can turn karma. Karma is created by the mind, and karma is turned by the mind. If the mind cannot turn karma, then it is bound by karma; if karma is not turned by the mind, then karma can bind the mind. Why can the mind turn karma? When the mind accords with the Way and the mind accords with the Buddha, it can turn karma. Why can karma bind the mind? When the mind rests in its habitual portion and idly produces and receives, then it is bound by karma. All realms present before us, all future retributions that come, are all experienced by karma and all manifested by the mind.

The mind can create karma, and the mind can also turn karma. Karma is created by the mind, and karma is also turned by the mind. If the mind cannot turn karma, it is controlled by karma; if karma is not turned by the mind, then it can control the mind. Then how can the mind turn karma? When the mind accords with the Way and the mind accords with the Buddha, it can turn karma. How then can karma control the mind? If the mind still follows its habitual tendencies, drifting with the tide in producing and receiving, then it is controlled by karma. All realms present before us, all future retributions that come, are all experienced by karma and all manifested by the mind.
[Binds the mind] To control the mind.

For example, hearing slander without anger is turning karma with the mind; hearing slander and growing angry is karma coming to bind the mind. The ancients said: “Follow conditions to dissolve old karma; be sure not to create new misfortunes.” If the mind turns karma, that is dissolving old karma; if karma binds the mind, that is creating a new misfortune. Whether one dissolves karma or creates karma, and the rise and fall of one's lot, all rest wholly in this one thought. This very crest of the storm is the finest time for practicing and for testing one's practice!

Because all things are experienced by karma, the realms before us and the retributions that come are all fixed, since karma can bind the mind. Because all things are manifested by the mind, the realms before us and the retributions that come are all unfixed, since the mind can turn karma. If, at the very time when karma is able to bind the mind and the realm before us and its retribution are fixed, one suddenly arouses the vast mind and practices the real practice, the mind according with the Buddha and the mind according with the Way, then the mind can turn karma, and the realm before us and its retribution, though fixed, become unfixed.
