Again, when the mind can turn karma and the realm before us and its retribution are unfixed, if the vast mind suddenly retreats and the real practice falls short, then karma can bind the mind, and the realm before us and its retribution, though unfixed, become fixed.

Since all realms are experienced by karma, therefore when circumstances come and their retribution arises (karmic retribution), it is fixed — this is because karma can control the mind. Since all realms are manifested by the mind, therefore when circumstances come and their retribution arises, it is unfixed — this is because the mind can turn karma. If, at the very time when karma can control the mind and the circumstance before us and its retribution are fixed, one suddenly arouses the bodhi-mind and practices the real practice, the mind according with the Buddha and the mind according with the Way, then the mind can turn karma, and the retribution of the circumstance before us, though fixed, becomes unfixed. Again, when the mind can turn karma and the circumstance before us and its retribution are unfixed, if the vast mind suddenly retreats and the real practice falls short, then karma can control the mind, and the retribution of the circumstance before us, though unfixed, becomes fixed.

Yet karma was created in the past, and to this there is nothing one can do; fortunately, whether one will arouse the mind or not — the switch lies in myself. Creating karma or turning karma is not up to anyone else.”

Yet karma was created in the past, and this is beyond recovery; fortunately, whether one will arouse the mind and whether one's practice is real — the initiative lies with me. When circumstances come before us, whether to create a new misfortune or dissolve old karma is also entirely up to me, and not up to others.

The coming of circumstances is experienced by old karma; but how to deal with them — the initiative lies with oneself. Yet it is not that you can deal with them however you wish, or turn karma just by wanting to. It is like waging a battle: who does not wish to win? The key lies in strength. Therefore, to be able to deal rightly with circumstances, one must arouse the bodhi-mind, practice the real practice, let the mind accord with the Buddha and the mind accord with the Way, and only then have the strength to turn karma and to turn the circumstances. This passage of Master Chewu clarifies the principle of reforming one's destiny. Savor it repeatedly, and practice it continuously. Examine yourself often:
Is this karma binding the mind, or is the mind turning karma?

Remember: when circumstances come before us, this is karma coming to bind the mind, making you receive retribution and create a new misfortune; when the mind rests on the Buddha-name and is not drawn away, this is the mind turning karma (no retribution, or a light retribution), and moreover dissolving old karma — weakening and even uprooting the karma-seeds in the alaya-vijnana.
As when we now arouse the mind to recite the Buddha and seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Either contemplate the dependent and proper retributions, or hold the Name,
thought after thought continuous

. When contemplation and recitation reach the utmost, then the mind accords with the Buddha, and in accord after accord, reaching the extreme of that accord, the mind can turn karma. Then the former realm of Sahā is turned into the Land of Ultimate Bliss; the retribution of the womb-prison is turned into the lotus-flower; and one becomes a person free in the Land of Bliss! But if at just that time the mind should by chance lose its clear awareness, or suddenly give rise to regret and retreat, and no longer accord with the Buddha, then karma can bind the mind, and the former realm remains as before, the retribution that comes still remains, and one is still a suffering sentient being of the endurance-realm.

Just as we now arouse the mind to recite the Buddha and seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Either contemplate the adorned majesty of the Land of Ultimate Bliss's dependent and proper retributions (such as the various contemplations in the Sutra of the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life), or hold the Name, thought after thought continuous (not interrupted by false thoughts). When contemplation and recitation reach the utmost, then the mind accords with the Buddha, and in accord after accord, reaching the extreme of that accord, the mind can turn karma. Then the realm of the Sahā world is turned into the realm of the Land of Ultimate Bliss; the retribution of the womb-prison at death is turned into metamorphic birth in the lotus-flower. This is then a person free in the Land of Ultimate Bliss! But if at the time when the former realm comes and its retribution arises, the mind should by chance lose its clear awareness, or suddenly give rise to regret and retreat, and no longer accord with the Buddha, then karma can bind the mind. Then the former realm remains as before and the retribution that comes still remains, and one is still a suffering sentient being of the Sahā world.

[Dependent and proper] The dependent retribution and the proper retribution. The land, houses, utensils and the like of this world are what the body depends on, called the “dependent retribution”; the body itself, which is what one's karma in the past has brought about, is called the “proper retribution.” [The endurance-realm] The Sahā world; “Sahā” is translated into Chinese as “endurance.”
Master Chewu here reveals the secret of turning karma:

“Either contemplate the dependent and proper retributions, or hold the Name, thought after thought continuous. When contemplation and recitation reach the utmost, then the mind accords with the Buddha, and in accord after accord, reaching the extreme of that accord, the mind can turn karma.”
Please note:
“thought after thought continuous”
, this is the key.

Therefore, when one recites the Buddha until there is a response, not only at the end of life will one surely be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, but even now one can already reform one's own destiny.
Then we who are determined to leave the world, who seek rebirth in the Pure Land — can we fail to be startled into vigilance and rouse ourselves to strive on!”
Then, having understood this principle, we who are determined to leave the Sahā world and seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss — can we fail to be wary and earnest, and press forward bravely?

The vow is supreme: In the Pure Land practice, the vow is supreme. If what one arouses is a real vow, then faith is already within it. Since faith and vow are real, the practice arises of itself (for if one does not practice diligently, the faith and vow are not real). For this reason, of the three provisions of faith, vow, and practice, the single word “vow” encompasses them all.
In the Pure Land approach, the vow is most important.
In the Pure Land approach, the vow is the most important.

Whoever makes a vow will in the end surely fulfill it. For example, Udraka Ramaputra practiced the concentration of neither thinking nor not-thinking by the waterside beneath a grove. Each time his meditation was about to be accomplished, he was startled by the fishes leaping and the birds calling. So he made an evil vow: “In a life to come, I shall become a flying marten, entering the grove to eat the birds and diving into the water to eat the fishes.” Afterward, when his concentration of neither thinking nor not-thinking was accomplished, he was born in the heavens and lived for eighty thousand great kalpas. When that heavenly reward came to an end, he fell and became a flying marten, going into the grove and the water to feed on fish and birds. This was an evil vow, going against his own nature, and yet it still had such great power that after a vast span of eighty thousand kalpas it was fulfilled. How much more so the good vow that accords with one’s true nature!

Whoever makes a vow will in the end surely fulfill it. For example, Udraka Ramaputra practiced the concentration of neither thinking nor not-thinking by the waterside beneath a grove. Each time his meditation was about to be accomplished, he was startled by the fishes leaping and the birds calling. So he made an evil vow: “In a life to come, I shall become a flying marten, entering the grove to eat the birds and diving into the water to eat the fishes.” Later, when his concentration of neither thinking nor not-thinking was accomplished, he was accordingly reborn in the heaven of neither thinking nor not-thinking, and lived for eighty thousand great kalpas. When that heavenly reward of life came to an end, he fell and became a flying marten, going into the grove and the water to feed on birds and fishes. This was an evil vow, contrary to his own nature, and yet it possessed such great power that, even after a vast span of eighty thousand kalpas, it was able to fulfill his wish. How much more so the good vow, in accord with one’s true nature, to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss!

[Udraka Ramaputra] A person’s name, also translated as Uddaka Ramaputra. [Concentration of neither thinking nor not-thinking] That is, the concentration of the station of neither thinking nor not-thinking, which leads to rebirth in the heaven of the station of neither thinking nor not-thinking in the formless realm. This meditation is extremely still, and thoughts, though present, are as if absent, whence its name.

The Record of Spiritually Gifted Monks relates: a monk, before a stone Buddha, jokingly made a vow, saying: “If in this life I cannot escape birth and death, may I in my next life be a mighty minister.” Later he indeed became a great general. This was a vow made in jest, and it was still fulfilled in the end. How much more so a vow made with utmost sincerity!

The Record of Spiritually Gifted Monks relates: a monk, before a stone-carved image of the Buddha, jokingly made a vow, saying: “If in this life I cannot put an end to birth and death, may I in my next life be a mighty minister.” Later he indeed became a great general. This was a vow made in jest, and it was still fulfilled in the end. How much more so a vow made with utmost sincerity, to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss!

It further relates: a monk, broadly learned in the sutras and treatises, yet finding no opportunity wherever he went, sighed and lamented. A monk beside him said: “You study the Buddha’s Dharma. Have you alone not heard that, before perfecting the fruit of Buddhahood, one should first form connections with beings? Though you are clear on the Buddha’s Dharma, what can be done if you have no connection with beings?” The monk said: “Shall I then be stuck here for the rest of my life?” The monk beside him said: “I will do it on your behalf.” He asked the monk what he had in store. He replied: “Nothing else — I have only a piece of cloth left.” He said: “That is enough.” So he sold the cloth and bought food, led the monk to a deep grove where there were many birds and insects, laid the food on the ground, and taught him to make a vow. Then he instructed him: “You may begin teaching only after twenty years.” The monk did as he was told, and only after twenty years did he begin teaching. Those he converted were mostly youths, for they were all the birds and insects that had partaken of the food. Such is the inconceivable power of the vow! If the vow of another could gather in those birds and insects, enabling them to escape their different realm and enter the human path, how could one’s own vow fail to save oneself?

The Record of Spiritually Gifted Monks further relates: a monk, though broadly learned in the sutras and treatises, had no opportunity to spread the Dharma wherever he went, and so lamented over himself without cease. A monk beside him said: “You study the Buddha’s Dharma. Have you never heard of ‘before perfecting the fruit of Buddhahood, first form connections with beings’? Though you are well versed in the Buddha’s Dharma, what is to be done if you have no connection with beings?” This monk said: “Shall I then, in this lifetime, never have an opportunity to spread the Dharma?” The monk beside him said: “I will cultivate connections with beings on your behalf.” Thereupon he asked this monk what he had in store. He replied: “Nothing else — only a piece of cloth is left.” The monk beside him said: “That is quite enough.” So he sold the cloth to buy food, led this monk to a deep grove, and in a place where there were many birds and insects, laid the food on the ground, and taught him to make a vow, wishing to be able to spread the Dharma and universally save sentient beings. Then he instructed him: “Only after twenty years may you begin teaching and spreading the Dharma.” This monk, as instructed, began spreading the Dharma only after twenty years. Those who came to hear him and be converted were mostly youths, because in their former lives they had been the birds and insects that had partaken of the food in the deep grove. All this shows the inconceivable power of the vow! If the vow of another could gather and transform those birds and insects, enabling them to escape their different realm and enter the human path, how could one’s own vow fail to save oneself?

The Buddha, through forty-eight great vows, brought himself to Buddhahood. And the vow I have made accords exactly with the Buddha’s vow to gather in sentient beings. This being so, one can reach rebirth by means of the vow alone, to say nothing of the Buddha’s inconceivable great compassion and great sorrow.

Amitābha Buddha, in his causal stage, made forty-eight great vows to save suffering sentient beings, and in reliance upon them cultivated and attained the fruit of Buddhahood, realizing the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. And the vow I have made, to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, accords exactly with Amitābha Buddha’s great vow to gather in and transform sentient beings. Therefore, by this vow alone one can reach rebirth, to say nothing of Amitābha Buddha’s inconceivable great compassion and great sorrow.

Please note: “by this vow alone one can reach rebirth” — here the vow spoken of is a true vow, a vow possessing great power. As the following instruction of the Master Chewu shows: if the vow one makes is a true vow, then faith is already within it. Faith and vow being true, the practice arises of itself. For this reason, of the three provisions of faith, vow, and practice, the single word “vow” encompasses them all. Therefore, if a vow does not contain faith, cannot give rise to practice of itself, and cannot press through thorns and brambles straight toward the destination, then it is but a false vow.

Such as Yingke, a man who made no distinction of wine and meat. Later he read the Biographies of Rebirth — with each biography he read, he gave a nod of assent — and thereupon gave up food and chanted the Buddha’s name. On the seventh day he was moved to have the Buddha appear and comfort him, saying: “You still have ten years of life; you should diligently chant the Buddha’s name. In ten years I will come to receive you.” Yingke said: “The Sahā world is defiled and evil; it is easy to lose right mindfulness. I wish to be reborn early in the Pure Land and to attend upon the sages.” The Buddha said: “Since your resolve is thus, in three days I will come to receive you.” After three days he indeed attained rebirth.

For example, the Chan master Yingke of the Song dynasty was a man who made no distinction of wine and meat. Later he read the Biographies of Rebirth, and with each biography he read, he gave a nod of assent. Thereupon he sat facing west and, giving up food, chanted the Buddha’s name. On the seventh day (which should be the third day), he was moved to have Amitābha Buddha appear and comfort him, saying: “You still have ten years of life; you should diligently chant the Buddha’s name. In ten years I will come to receive you.” Yingke said to the Buddha: “The Sahā world is defiled and evil; it is easy to lose right mindfulness. I wish to be reborn early in the Pure Land and to attend upon the sages.” The Buddha said: “Since that is your wish, in three days I will come to receive you.” On the third day, the Chan master Yingke asked the assembly to recite the Amitābha Sutra, and said: “Amitābha Buddha and all the holy assembly have arrived.” Then he passed away in stillness.
The matter of Master Yingke originates from the Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, transcribed as follows:
Yingke. He studied under Master Yao of Mount Zhe (
zhá

)chuan, and widely visited the teachings and the Chan school. Owing to illness he returned to his teacher (from context, “returned to his teacher” seems redundant and may be a copying error), and made no distinction of wine and meat. He thought privately that his precept practice was incomplete, and feared he might drift through transmigration. He had his co-residents take out the Biographies of Rebirth in the Pure Land compiled by Master Jiezhushu (Master of the Precept Bead), and read them beside his bed — with each biography he read, he gave a nod of assent. Thereupon he chose a room, set a meditation seat facing west, and without eating chanted the Buddha’s name for three days. In a dream the Buddha and the great bodhisattvas said to him: ‘You still have ten years of life, and should exert yourself.’ Yingke said to the Buddha: ‘Even were there a hundred years, the Jambudvipa world is defiled and evil, and it is easy to lose right mindfulness. My wish is to ascend early to the Land of Peace (Sukhavati) and to attend upon the assembly of sages.’ The Buddha said: ‘Since your resolve is thus, in three days I will come to welcome you.’ At the appointed time, he had the assembly recite the Amitābha Sutra. The master said: ‘The Buddha and the assembly have all arrived.’ Then he passed away in stillness.”

Further, the Chan master Huaiyu, who diligently cultivated the pure karma. One day he saw Buddhas and bodhisattvas filling the empty sky, and one person came bearing a silver dais. Huaiyu thought: “All my life I have been diligent, and my resolve is upon the golden dais; why is it not so now?” The silver dais thereupon vanished. Huaiyu applied himself all the more diligently, and after twenty-one days he again saw Buddhas and bodhisattvas filling the empty sky, and the one who had before borne the silver dais now came bearing a golden dais. Huaiyu then passed away in stillness.

Again, the Chan master Huaiyu diligently cultivated the pure karma. One day he saw Buddhas and bodhisattvas filling the empty sky, and one person came bearing a silver dais. The Chan master Huaiyu thought within: “All my life I have chanted the Buddha’s name in diligence, and my resolve is upon rebirth upon a golden dais; why is it not a golden dais now?” The person bearing the silver dais then vanished. The Chan master Huaiyu chanted the Buddha’s name all the more diligently. On the twenty-first day he again saw Buddhas and bodhisattvas filling the empty sky, and the one who had before borne the silver dais now came bearing a golden dais. The Chan master Huaiyu thereupon passed away in stillness.

Liu Yimin, in reliance on the East Forest (Donglin), formed a society and chanted the Buddha’s name. One day, as he was thinking of chanting the Buddha’s name, he saw the Buddha manifest himself. Liu thought: “How might I have the Tathagata stroke my head with his hand?” The Buddha thereupon stroked his head with his hand. He again thought: “How might I have the Tathagata cover my body with his robe?” The Buddha thereupon covered his body with his robe.

Liu Yimin studied under the great master Huiyuan of the East Forest temple on Mount Lu (the founding patriarch of the Lotus school), and formed a society to chant the Buddha’s name. One day, as he was contemplating and chanting the Buddha’s name, he saw Amitābha Buddha manifest himself. Liu Yimin thought within: “How might I obtain the Tathagata’s laying his hand upon my head?” Amitābha Buddha thereupon stroked his head with his hand. He again thought within: “How might I obtain the Tathagata’s covering my body with his robe?” Amitābha thereupon covered his body with his robe.

[Liu Yimin] A man of the Jin dynasty, named Chengzhi, styled Zhongsi, a native of Pengcheng (Tongshan county, Jiangsu). He lost his father young and served his mother with utmost filial piety. He excelled in the teachings of Laozi and Zhuangzi, and would not casually mingle with the vulgar world of his time; together with Zhou Xuzhi and Tao Yuanming he was acclaimed as one of the Three Recluses of Xunyang. He first served as a military adjutant; the princes and great ministers of the time one after another recommended him for higher office, but Liu Chengzhi firmly declined each time. At that time the great master Huiyuan dwelt at the East Forest temple on Mount Lu, cultivating the samādhi of Buddha-recitation, and so Liu Chengzhi went to rely upon him. The great master Huiyuan said: “Official rank and emolument are glorious; why not take them?” Liu Chengzhi said: “The Jin dynasty has not the firmness of a rock, yet sentient beings face the peril of piled eggs; why should I go and hold office?” At that time the Liu Song emperor Liu Yu of the southern dynasty, seeing that Liu Chengzhi would not submit to official rank and emolument, therefore called him “Yimin” (the remaining one), to praise his lofty and pure virtue. Later, north of the Western Forest mountain stream, Liu Yimin built a meditation dwelling for himself, and devoted himself to investigating the profound meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma, while strictly observing the precepts, and composed a poem on the samādhi of Buddha-recitation. After dwelling half a year, in meditation he saw Amitābha Buddha emit light illuminating the earth, all turning to golden color. After another fifteen years, as he was chanting the Buddha’s name, he saw Amitābha Buddha touch his body with the light of his white hair-mark, and lower his hand to express comfort and welcoming. Liu Yimin thought: “How might I obtain the Tathagata’s laying his hand upon my head, and covering my body with his robe?” No sooner had the words been uttered than Amitābha Buddha stroked his head with his hand and covered his body with his robe. On another day, he dreamed of entering the seven-jewel lotus pond, seeing blue and white lotuses, the pool water clear and translucent. There was a person with a halo around his head and a swastika on his chest, pointing to the pool and saying: “This is the water of the eight qualities of merit; you may drink of it.” Liu Yimin thereupon drank of the water and found it very sweet. On waking, a strange fragrance issued from his pores. He then said to others: “The causes and conditions for my rebirth in the Pure Land have arrived!” He then asked monks to recite the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma, several hundred times. Liu Yimin faced the Buddha image and burned incense, bowing again and again and praying: “By means of the bequeathed teaching of Śākyamuni Buddha, I have come to know the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and Amitābha Buddha. This incense should first be offered to Śākyamuni Buddha, then to Amitābha Buddha, and next to the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma, because the reason I am able to attain rebirth in the Pure Land is due to the merit of this sutra. And I make the vow that together with all sentient beings, we shall be reborn together in the Western Pure Land.” Having said this, he took leave of the assembly, and lying on his bed facing west with palms joined, he peacefully passed away. This was in the sixth year of the Yixi era of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin (

), at the age of fifty-nine. Six years later, the great master Huiyuan, when seated in meditation in his hermitage, saw Amitābha Buddha in meditation, his body vast, filling the empty sky, with Avalokitesvara and Mahasthamaprapta standing in attendance to left and right. Liu Yimin and the monastic and lay members of the Lotus Society who had already passed on stood before the Buddha, and, bowing to the great master Huiyuan, said: “The master took the resolve first; how is it you have come so late?” The great master Huiyuan passed away seven days later. [Forming a society to chant the Buddha’s name] The founding patriarch of the Lotus school, the great master Huiyuan, led the assembly at the East Forest temple on Mount Lu in the practice of the Pure Land, digging a pool and planting lotuses. On the pool he set a twelve-leaf lotus which, turning with the water, served as a clepsydra, with the periods of day and night marked off as the divisions for walking meditation and practice. From that time on, gentlemen of pure faith from the four directions, hearing of the great master Huiyuan’s lofty conduct and virtue, came to find refuge with him, one hundred and twenty-three men in all. The great master Huiyuan said: “You noble ones have come here to cultivate. Can you be without the intention to seek rebirth in the Pure Land
Therefore he reverently made images of the Three Holy Ones of the West, built a hall, and gathered the Lotus Society, having Liu Yimin compose a vow text, which was carved upon stone.

Alas! The Buddha, toward sentient beings, reaches everywhere without exception — truly he may be called the great compassionate father and mother! If one wishes to be reborn quickly, he lets him be reborn quickly; if one wishes a golden dais, he changes it to a golden dais; if one wishes the hand to stroke the head, he strokes the head; if one wishes the robe to cover the body, he covers the body. Since the Buddha is compassionate toward all sentient beings, how could he alone not be compassionate toward me? Since the Buddha fulfills the vows of all sentient beings, how could he alone not fulfill my vow? The great compassionate heart makes no choosing — how could there be such a principle?

Alas! The Buddha, toward sentient beings, reaches everywhere without exception — truly he may be called the great compassionate father and mother! If one wishes to be reborn quickly, he lets him be reborn quickly; if one wishes to be reborn upon a golden dais, he lets him be reborn upon a golden dais; if one wishes the Tathagata to lay his hand upon the head, he strokes the head; if one wishes the Buddha’s robe to cover the body, he covers the body. Since the Buddha is compassionate toward all sentient beings, how could he alone not be compassionate toward me? Since the Buddha fulfills the vows of all sentient beings, how could he alone not fulfill my vow? The great compassionate heart of Amitābha Buddha makes no distinction or choosing — of course he will be compassionate toward me and fulfill my vow.

Therefore, if one can truly make a vow, then faith is already within it. Faith and vow being true, practice arises of itself without expecting to turn. For this reason, of the three provisions of faith, vow, and practice, the single word “vow” encompasses them all.

Therefore, if the vow one makes is a true vow, then faith is already within it. Faith and vow being true, practice arises of itself. For this reason, of the three provisions of faith, vow, and practice, the single word “vow” encompasses them all.
Cherish every thought: whenever a single thought arises, it is a seed of the ten realms — can one fail to cherish it?

What in the world is most to be cherished is nothing other than the spirit. What in the world is most to be treasured is nothing other than time. A single thought of purity is the causal arising of the Buddha-realm; a single thought of defilement is the cause of birth in the nine realms. Whenever a single thought arises, it is a seed of the ten realms — can one fail to cherish it?
What in the world is most to be cherished is nothing other than the spirit. What in the world is most to be treasured is nothing other than time. A single thought of purity (
this single, pure and unadulterated thought of Buddha-recitation

) is the causal arising of entry into the Buddha-realm; a single thought of defilement is the karmic cause of birth in the nine realms. Whenever a single thought arises, it is a seed of the ten realms (hell, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, devas, sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas) — how can one fail to cherish and treasure this single thought?

[A single thought of purity is the causal arising of the Buddha-realm] This single, pure and unadulterated thought of Buddha-recitation is the causal arising of becoming a Buddha. This is because, having been reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one becomes a Buddha in that very life.

The day has passed, and life diminishes along with it. An inch of time is an inch of life-light — can one fail to treasure it? If one truly knows that the spirit is to be cherished, one will not use it carelessly, and will hold fast to the Buddha’s name in thought after thought. If time is not to be idly spent, then one must cultivate the pure karma moment after moment.

When a day passes, life decreases along with it by a day. An inch of time is an inch of life-light — how can one fail to treasure time? If one truly knows that the spirit is precious, one will not waste the spirit, and will hold fast to the Buddha’s name in thought after thought. If time is not to be passed in vain, one must cultivate the pure karma moment after moment.
[The day has passed, and life diminishes along with it] The gatha of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra “Admonition to the Assembly” says:
“The day has passed, and life diminishes along with it. Like a fish in a dwindling pool, what joy is there
(this)
? O great assembly: be diligent and vigorous, as if saving your head from fire! Ever mindful of impermanence
(ever mindful of the coming of death)
, be on no account given to indolence
(never give way to indulgence and pleasure)

[A fish in a dwindling pool] A fish in a pool whose water is daily drying up. [As if saving your head from fire] When the oil-soaked hair is ablaze with a great fire and death presses close, to chant the Buddha’s name is to be eager (diligent and vigorous), urgently to extinguish this fire of death, and to accomplish the unbroken continuity of mindfulness before falling into unconsciousness and death. [Impermanence] That which has no permanent abiding; it also refers to death and the demon that seizes the soul. [Indolence] To give oneself over to indulgence and pleasure.

If one were to set aside the Buddha’s name and instead cultivate the holy practices of the Three Vehicles, that too would be wasting the spirit, and would be fitting a bow of a thousand jun’s force to shoot a mouse — how much more so to create the karma of the six destinies of birth and death! If one were to set aside the pure karma and instead seek the petty fruits of the provisional vehicle, that too would be passing time in vain, and would be trading a wish-fulfilling jewel for a single meal and a single garment — how much more so to seek the defiled fruits of the human and heavenly destinies!

If one were to set aside reciting the Buddha’s name and instead cultivate the holy practices of the Three Vehicles (the vehicle of sravakas, the vehicle of pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of bodhisattvas), that too would be wasting the spirit, like using a great bow that requires the strength of a thousand jun’s merely to shoot a small mouse — how much more so if one uses this spirit to create the karma of the six destinies, of birth and death and transmigration! If one were to set aside the pure karma and instead seek the petty fruits of the provisional vehicle (the expedient teachings), that too would be passing time in vain, and would be trading a wish-fulfilling jewel for a single meal and a single garment — how much more so to seek the defiled fruits of the human and heavenly destinies!

[A jun] Thirty jin make a jun; a thousand jun is thirty thousand jin. “A thousand jun” is commonly used to describe the weight of an object or the greatness of strength. [Fitting a bow of a thousand jun’s force to shoot a mouse] Using a great bow that requires the strength of a thousand jun’s to shoot a small mouse. [To release the trigger] To pull the trigger. [Xi (shrew-mouse)] The smallest kind of mouse. [Defiled fruit] “Defilement” is another name for affliction; “defiled” means possessing affliction; “defiled fruit” is the fruit in which birth and death are not yet ended.

Thus cherishing, thus treasuring, the mind becomes concentrated and the Buddha is easily moved, the practice diligent and the karma easily perfected. If one truly attains rebirth in the Pure Land and sees Amitābha Buddha face to face, then, constantly receiving his teaching and personally hearing his compassionate voice, one will wondrously awaken the mind and deeply realize the dharma-realm. Extending a single thought into a long kalpa, and drawing a long kalpa into a single thought — thought and kalpa interpenetrate, and one attains great freedom. Is this not reaping the reward of one’s own cherishing and treasuring?

Thus cherishing the spirit, thus treasuring time, the mind becomes concentrated and single, and Amitābha Buddha is easily moved to respond; the practice (holding fast to the Buddha’s name) is diligent, and the pure karma is easily brought to perfection. If one truly attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and sees Amitābha Buddha face to face, constantly receiving his teaching and personally hearing his compassionate voice, then naturally one will wondrously awaken the mind and deeply realize the dharma-realm. Extending a brief single thought into a long kalpa, and drawing a long kalpa into a brief single thought — thought and kalpa interpenetrate (transcending space and time), and one attains great freedom. Is this not oneself enjoying the reward of one’s own cherishing of the spirit and treasuring of time?

Surpassing all other paths: the single path of the Pure Land does not, at the outset, require awakening, and at the end does not await the arising of wisdom. It needs no repentance of karma, and no cutting off of affliction. It is to the utmost simplified and essential, and to the utmost direct and quick. And upon its realization, it is to the utmost vast, and to the utmost ultimate.

Now, one sees the Way, and thereafter cultivates the Way; one cultivates the Way, and thereafter realizes the Way. This is the same path of the thousand sages, a settled principle that never changes through the ages. But how can seeing the Way be spoken of lightly! If one follows the teachings of the doctrinal school, one must open the perfect understanding; if one follows the Chan school, one must penetrate straight through the final checkpoint. Only then can one speak of cultivating the Way. Otherwise, one is blindly practicing and blindly training, and cannot but run against walls and knock over beams, falling into pits and pitfalls.

Seeing the Way and thereafter cultivating the Way, cultivating the Way and thereafter realizing the Way — this is the common path of the multitude of sages (those who have severed delusion), and a settled principle that never changes through the ages. Yet how could seeing the Way be easy! If one follows the requirements of the doctrinal approach, one must open the perfect understanding to count as seeing the Way; if one follows the Chan school, one must penetrate straight through the final checkpoint to count as seeing the Way. Only after seeing the Way can one speak of cultivating the Way. Otherwise, one is blindly practicing and blindly training, and cannot but meet obstacle upon obstacle (running against walls and knocking over beams), and may even stray onto a wrong path (falling into pits and pitfalls).

[Doctrinal school] That is, the text-based school. [Chan school and text-based school] The Chan school refers specifically to the mind-to-mind transmission of the Chan lineage; the text-based school refers to all the theories and methods under the spoken teaching of Śākyamuni Buddha. Apart from the Chan school, all the others (the Vinaya school, the Avatamsaka school, the Tiantai school, the Three Treatise school, the Dharma-character school, and the True Word school) belong to the text-based school. Moreover, the Chan school emphasizes understanding the mind and seeing the nature, while the text-based school emphasizes opening the perfect understanding. [Final checkpoint] The Chan school has the doctrine of three checkpoints: the first checkpoint (breaking through the fundamental inquiry), the middle checkpoint, and the final checkpoint (the last checkpoint). If a practitioner can completely exhaust the feelings of the ordinary mind and clearly see that all dharmas are false and unreal, and awaken to the original source of his own mind-nature (the original face, the original scenery), this is called “breaking through the first checkpoint,” or breaking through the fundamental inquiry, also called seeing the nature. Next, after seeing the nature, if one continues to work at practice, so that one is not only not obstructed by “existence,” but also does not cling to “emptiness,” this is called “passing through the middle checkpoint,” also called the great death and the great life. After this, if one continues to work and refine, brushing away the traces of awakening, and attains the state of the non-duality of stillness and illumination, of the unimpeded interpenetration of emptiness and existence, so that even with the five desires before him, he acts freely without losing his original nature — this is “passing through the final checkpoint.” Breaking through the first checkpoint, one sees the dharma-body; breaking through the middle checkpoint, one realizes the dharma-body; breaking through the final checkpoint, one penetrates the dharma-body.

[The great death and the great life] A term used in the Chan school, meaning the great life after the great death; it is synonymous with the phrases “a great death once,” and “revival after death.” To know that true emptiness is originally without a single thing, this is the great death; to know the wonderful existence and the interpenetration of emptiness and existence, this is the great life. The Blue Cliff Record says: “One must first die the great death, and then become alive again.” [The five desires] Form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Form refers to beautiful appearances; sound refers to melodious voices; smell refers to fragrant scents; taste refers to delicious flavors; touch refers to the physical comfort of the body. Because these five can cause one to give rise to a mind of greed and desire, they are called the five desires.

Only the single path of the Pure Land is not so. “Going west from this world, passing through ten trillion Buddha-lands, there is a world called Ultimate Bliss. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who is now teaching the Dharma.” Only make the vow and hold the name, and one attains rebirth. This is the realm personally known and personally seen by the Buddha’s mind and the Buddha’s eye, not something that the sages of the Three Vehicles can know or see. One should only deeply trust the Buddha’s words, and in reliance upon them make the vow and hold the name. This is to take the Buddha’s knowing and seeing as one’s own knowing and seeing, without the need to seek another gate of awakening.

Only the Pure Land approach need not first require seeing the Way. The sutra says: “Going west from this world, passing through ten trillion Buddha-lands, there is a world called Ultimate Bliss. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who is now teaching the Dharma.” Only make the vow and hold the name, and one attains rebirth and puts an end to birth and death. This is the realm personally known and personally seen by the Buddha’s mind and the Buddha’s eye, not something that the sages of the Three Vehicles can know or see! One should only deeply trust the Buddha’s words, and in reliance upon them make the vow and hold the name. This is to take the Buddha’s knowing and seeing as one’s own knowing and seeing, without the need to seek another gate of awakening, and directly to put an end to birth and death.

The other paths of cultivation must, after awakening, practice in accordance with the Dharma, gather the mind to achieve concentration, from concentration bring forth wisdom, and by wisdom sever delusion. The wisdom that arises may be superior or inferior, and the delusion severed may be deep or shallow; only then can one speak of regressing or not regressing. Only in this single path of the Pure Land does one, solely by a mind of faith and vow, hold fast to the name, and when holding reaches single-mindedness without confusion, the pure karma is then great in its accomplishment, and rebirth after death is certain. Once one attains rebirth, one never regresses.

The other paths of cultivation must, after awakening, practice in accordance with the Dharma, gather the mind to achieve concentration, from concentration bring forth wisdom, and by wisdom sever delusion. Because the wisdom brought forth may be superior or inferior, the delusion severed may accordingly be deep or shallow; only then can one speak of whether the merit and wholesome roots regress. Only the Pure Land approach, solely by a mind of faith and vow, holds fast to the name; when holding reaches single-mindedness without confusion, the pure karma is then great in its accomplishment, and rebirth at the moment of death is certain. Once one attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one never regresses.
[No regression] Merit and wholesome roots only increase and never regress.

Further, the other paths of cultivation must first repent the present karma. If the present karma is not repented, it can obstruct the Way, and then there is no path for advancing. Those who cultivate the pure karma attain rebirth together with their karma, and need not repent. Because a single thought of single-hearted Buddha-recitation can extinguish the heavy karma of birth and death of eighty billion kalpas.

Further, the other paths of cultivation must first repent the present karma. If the present karma is not repented away, it can obstruct the Way, and then there is no path of advancing. Those who cultivate the pure karma attain rebirth together with their karma, and need not repent. Because a single thought of single-hearted Buddha-recitation can extinguish the heavy karma of birth and death of eighty billion kalpas.

Further, the other paths of cultivation must sever affliction. If the afflictions of false views and false thinking are not eliminated in the very least, then the birth-and-death of the delimited mode is not ended, and one cannot escape the common land. Only by cultivating the pure karma does one emerge horizontally from the three realms. Without severing affliction, from this common land one is born in that common land. Once born in that land, the very root and stock of birth and death is forever cut off.

Further, the other paths of cultivation must sever affliction. If the afflictions of false views and false thinking are not eliminated in the very least, then the birth-and-death of the delimited mode is not ended, and one cannot escape the Sahā world. Only by cultivating the pure karma does one emerge horizontally from the three realms; without the need to sever affliction, one goes from the common land of sages and ordinary beings of the Sahā world to be reborn in the common land of sages and ordinary beings of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once born in that land, the afflictions of false views and false thinking (the very root and stock of birth and death) are forever cut off.

Once born in that land, one constantly sees the Buddha and constantly hears the Dharma. Clothing, food, dwelling, and abode all come of themselves. The water, the birds, and the groves all expound the Dharma. In the common land, one sees horizontally the three higher Pure Lands, and dwells in one assembly with the multitude of superior ones, perfectly realizing the three kinds of non-regression, and in a single life fills the Buddha’s position.

Once born in the common land of sages and ordinary beings of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one constantly sees the Buddha and constantly hears the Dharma. Clothing, food, dwelling, and abode come of themselves. The water, the birds, and the groves all expound the Dharma. Though one is born in the common land, one can see horizontally the Land of Expedient Remaining, the Land of Real Reward, and the Land of Eternal Stillness and Light, and dwell in one assembly with the multitude of superior ones, perfectly realizing the three kinds of non-regression (non-regression of position, non-regression of practice, and non-regression of thought), and in a single life can become a Buddha.

[The three kinds of non-regression] First, non-regression of position: having broken the false views and entered the state of the noble ones, one will never again fall back to the former position of the ordinary person. Second, non-regression of practice: having broken the false thinking and the delusion of dust and sand, one now devotes oneself solely to saving all sentient beings, and will never again fall back to the former position of the two vehicles. Third, non-regression of thought: having realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, one’s thought abides in this true wisdom, and will never again fall away.

If this is so, then the single path of the Pure Land, at the outset, spares the search for the gate of awakening, and at the end does not await the arising of wisdom. It needs no repentance of karma, and no cutting off of affliction. It is to the utmost simplified and essential, and to the utmost direct and quick. And upon its realization, it is to the utmost vast, and to the utmost ultimate. The student should carefully savor and minutely weigh this, and not, through a momentary arrogance, lose this most excellent and greatest benefit.

As described above, the Pure Land approach, at the very beginning, spares the link of awakening, and at the end needs no attainment of wisdom from concentration nor severing of delusion by wisdom; it needs no repentance of karma, and no cutting off of affliction. This is an extremely simplified and essential, and extremely direct and quick approach. And upon realization, its fruit is again extremely vast, and extremely ultimate. The student should carefully realize the above principle and minutely choose the approach to be studied, and not through a momentary arrogance and self-conceit lose this most excellent and greatest benefit!
Karma senses, the mind manifests: all dharmas are only sensed by karma and only manifested by the mind.

A poor man, looking into the distance, saw a string of cash and went toward it to pick it up — it was a snake. He stood staring beside it. Another man came, got a string of cash, and carried it off. Now, the cash was not a snake, yet a snake appeared. This was only because of karma sensed and mind manifested. The snake on the cash was indeed karmically sensed and mentally manifested. And the cash on the snake — was that alone not also karmically sensed and mentally manifested?

A poor man, looking into the distance, saw a string of cash on the ground, so he went over to pick it up, only to find it was a snake. So he stood beside it staring. Another man came, saw that it was a string of cash, and picked it up and took it away. The cash was not a snake, yet it appeared as a snake — this is only because of karma sensed and mind manifested. Seeing the cash as a snake is indeed karmically sensed and mentally manifested. And seeing the snake as cash — is that not also karmically sensed and mentally manifested?

The snake on the cash is the private false vision of one person. The cash on the snake is the common false vision of many people. The falseness of one person’s false vision is easy to know. The falseness of many people’s false vision is hard to know. But by applying the easy to the hard, the hard also becomes easy to know. If this is so, then a snake is indeed a snake, and the cash is also a snake. Pushing further from here, within, the sense-organs and body; without, the realms; from one direction to the ten directions; and on to the four great continents and the three thousand great thousand worlds — all are this snake on the cash.

Seeing the cash as a snake is the private false vision caused by one person’s separate karma. And seeing the snake as cash is the common false vision of many people’s shared karma. The falseness of one person’s false vision is easy to know as false. The falseness of many people’s false vision, however, is very hard to know as false. But by using what is easy to know to illustrate what is hard to know, the hard to know also becomes easy to know. Therefore, a snake is indeed a snake, but from the standpoint of true reality, the cash is also a snake. Pushing the reasoning further from here, within, the body composed of the six sense-organs combined; without, all the realms; from one direction to the ten directions; and on to the four great continents and the three thousand great thousand worlds — all are the common false vision of shared karma.

[Shared karma and separate karma] Shared karma is the karmic cause that brings into being a common retribution; separate karma (individual karma) is the karmic cause that brings into being a retribution distinct and different for each.

But since the snake of mind-only has appeared, it can sting people; and since the cash of mind-only has appeared, it can be enjoyed. This does not mean that, being mind-only, there is no external realm. Moreover, the defiled suffering of the Sahā world and the pure bliss of the Land of Peace are both manifested by the mind. Since the defiled suffering of mind-only has appeared, one meets great oppression. Since the pure bliss of mind-only has appeared, one obtains great enjoyment. Since both defiled suffering and pure bliss are manifested by the mind, why not forsake the defiled suffering of mind-only and take up the pure bliss of mind-only, instead of passing through long kalpas, content to be assailed by the eight sufferings?

But since the serpent of the mind-only has already appeared, it is able to bite; since the money of the mind-only has already appeared, it is available to be enjoyed. If it were not mind-only, there would be no external world at all. Moreover, the defiled suffering of the Sahā world and the pure bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss are likewise both manifested by the mind alone. Since the defiled suffering of the mind-only has appeared, one undergoes great oppression; since the pure bliss of the mind-only has appeared, one enjoys great benefit. Since both defiled suffering and pure bliss are manifested by the mind alone, why not abandon the defiled suffering of the mind-only and take up the pure bliss of the mind-only, yet still deliberately endure the torment of the Eight Sufferings through long kalpas!

[The Eight Sufferings] The suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of sickness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what one loves, the suffering of meeting with what one hates, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the blazing of the five aggregates.

blocks.text: 13. The Power of the Mind and the Power of Karma

inline.s: The power of the mind and the power of karma: At the critical juncture of birth and death, there are but two powers — the power of the mind and the power of karma. The power of karma is the greatest, yet the power of the mind is even greater. A person who recites the Buddha's name must make the power of the mind greater than the power of karma before he can bring about the Buddha's appearance to receive and guide him.

[At the critical juncture of birth and death, there are but two powers. The first: thoughts are many and various, and where the mind leans most heavily it falls — this is the power of the mind. The second: as a man in debt is seized first by his strongest creditor, so among the many karma the strongest draws one onward — this is the power of karma. The power of karma is the greatest, yet the power of the mind is even greater. Because karma has no self-nature and relies entirely upon the mind; the mind can create karma and the mind can turn karma. Therefore only when the power of the mind is concentrated and the power of karma is strong can they pull one into rebirth. If with a concentrated mind one cultivates the pure karma, then the pure karma becomes strong; with the mind weighed down and the karma strong, one heads only for the Western Land. Thus when one's life comes to an end at death, one will certainly be reborn in the Western Land and nowhere else. Like a great tree or a great wall that has leaned westward all along — if it falls some day, it will never fall in any other direction.]

At the critical juncture of birth and death, only two powers are at work. The first: thoughts are many and various, and at the moment of rebirth whichever thought weighs most heavily goes to the place that corresponds to it — this is the working of the power of the mind. The second: as a man in debt repays first the greatest debt, so among the many karma at the moment of rebirth whichever karma is strongest goes to the place corresponding to it — this is the working of the power of karma. The power of karma is the greatest, yet the power of the mind is even greater. This is because karma has no self-nature and relies entirely upon the mind. The mind can create karma, and the mind can also turn karma. Therefore the power of the mind pushes the consciousness toward where the thoughts weigh most heavily, while the power of karma pushes the consciousness toward where the karma is strongest; both together determine the place of rebirth. If with a heavy, concentrated mind one cultivates the pure karma, then the pure karma is strong; and with the mind heavy upon rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and the pure karma strong, both the power of the mind and the power of karma push the consciousness toward the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Thus when one's life comes to an end, the consciousness will certainly be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and nowhere else. This is like a great tree or a great wall, which normally leans westward; if it falls some day, it will only fall to the west.

[What is a concentrated mind? We who cultivate the pure karma treasure faith above depth and vows above earnestness. Because faith is deep and vows are earnest, no false doctrine can shake or confuse, and no circumstance or condition can lure or turn us. If while earnestly cultivating the pure karma Bodhidharma the Great Master should suddenly appear before us and say: “I have the Chan of directly pointing to the human mind, seeing the nature, and becoming Buddha. You have only to set aside Buddha-recitation, and I shall transmit this Chan to you,” we should simply bow to the patriarch and reply: “I have already received the Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation from Śākyamuni Tathagata and have vowed to uphold it my whole life without change. Although the patriarch has a profound and subtle Chan teaching, I dare not violate my own original vow.” Even if Śākyamuni Tathagata were suddenly to appear and say: “What I earlier taught as the Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation was merely an expedient for that time. Now there is a yet more supreme Dharma-door surpassing it. You should set aside Buddha-recitation for now and I shall teach you the supreme Dharma,” we should likewise bow to the Buddha and declare: “I have already received the World-Honored One's Dharma-door of pure karma and have vowed, so long as a single breath remains, never to change. Although the Tathagata has a supreme Dharma, I dare not violate my own original vow.” Even when the Buddha and the patriarchs appear in person, one does not change his faith; how much less can the false, deluded doctrines of Mara and the heterodox teachers shake or confuse it! To have faith like this may indeed be called deep faith.]

So then, what is a concentrated mind? We who cultivate the pure karma treasure faith above depth and vows above earnestness, and because faith is deep and vows are earnest, no false doctrine can confuse or shake us, and no circumstance or condition can lure or turn us. If while earnestly cultivating the pure karma Bodhidharma the Great Master should suddenly appear before us and say: “I have the Chan of directly pointing to the human mind, seeing the nature, and becoming Buddha. You have only to give up Buddha-recitation and I shall transmit this Chan to you,” we should simply bow to the patriarch and answer: “I have already received the Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation from Śākyamuni Tathagata and have vowed to uphold it my whole life without change. Although the patriarch has a profound and subtle Chan teaching, I dare not violate my own original vow.” Even if Śākyamuni Tathagata were suddenly to appear and say: “What I earlier spoke as the Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation was merely an expedient for a time. Now I have a yet more supreme Dharma-door surpassing Buddha-recitation. You have only to give up Buddha-recitation and I shall teach you the supreme Dharma,” we should likewise bow to the Buddha and report: “I have already received the World-Honored One's Dharma-door of pure karma and have vowed, so long as a single breath remains, never to change. Although the Tathagata has a supreme Dharma, I dare not violate my own original vow.” Even when the Buddha and the patriarchs appear and still do not change what one believes, how much less can Mara and the heterodox teachers, with their false, deluded doctrines, confuse or shake one! To have faith like this may be spoken of as deep faith.

[If a red-hot iron wheel were spinning above one's head, one would not, because of this suffering, retreat from the vow to be reborn. If the supreme, wonderful five desires of a wheel-turning king appeared before one, one would not, because of this bliss, retreat from the vow to be reborn. These are the extremes of adversity and prosperity, and yet they do not change one's vow — how much less could the trivial favorable and adverse circumstances of the world lure one away! To have a vow like this may indeed be called an earnest vow.]

If a red-hot iron wheel were spinning above one's head, one would not, because of the menace of this suffering, retreat from the vow to be reborn. If the supreme, wonderful five desires of a wheel-turning king appeared before one, one would not, because of the allure of this bliss, retreat from the vow to be reborn. These extreme adverse and favorable circumstances still cannot change one's vow — how much less could the trivial favorable and adverse circumstances of the world lure and turn one! To have a vow like this may be spoken of as an earnest vow.

[Deep faith and earnest vows are what is called a concentrated mind. Cultivating the pure karma with these, the pure karma is certain to be strong. Because the mind is concentrated it easily becomes pure; because the karma is strong it easily ripens. If the pure karma of the Land of Ultimate Bliss ripens, then the defiled conditions of the Sahā world are exhausted. If the defiled conditions are truly exhausted, then at the moment of death, even if one wished the realms of samsara to appear again, they cannot. If the pure karma has truly ripened, then at the moment of death, even if one wished the Pure Land of Amitābha not to appear, it cannot.]

Deep faith and earnest vows — this is what is called a concentrated mind. Cultivating the pure karma with them, the pure karma is certain to be strong. Because the mind is concentrated it easily becomes single and pure; because the karma is strong the karma easily ripens. If the pure karma of the Land of Ultimate Bliss ripens, then the defiled conditions of the Sahā world are exhausted. If the defiled conditions are truly exhausted, then at the moment of death, even if one wished the realms of samsara to appear again, they cannot. If the pure karma has truly ripened, then at the moment of death, even if one wished the Pure Land of Amitābha not to appear, it cannot.

[But this faith and vow must be maintained with constant practice through ordinary days, so that at the final moment one will not enter a wrong path. There was an ancient worthy who, as he was about to die, was received in succession by the young attendants of the Six Desire Heavens, yet he went with none of them, only fixing his mind upon awaiting the Buddha. When the Buddha later appeared, he said: “The Buddha has come,” and with hands joined he passed away. Now at the very moment of death, when the four elements are dissolving, what a time that is! When the heavenly attendants of the Six Desire Heavens come to receive one after another, what a state that is! If one's faith and vow have not reached complete firmness in ordinary days, when facing such a time and such a state, could one still forcibly maintain mastery? An ancient worthy like this may truly be called a model for all who cultivate the pure karma through the ages.]

And yet such deep faith and earnest vows must be maintained with constant practice through ordinary days, so that at the final moment one will naturally not enter a wrong path. For example, an ancient worthy, as he was about to die, was received in succession by the heavenly attendants of the Six Desire Heavens, yet he went with none of them, only fixing his mind upon awaiting the arrival of Amitābha Buddha. Only when Amitābha Buddha appeared before him did he say: “The Buddha has come,” and with hands joined he passed away. Now at the moment of death, when the four elements dissolve, what a time that is! When the heavenly attendants of the Six Desire Heavens come to receive one after another, what a state that is! If in ordinary days one's faith and vow have not reached complete firmness, when facing such a time and such a state, where could one forcibly maintain mastery? An ancient worthy like this may truly be called a model for all who cultivate the pure karma through the ages.

blocks.text: 14. Practicing the Way Within the Dream

inline.s: Practicing the Way within the dream: use the illusory to depart from the illusory; when illusion is exhausted, the dream awakens.

[A Chan practitioner once asked: “All dharmas are like a dream. The Sahā world is indeed a dream, and the Land of Ultimate Bliss is also a dream. Since both are dreams, what benefit is there in practicing?”

A Chan practitioner asked: “All dharmas are like a dream. The Sahā world is indeed a dream, and the Land of Ultimate Bliss is also a dream. Since both are dreams, what benefit is there in cultivating within the dream?”

[I replied: “Not so. Before the seventh ground, one practices the Way within a dream. The great dream of ignorance is one from which even an equal-enlightenment bodhisattva still sleeps. Only the Buddha alone may be called the Great Awakened One. While the eye of the dream has not yet opened, suffering and bliss appear quite real. Better than dreaming of the extreme suffering of the Sahā world is dreaming of the wonderful bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Moreover, the dream of the Sahā world goes from dream into deeper dream — dream upon dream, sinking ever more deeply. The dream of the Land of Ultimate Bliss goes from dream into awakening — awakening upon awakening, gradually reaching the Great Awakening. Although both are dreams, the one who dreams them is not the same; how can they be discussed as one?”

I replied: “You are mistaken. Before the seventh ground, bodhisattvas all practice the Way within a dream. The great dream of ignorance is one from which even an equal-enlightenment bodhisattva has not fully awakened. Only the Buddha alone may be called completely awake (the Great Awakening). While the eye of the dream has not yet opened, the suffering and bliss within the dream appear quite real. Better than dreaming of the extreme suffering of the Sahā world is dreaming of the wonderful bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Moreover, the dream of the Sahā world goes from dream into deeper dream — dream upon dream, ever more lost. The dream of the Land of Ultimate Bliss goes from dream into awakening — awakening upon awakening, gradually becoming completely awake. Although the Sahā world and the Land of Ultimate Bliss are both dreams, the nature of the two dreams is utterly different; how can they be lumped together?”
Faith is especially essential: in the great ocean of the Buddha-Dharma, faith is what allows entrance. In the single gate of the Pure Land, faith is especially essential.

[In the great ocean of the Buddha-Dharma, faith is what allows entrance. In the single gate of the Pure Land, faith is especially essential. Because the recitation of the Buddha's name is the profound practice-ground of all the Buddhas. Except for the bodhisattva bound for Buddhahood in one lifetime, who may know a small portion of it, all the other sages and worthies can only follow it in faith — it is not within the reach of their wisdom, how much less that of inferior common mortals!]

In the great ocean of the Buddha-Dharma, only faith allows entrance. In the Pure Land Dharma-door, faith is all the more essential. Because the recitation of the Buddha's name is the profound practice-ground of all the Buddhas. Except for the equal-enlightenment bodhisattva, who knows a portion of it, all the other sages and worthies should only follow it in deep faith — for its principle is not within the reach of their wisdom, how much less that of inferior common mortals!

[Bodhisattva bound for Buddhahood in one lifetime] That is, the bodhisattva of one more rebirth — the equal-enlightenment bodhisattva — who, at the end of this very life, is able to fill the Buddha's seat.

[Moreover, of the eleven wholesome dharmas, faith occupies the first place; before faith there is no other wholesome dharma. Of the fifty-two stages, faith is the beginning; before the stage of faith there is no other sage-stage. Therefore the bodhisattva composed the Awakening of Faith, and the patriarch wrote the Inscription on Faith — taking the single dharma of faith as the essential gate for entering the Way. In former times Wang Zhonghui asked Yang Wuwei: “How can one's Buddha-recitation become uninterrupted?” Yang replied: “After a single moment of faith, one no longer doubts.” Wang departed joyfully. Before long, Yang dreamed that Zhonghui came to thank him, saying: “Through your instruction I gained great benefit, and I have now been reborn in the Pure Land.” Yang later met Zhonghui's son and asked about the circumstances of Zhonghui's passing and the time of it — which turned out to be the very day Yang had the dream. Alas! How great is the meaning of the moment of faith!]

Moreover, of the eleven wholesome mental factors, faith occupies the first place; before faith there is no other wholesome dharma. Of the fifty-two stages, faith is the beginning; before the stage of faith there is no other sage-stage. Therefore the bodhisattva Asvaghosa composed the Awakening of Faith, and the Third Patriarch of the Chan school, Sengcan, wrote the Inscription on Faith — each taking the single dharma of faith as the essential gate for entering the Way. In former times Wang Zhonghui asked Yang Wuwei: “How can one's Buddha-recitation become uninterrupted?” Yang Wuwei replied: “After a single moment of faith, one no longer doubts.” Wang Zhonghui departed joyfully. Before long, Yang Wuwei dreamed that Zhonghui came to thank him, saying: “Through your instruction I gained great benefit, and I have now been reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.” Yang Wuwei later met Zhonghui's son and asked about the circumstances and the time of Zhonghui's passing — which turned out to be the very day Yang Wuwei had the dream. Alas! How important faith is!

[The Eleven Wholesome Dharmas] That is, the eleven wholesome mental factors, one of the six groups of mental factors established by the Consciousness-Only school, namely: faith, shame, dread of blame, absence of greed, absence of anger, absence of delusion, diligence, tranquility, non-laxity, equanimity in relinquishment, and non-harmfulness. [Mental Factors] An abbreviation for the dharmas belonging to the mind — the various mental phenomena that belong to the mind, fifty-one in all. [Fifty-Two Stages] The stages a bodhisattva passes through from a common mortal to Buddhahood, fifty-two in all: the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment. [Yang Wuwei] Yang Jie, style name Cigong, a man of Wuwei in Jiangsu, who called himself “Master Wuwei.” During the Yuanfeng era of Emperor Shenzong of the Northern Song, he held the office of “Taichang”
in charge of the affairs of ritual, music, the suburban temples, and the altars of soil and grain

. After his great awakening, he turned his heart to the Pure Land. He wrote the Preface to the Ten Doubts of the Tiantai School, the Record of the Amitābha Pavilion, Thirty Hymns in Praise of the Land of Peace and Nurture, and the Preface to the Collection Resolving Doubts on the Pure Land, widely proclaiming the contemplation doctrines of the Western Land to guide those of future ages. In his later years he painted an image of Amitābha Buddha and carried it with him for contemplation and recollection. On the day of his death, his sincerity brought the Buddha to welcome him, and he passed away seated upright.

[The monk Dharmakara, before the Buddha World-Self-Ruling King, made forty-eight great vows in accordance with his nature. Relying upon these vows, through countless long kalpas he cultivated the great practices, until cause was complete and fruit fulfilled, and he himself became a Buddha. Dharmakara's name changed to Amitābha, and the world changed to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. What makes Amitābha Amitābha is that he has deeply realized the mind-only self-nature. Yet are not this Amitābha and this Land of Ultimate Bliss the mind-only Amitābha and the mind-only Land of Ultimate Bliss of the self-nature? But this mind-nature is equally shared by living beings and Buddhas; it belongs not particularly to the Buddha, nor particularly to living beings.]

The monk Dharmakara, before the Buddha World-Self-Ruling King, made forty-eight great vows in accordance with his nature. Relying upon these forty-eight great vows, through countless long kalpas he cultivated the great practices, until cause was complete and fruit fulfilled and he became a Buddha. At that time Dharmakara's name changed to Amitābha Buddha, and the world changed to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. What makes Amitābha Buddha Amitābha Buddha is that he has deeply realized the mind-only self-nature. Yet is not this Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha the mind-only Land of Ultimate Bliss of the self-nature Amita? But this mind-nature is equally shared by living beings and Buddhas; it belongs not particularly to a Buddha, nor particularly to living beings.
[The monk Dharmakara] The name of Amitābha Buddha when, in the causal stage, he left home before the Buddha World-Self-Ruling King and practiced the bodhisattva path.

[If one attributes the mind to Amitābha, then living beings are the living beings within Amitābha's mind. If one attributes the mind to living beings, then Amitābha is the Amitābha within living beings' minds. When the living being within Amitābha's mind recites the Amitābha within the living being's mind, how could the Amitābha within the living being's mind not respond to the living being within Amitābha's mind?]

If one attributes the mind to Amitābha Buddha, then living beings are the living beings within Amitābha Buddha's mind. If one attributes the mind to living beings, then Amitābha Buddha is the Amitābha Buddha within living beings' minds. When the living being within Amitābha Buddha's mind recites the Amitābha Buddha within the living being's mind, how could the Amitābha Buddha within the living being's mind not respond to the living being within Amitābha Buddha's mind?

[But the Buddha, awakened to this mind, is like a man who is awake. Living beings, deluded about this mind, are like men in a dream. Apart from the man who is awake, there is no other man in the dream. How could there be, apart from the man in the dream, another man who is awake? But the man in the dream should not take himself to be real, nor should he, apart from the man in the dream, seek another man who is awake; he should only ever remember the man who is awake. Remembering again and again, he will see the great dream gradually awaken and the eye of the dream open wide. Then the man in the dream who is able to remember is the very man who is awake whom he remembers. But the man who is awake is not the man in the dream. The men in the dream are many; the man who is awake is only one. The Tathagatas of the ten directions share one single dharmakāya; one mind, one wisdom, and likewise the powers and the fearlessnesses. This is the Dharma of at once one and many, ever the same and ever distinct, naturally and spontaneously wonderful. The essential meaning of Buddha-recitation is roughly this.]

But the Buddha, awakened to this mind, is like a man who is awake; living beings, deluded about this mind, are like men in a dream. Apart from the man who is awake, there is no other man in the dream. Apart from the man in the dream, how could there be another man who is awake? But the man in the dream should not take the affairs of the dream to be real, nor should he, apart from the man in the dream, seek another man who is awake; he should only always remember the man who is awake (the Buddha). Remembering again and again, he will see the great dream gradually awaken and the eye of the dream open wide. Then the man in the dream who is able to remember is the very man who is awake whom he remembers. But the man who is awake is not the man in the dream. The men in the dream are many; the man who is awake is only one. The Tathagatas of the ten directions share one single dharmakāya; one mind, one wisdom, and likewise the powers and the fearlessnesses. This is the Dharma of at once one and many, ever the same and ever distinct, naturally and spontaneously wonderful. The essential meaning of Buddha-recitation is roughly this.

blocks.text: 17. The Perfect Interfusion of Phenomenon and Principle

inline.s: The perfect interfusion of phenomenon and principle: “Reborn — one is certainly reborn; gone — one truly does not go.”

[The two statements “Reborn — one is certainly reborn; gone — one truly does not go” are held to speak: the first of phenomenon, the second of principle. Phenomenon is phenomenon that is identical to principle, meaning that to be born is not to be born — not that birth is taken simply as birth. Principle is principle that is identical to phenomenon, meaning that not to go is to go — not that not-going is taken simply as not-going. Read the two statements as one, then phenomenon and principle are perfectly interfused, so that joined they are doubly beautiful. Read the two statements as two, then phenomenon and principle are split apart, so that separated they are doubly injured. If one does not join these two statements as one, one should expand them into four statements: Reborn — one is certainly reborn, yet born without birth; gone — one truly does not go, yet not-going is to go.]

Reborn — one is certainly reborn; gone — one truly does not go,” these two sentences: the first speaks of phenomenon, the second speaks of principle. Phenomenon does not depart from principle — the “birth” of “reborn — one is certainly reborn” is non-birth, not taking birth simply as birth. Principle does not depart from phenomenon — the “not going” of “gone — one truly does not go” is going, not taking not-going simply as not-going. Read the two sentences as one, then phenomenon and principle are perfectly interfused — the so-called joined, doubly beautiful. Read the two sentences as two, then phenomenon and principle are split apart — the so-called separated, doubly injured. If one does not join these two sentences as one, one should expand these two sentences into four: Reborn — one is certainly reborn, yet born without birth; gone — one truly does not go, yet not-going is to go.

The Diamond Sutra says: “All conditioned appearances are false and unreal.” Rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is an affair within the dream of ignorance, so it too is an illusion. The characteristic of an illusion is that the appearance exists while the essence is non-existent — that is, the phenomenon exists while the principle is non-existent. The passage “Reborn — one is certainly reborn; gone — one truly does not go” speaks of rebirth from the two aspects of phenomenon and principle. From the aspect of phenomenal appearance, “reborn — one is certainly reborn” — one truly is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; from the aspect of principle, “gone — one truly does not go” — in reality there is no such affair as going to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore the passage “Reborn — one is certainly reborn; gone — one truly does not go” must be read as one sentence, speaking of the two aspects of phenomenon and principle. If read as two sentences, they become two mutually contradictory and confusing statements. So if not read as one sentence, one should expand them into four: Reborn — one is certainly reborn, yet born without birth (birth is illusion; in reality one was not born); gone — one truly does not go, yet not-going is to go (though on the essential principle one does not go, on the phenomenal appearance one goes).

In this book, Master Chewu often explains the principles of the Pure Land from the standpoint of the true reality of all dharmas, so it is best to read it after completing the four courses — the Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra, the Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra, the Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, and the Selected Annotations on the Buddha-Treasure Sutra — in the stage of “Prajñā that Destroys Delusion” of “Practicing Accordingly,” and it will then be easy to understand.

[Though they be four statements, the meaning is no more; joined as one statement, the meaning is no less. All in all it is just the perfect interfusion of phenomenon and principle. Rather than cling to the principle of “gone — one truly does not go,” it is better to cling to the phenomenon of “reborn — one is certainly reborn.” Why? Because clinging to phenomenon while being blind to principle still does not fail to gain the merit of entering a grade. But if one clings to principle and abandons phenomenon, one inevitably incurs the reproach of falling into emptiness. This is because phenomenon has the power to accord with principle, while principle has no power to stand alone. To take birth as birth is to fall into the eternalist view; to take not-going as not-going (denying even the phenomenal appearance) is to fall into the nihilist view. Though nihilism and eternalism are equally wrong views, the fault of the nihilist view is the deeper and heavier, and so it is better to cling to phenomenon. Yet after all, nothing is better than to perfectly comprehend the two statements together.]
