“Reborn — one is certainly reborn, yet born without birth; gone — one truly does not go, yet not-going is to go,” though they be four statements, the meaning is not increased. Joined as one statement, the meaning is not decreased. Whether four statements or one, all are but bringing about the perfect interfusion of phenomenon and principle. If one cannot achieve this perfect interfusion, then rather than cling to the principle of “gone — one truly does not go,” it is better to cling to the phenomenon of “reborn — one is certainly reborn.” Why? Because clinging to phenomenon while not understanding principle still has the effect of rebirth in the Pure Land. But if one clings to principle and abandons phenomenon, one inevitably incurs the reproach of falling into emptiness and cannot be reborn in the Pure Land. This is because phenomenon originally contains principle within it — only this person does not understand; while principle can never stand apart from phenomenon — principle without phenomenon is empty talk and fallacious theory. If one thinks of birth as birth, one falls into the eternalist view; if one thinks of not-going as absolute not-going (denying even the phenomenal appearance), one falls into the nihilist view. Though nihilism and eternalism are equally wrong views, nevertheless the fault of nihilism is deep and heavy, and so it is better to cling to phenomenon as having effect. Of course, although practicing by clinging to phenomenon has effect, it is still not as good as perfectly comprehending, from both phenomenon and principle, the two statements “Reborn — one is certainly reborn; gone — one truly does not go.” (Because one who clings to phenomenon without understanding principle may be reborn, but the grade is not high; one who clings to phenomenon yet understands principle — comprehending the first meaning — is reborn in the highest grade.)

blocks.text: 18. The Single Thought at the Moment of Death

inline.s: The single thought at the moment of death: the thousand recitations and the ten thousand recitations, even the day-long and year-long recitation — all are for nothing but to ripen this single thought of Buddha-recitation, in order to ensure that this thought appears at the moment of death.

[Our present single thought is dependently arisen and without self-nature; without self-nature yet dependently arisen. If it is not born in the Buddha-realm, then it is born in the nine realms. From the standpoint of dependent arising without self-nature, living beings and Buddhas are equally one emptiness. From the standpoint of no self-nature yet dependent arising, the ten realms differ vastly in superiority and inferiority.]

Our present single thought arises from causes and conditions and has no self-nature (it is an illusion); though without self-nature, it nonetheless arises following causes and conditions. If it is not born in the Buddha-dharmarealm, then it is born in the nine dharmarealms. From the standpoint of dependent arising without self-nature, living beings and Buddhas are equal, all being one emptiness. From the standpoint of no self-nature yet dependent arising, within the ten dharmarealms the superiority or inferiority of each is vastly disproportionate.

[No self-nature] “No self-nature” means that there is no real substance — it is an illusion, like the affairs of a dream. The Lotus Sutra says: “Know that all dharmas are ever without self-nature.” The Surangama Sutra says: “All illusions become without self-nature.”

[When King Ajitavati was dying, because a servant brushing away flies brushed his face with a whisk, a single thought of anger arose, and because of this he fell and became a poisonous snake. A woman, crossing a river, lost her footing; her child fell into the water, and in rescuing the child she sank with him. Because of her compassionate thought, she was reborn in heaven. When a single thought of compassion or anger thus divides heaven from the animal realm, how can this dependently arisen single thought at death be anything but a matter for care? If with this thought one turns the mind to recite Amitābha and seek rebirth in the Pure Land, how could one fail to see the Buddha and be reborn?]

When King Ajitavati was dying, because the servant brushing away flies carelessly brushed his face with a fan, a single thought of anger arose, and because this dying thought was one of anger, he fell and became a poisonous snake. A woman, crossing a river, lost her footing; her child fell into the water, and because she retrieved the child, both she and the child were submerged. Because her dying thought was one of compassion, this woman was reborn in heaven. When the dying thought is compassion or anger, the compassionate one is born in heaven and the angry one is born among animals — this distinction follows. How can one not be careful with this dependently arisen single thought at death? If at death, with this thought, one turns the mind to recite Amitābha Buddha and seek rebirth in the Pure Land, how could one fail to see the Buddha and be reborn?

[No self-nature] The meaning of “all dharmas are without self-nature” is that all dharmas have no real substance, all being illusions, like the affairs of a dream. No self-nature is also called no-nature. The Consciousness-Only Treatise says: “All dharmas are without self-nature.” The Lotus Sutra says: “Know that all dharmas are ever without self-nature.” The Surangama Sutra says: “All illusions become without self-nature.” [King Ajitavati] That is, King Ajitashatru, who throughout his life built countless stupas, made offerings to the Three Jewels, upheld the true Dharma, and accumulated vast merit. At death, because his attendant carelessly brushed his face with a fan, anger arose, and he fell and became a poisonous snake. This matter is found in the Miscellaneous Similes Sutra.
[The dependently arisen single thought at death] The single thought, at the moment of death, that determines where the consciousness is reborn.

[But this single thought cannot be gained through luck. It must be preserved with sincerity and maintained with constant practice. Therefore we, in this single “Amitābha,” recite a thousand times and ten thousand times, even day-long and year-long — all for nothing but to ripen this single thought. If this single thought ripens to purity, then at the moment of death there is only this thought and no other. Master Zhiyi says: “The mind in concentration at death is the mind that receives rebirth in the Pure Land.” Now when there is only this one thought and no other, is this not the mind in concentration? If the thought is thus, then not seeing Amitābha, whom else would he see? Not being reborn in the Pure Land, where else would he be reborn? I fear only that we do not have confidence in ourselves.]

But this single thought at death cannot be gained through luck. It must be preserved with sincerity and maintained with constant practice. Therefore we, in this single “Amitābha Buddha,” recite a thousand times and ten thousand times, even day-long and year-long — all for nothing but to ripen this single thought of Buddha-recitation, in order to ensure that the thought at death is a thought of Amitābha Buddha. If this single thought of Buddha-recitation ripens to purity, then at the moment of death there is only this thought of Buddha-recitation and no other. Master Zhiyi says: “The mind in concentration at death is the mind that receives rebirth in the Pure Land.” Now when there is only the thought of Buddha-recitation and no other thought, is this not the mind in concentration? Since at death it is the mind in concentration, then not seeing Amitābha Buddha, whom else would he see? Not being reborn in the Pure Land, where else would he be reborn? I fear only that we have not truly believed in the above principle; if we truly believed, how could we not be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss?

[Ripening this single thought] This means achieving what the bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta called “pure thoughts continuing without interruption,” which is what Master Shandao (the second patriarch of the Pure Land school) called “thought after thought continuous.” (Note: “thought after thought continuous” means that each thought of Buddha-recitation continues into the next; it does not mean the condition of mouthing the Buddha's name while the mind is given over to delusive thinking.) Master Shandao says: “Therefore the Great Sage (Śākyamuni Buddha), in his compassion and pity, directly urged single-minded recitation of the name; precisely because reciting the name is easy, when it is continuous one is reborn. If one can make thought after thought continuous, making the end of life the term, then ten in ten are reborn, a hundred in a hundred are reborn. … If all people will earnestly reflect, then whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, they must be diligent and strict with themselves, never ceasing by day or night — the former thought ends with life, the latter thought is born, ever enjoying the Dharma-bliss of the unconditioned, even reaching Buddhahood. Is this not blessed?” (Quoted from The Essentials of Buddha-Recitation.) Therefore, thought after thought continuous in daily life is the guarantee of right mindfulness clearly present at death; and right mindfulness clearly present at death is the key to rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Master Shandao composed the Essay on Right Mindfulness at Death, saying: “The one who knows the return asked: Of the great affairs of the world, none surpasses birth and death. When one breath does not come, one belongs to the next life; a single mistaken thought and one falls into samsara. I have repeatedly received your instruction on the Dharma of rebirth through Buddha-recitation, and its principle is most clear. Yet I fear that when sickness comes and death arrives, my mind and consciousness may be scattered, and I still worry that others may disturb my right mindfulness and cause me to lose the pure cause. I humbly beg you to again make clear the path of return, so that I may escape the suffering of sinking. The master said: Good is your question! All people, when about to die, who wish to be reborn in the Pure Land must not fear death. Always think that this body is full of suffering and that impure evil karma entangles it in many ways. If one can abandon this defiled body and be reborn beyond in the Pure Land, receiving immeasurable bliss and being liberated from the bitter realm of birth and death, that is a most satisfying matter — like casting off a worn garment and receiving a precious robe. One should only let go of body and mind and give rise to no attachment. … When illness is grave and death approaches, relatives must not weep in tears or utter sighs of regret and distress, disturbing the mind and confusing the spirit and losing right mindfulness. They should only recite the Buddha's name in unison, and only after the breath has ceased may they grieve and weep. If there is the slightest thought of attachment to the world, it becomes a hindrance and one cannot be liberated. … I have often seen people in the world who in daily life recite, praise, and make vows to seek rebirth in the West with great diligence and sincerity. Yet when sickness comes, they fear death and speak no more of rebirth and liberation. Only when the breath fades and life ends and consciousness goes to the netherworld do they begin ten recitations. This is exactly like closing the door after the thief has gone — of what use is it? The matter of birth and death is great; one must exert one's own strength. If a single thought is mistaken, one suffers for kalpas — who can take one's place? Think on this, think on this!” (Quoted from the Longshu Pure Land Text.)

blocks.text: 19. The Essential Doctrine of the Dharma-Treasure

inline.s: The essential doctrine of the Dharma-treasure: The two statements “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha” are in truth the essential doctrine of the Dharma-treasure of all the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times.

[Once the two statements of the Contemplation Sutra, “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha,” are raised, then the meanings beyond the words — “the mind not making the Buddha, the mind not being the Buddha; the mind making the nine realms, the mind being the nine realms; the mind not making the nine realms, the mind not being the nine realms” — are all made clear. Alas! If one truly understands this principle and still does not recite the Buddha's name, then there is nothing I can do with him.]

In the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the Buddha said: “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha.” The meanings beyond the words — “this mind not making the Buddha, this mind then not being the Buddha; this mind making the nine realms, this mind then being the nine realms; this mind not making the nine realms, this mind then not being the nine realms” — are then perfectly clear. Alas! If one truly understands this principle and still does not recite the Buddha's name, then there is nothing I can do with him.

[This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha] In the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life the Buddha said: “Next you should contemplate the Buddha. Why? Because the Tathagatas of all the Buddhas are the dharmakāya realm, entering into the thoughts of all living beings. Therefore, when you living beings think of the Buddha, this mind is endowed with the thirty-two marks and the eighty secondary signs. This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. The ocean of the Buddhas' correct and universal knowledge is born from the thought.” [Correct and universal knowledge] One of the Buddha's ten honorable titles: correct and universal knowledge, truly knowing all dharmas. [Then there is nothing I can do with him] (For such a person) I truly can do nothing with him; “none” means to have nothing.

[The two statements of the Contemplation Sutra, “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha,” are not only the essential doctrine and Dharma-essentials of that one sutra, but in truth the essential doctrine of the great Dharma of the entire teaching of Śākyamuni Tathagata's lifetime; not only the essential doctrine of the Dharma-treasure of the one Buddha Śākyamuni, but in truth the essential doctrine of the Dharma-treasure of all the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times. This doctrine once penetrated, what doctrine is not penetrated? This Dharma once made clear, what Dharma is not clear? It is the saying that though one's learning be not extensive, one may rank with the highest worthies.]

The two statements of the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha,” are not only the essential doctrine and Dharma-essentials of that one sutra, but in truth the essential doctrine of the great Dharma of the entire teaching of Śākyamuni Tathagata's lifetime; not only the essential doctrine of the Dharma-treasure of the one Buddha Śākyamuni, but in truth the essential doctrine of the Dharma-treasure of all the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times. This doctrine once penetrated, what doctrine is not penetrated? This Dharma once made clear, what Dharma is not clear? Therefore by firmly grasping the two statements “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha,” and with such faith, such understanding, such practice, though one's learning be not extensive, one may reach the station of the highest worthies.
[Dharma-treasury] Refers to the teaching spoken by the Buddha. Dharma means the teaching; treasury is the general term for the scriptures.
Absolute and perfectly interfused: a single recitation of the Buddha’s name is absolute and perfectly interfused, inconceivable.

[The true dharma has no nature of its own; defilement and purity follow conditions. Since the one true, in its entirety, becomes the ten realms, the ten realms in their entirety are just the one true. Therefore one who is skilled at discussing mind and nature will never forsake cause and effect, and one who deeply believes in cause and effect will in the end greatly illumine mind and nature. Such is the inevitable tendency of principle and circumstance. The single thought of our present mind that is able to recite is wholly true become false, and wholly false is just true; all day long it follows conditions, all day long it does not change.]

The dharma of true suchness has no self-nature of its own; whether defiled or pure, all arises in dependence upon conditions. Since the one true, in its entirety, becomes the ten dharma-realms, the ten dharma-realms in their entirety are the one true. Therefore one who is skilled at discussing mind and nature will never forsake cause and effect, and one who deeply believes in cause and effect will in the end greatly illumine mind and nature — such is the inevitable tendency of principle. The single thought of our present mind that is able to recite: with one deluded thought, the whole of the true becomes false; with one awakened thought, the whole of the false returns to the true. Though the mind follows conditions and changes all day long, the essence of the mind is forever that same essence.

[True dharma] the dharma of true suchness. [The one true] the meaning of the solely real, that is, the true character of all dharmas. [Wholly true become false, wholly false is just true] The single thought of the present mind has two states, true and false. When the self-nature is master it is true; when habit-energy is master it is false. “Wholly true become false, wholly false is just true” means that the true and the false do not stand side by side: either it is wholly true or wholly false. With one deluded thought the whole of the true becomes false; with one awakened thought the whole of the false returns to the true.

[A single Buddha that is recited: the whole virtue establishes the name, and outside that virtue there is no name. By the name one summons the virtue, and outside the name there is no virtue. Outside the mind that recites there is no separate Buddha that is recited; outside the Buddha that is recited there is no separate mind that recites. The reciting and the recited are not two, yet living beings and Buddhas are clearly distinct. Originally it is free of the four propositions, originally cut off from the hundred negations. Originally it is everywhere, originally it contains everything. Absolute and perfectly interfused, inconceivable. The practitioner of the Lotus school should enter in faith from
(this)
point onward.]

The name of the Buddha that is recited is established wholly by the Buddha’s virtue, so outside the Buddha’s virtue there is no name. By the name one summons the Buddha’s virtue, so outside the name there is no Buddha’s virtue. Thus the Buddha’s name and the Buddha’s virtue wholly coincide. If one can bring it about that outside the reciting mind there is no separate Buddha recited, and outside the Buddha recited there is no separate reciting mind, then mind and Buddha wholly coincide, the reciting and the recited are not two, and living beings and Buddhas are clearly one body. Then, originally one is free of the four propositions, originally cut off from the hundred negations. Originally one is everywhere, originally one contains everything. Absolute perfect interfusion, inconceivable. The practitioner of the Lotus school should enter in faith from here.

This passage of Master Chewu’s instruction sets forth the virtue of the nature that living beings inherently possess. Yet only when the virtue of cultivation has efficacy does the virtue of the nature appear. Therefore in the annotation I have added such phrases as “if one can bring it about that...”, “then...”, and “then, originally...” so that it is easier to understand and easier to put into practice.

[The four propositions] The so-called four propositions are: existent, nonexistent, both existent and nonexistent, neither existent nor nonexistent. This is the phrase commonly used by the Chan school and others when explaining the principle that true emptiness is signless and unobtainable, in order to wipe out the deluded and erroneous views that cling to such dualities as existence and nonexistence. [The hundred negations] “Hundred” is a general term for a great number; “negations” refers to the various negations such as “not existent” and “not nonexistent”. It means that all words and phrases are not ultimately real; the intent is to sweep away living beings’ deluded attachments and cause them to awaken to the principle that all dharmas are ultimately real and unobtainable. [Cut off from relativity] Cut off from all relativities. Relativity means two sides standing in opposition, as with black and white, great and small, good and evil, and so forth. To be cut off from relativity is the equality of true suchness, in which no dharma is obtainable; hence it is cut off from all relativities, and is briefly called “cut off from relativity”. It is synonymous with “absolute”.
The grave fault of killing: creating heavy karma, giving rein to the killing mind, binding deep enmity, and reaping bitter fruit are all brought about by a single act of killing.

[The matter of killing living beings is of the deepest gravity. All living beings possess the Buddha-nature — can they be killed? To create heavy karma, to give rein to the killing mind, to bind deep enmity, and to reap bitter fruit: all are brought about by this one act of killing. Thus the killing mind grows ever fiercer and the karma of killing ever deeper, until by degrees one comes to kill people, and even to kill one’s own six close kin, and at last it accumulates into the great kalpa of swords and weapons. How pitiable! All of this comes from not knowing to abstain from killing.]

The matter of killing living beings is of the deepest gravity. All living beings possess the Buddha-nature; can living beings be killed? To create heavy karma, to give rein to the killing mind, to bind deep enmity, and to reap bitter fruit: all are brought about by this one word “kill”. If one does not abstain from killing, then the killing mind grows ever fiercer and the karma of killing ever deeper, until by degrees one will kill people, and even kill one’s own six close kin, and at last it accumulates into the great kalpa of swords and weapons. How truly pitiable! All of this is caused by not knowing to abstain from killing.
[The six close kin] Father, mother, elder brother, younger brother, wife, and children. It also refers generally to kinsfolk.

[If one but knows to abstain from killing, one cannot bear even to kill a domestic animal — how much less a human being! How much less one’s six close kin! If one cannot bear to kill even a domestic animal, whence would the great kalpa of swords and weapons ever come? He who kills another’s father, another will also kill his father. He who kills another’s elder brother, another will also kill his elder brother. To know that another’s father and elder brother may not be killed is also a gradual step toward abstaining from killing. But as for those who do not know that fathers and elder brothers may not be killed — it all begins from not abstaining from killing.]

If one knows to abstain from killing, one cannot bear even to kill a domestic animal — how much less a human being! How much less one’s six close kin! If one cannot bear to kill even a domestic animal, whence would the great kalpa of swords and weapons come? One should know that he who kills another’s father, another will also kill his father; he who kills another’s elder brother, another will also kill his elder brother. To know that another’s father and elder brother may not be killed is likewise to come gradually to abstain from killing. But those who do not know that fathers and elder brothers may not be killed — all of them begin from not abstaining from killing.

blocks.text: 22. The Way of Stimulus and Response

inline.s: The way of stimulus and response: the stimulus is the cause, the response is the fruit; where there is a stimulus there must be a response.

[The reason people do not abstain from killing is that they do not understand the principle of cause and effect. Cause and effect is stimulus and response. If I stir others with an evil mind, they respond with an evil mind. If I stir others with a good mind, they respond with a good mind. People know only that stimulus and response appears in this present life, and do not know that stimulus and response reaches through the three times. People know only that stimulus and response appears in the human path, and do not know that stimulus and response reaches through the six paths. If one truly knew that stimulus and response reaches through the three times and the six paths, then since throughout the six paths all are one’s fathers and elder brothers from many lives past — can killing go unrefrained?]

The reason people do not abstain from killing is that they do not understand the principle of cause and effect. Cause and effect is stimulus and response. If I stir others with an evil mind, others respond with an evil mind. If I stir others with a good mind, others respond with a good mind. People know only that stimulus and response appears in this present life, and do not know that stimulus and response reaches through the three times (past, present, and future). People know only that stimulus and response appears in the human path, and do not know that stimulus and response reaches through the six paths. If one truly knew that stimulus and response reaches through the three times and the six paths, then throughout the six paths all are one’s own fathers and elder brothers from many lives past — can killing go unrefrained?

Liao-Fan’s Four Lessons says: “One who is good at correcting his faults does not first prohibit the deed, but first understands its principle. If the fault lies in killing living beings, then one reflects: Heaven loves life, and all creatures cherish their own lives; to kill them to nourish myself, how can I be at peace? Moreover, when they are killed they first endure butchery and cutting, and then enter the cauldron, every kind of pain piercing to the marrow; while my own nourishment, spread out in rare and rich dishes, is gone as soon as it is eaten, whereas coarse vegetables and broth can fully fill the belly. Why then should I destroy their lives and diminish my own blessings? And again one reflects: creatures with blood and breath all contain a spiritual knowing; since they all have a spiritual knowing, they are all one body with me. Even if I cannot myself cultivate the highest virtue and cause them to honor and love me, how can I daily destroy their lives and cause them to hate and resent me without end? Once one thinks of this, one will grieve over one’s food and be unable to swallow it.”

The following situation is common: one wants to break the bad habit of eating meat, and yet cannot do it — what then? Master Yinguang tells of one case: “In the tenth year of the Republic, I went to Nanjing. Wei Meisun (a Hanlin scholar, then sixty years old) said to me: ‘The Buddha-Dharma, I do believe in; the Buddha, I am willing to recite; your Collected Writings I have also read — it is only that I cannot eat vegetarian food.’ I said: ‘The habits of the rich and noble are hard to forget. If you wish to eat vegetarian food, I beg you to read carefully the ‘Essay on the Pond for Releasing Life’ at Nanxun in my Collected Writings (the Essay on Rebuilding the Pond for Releasing Life at the Temple of Ultimate Bliss, Nanxun), and to read it again and again; then of yourself you will be unable to eat meat.’ This was spoken on the twelfth day of the eighth month. By the tenth month, on his sixtieth birthday, fearing that human feelings would stand in the way, he went to Mount Jin (note: Jinshan Temple) to pass his birthday, and when he returned home he became a lifelong vegetarian. The following year he began to promote the holding of Buddha-recitation and life-releasing assemblies at the Temple of the Clouds of Dharma, and now he is sixty-six. In charitable works he spares neither spirit nor effort, promoting them with all his might — whether founding a home for young children, or distributing gruel every year. And in the past two years, when the war broke out, he took in the old, the weak, and the women at the Temple of the Clouds of Dharma, put up several dozen mat sheds for them to live in, and cooked gruel for them. When the fighting ended he gave them traveling expenses according to the distance they had to go, and sent them home. Once there were more than a thousand people, another time more than two thousand. Every day after they had eaten the gruel, he had each of them recite the Buddha’s name and Guanyin’s name.” (From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Reply to the Lay Devotee Zhuoren)
See the appendix for the full text and translation of the Essay on Rebuilding the Pond for Releasing Life at the Temple of Ultimate Bliss, Nanxun.

[Even if one knows that stimulus and response reaches through the six paths, one still does not know that stimulus and response reaches through the mundane and the supramundane. If one stirs with a mind of no-self, then the fruits of the voice-hearer and the solitary realizer respond. If one stirs with the bodhi-mind and the six perfections and ten thousand practices, then the fruits of the bodhisattva realm respond. If one stirs with equal great loving-kindness and the great compassion of oneness, then the fruits of the Buddha realm respond. Alas! Can the way of stimulus and response ever be fully spoken?]

Even if one knows that stimulus and response reaches through the six paths, one still does not know that stimulus and response reaches through the mundane and the supramundane. Stirring with a mind of no-self, the fruits of the voice-hearer and the solitary realizer respond. Stirring with the bodhi-mind and the six perfections and ten thousand practices, the fruits of the bodhisattva realm respond. Stirring with equal great loving-kindness and the great compassion of oneness, the fruits of the Buddha realm respond. Alas! How could the way of stimulus and response ever be fully spoken?

The authentic tenets: the single phrase “Amitābha Buddha” takes mind-only as its tenet, takes Buddha-only as its tenet, takes absolute perfect interfusion as its tenet, and takes transcending emotion and cutting off views as its tenet.

[You should know that the single phrase “Amitābha Buddha” takes mind-only as its tenet. The meaning of this mind-only must be definitively established by the three means of valid cognition. The three means of valid cognition are: direct perception, inference, and scriptural authority.]

You should know that the single phrase “Amitābha Buddha” takes mind-only as its tenet. The meaning of this mind-only must be definitively established by the three means of valid cognition. The three means of valid cognition are: direct perception, inference, and scriptural authority.

[The three means of valid cognition] Direct perception, inference, and scriptural authority. Direct perception is the principle personally and actually verified; inference is the principle known through analogy and reasoning; scriptural authority is the principle spoken by the sages (the Buddhas).

[Direct perception means personally verifying that principle. Thus the Great Master Kumarajiva, at the age of seven, entered a Buddhist temple with his mother, saw the Buddha’s bowl, and joyfully placed it upon his head. Suddenly he thought: I am very young, and the Buddha’s bowl is very heavy — how can I hold it up? The instant this thought stirred, he cried out and set the bowl down, and so awakened to the truth that all dharmas are mind-only. The Korean Master Wonhyo came to this land to study. At night he lodged among the tombs, and grew very thirsty. In the bright moonlight he saw a pool of clear water, scooped it up with his hand and drank it, and found it wonderfully fragrant and sweet. At dawn the next day he saw that the water had seeped out from a grave, and his stomach turned and he vomited violently. Thereupon he awakened to the truth that all dharmas are mind-only, and returned to his own country to write his works. These are all instances of direct perception, personally verified.]

Direct perception means knowing the principle by personally verifying it. For example, the Great Master Kumarajiva, at the age of seven, entered a Buddhist temple with his mother, saw the Buddha’s bowl, and joyfully placed it upon his head. Suddenly he thought: I am very young, and the Buddha’s bowl is very heavy — how can I hold it up? The instant this thought arose, he cried out and the Buddha’s bowl fell to the ground, and so he awakened to the truth that all dharmas are mind-only. The Korean Master Wonhyo came to the Central Land to study. At night he lodged among the graves, and grew terribly thirsty. In the bright moonlight he saw a pool of clear water, scooped it up with his hand and drank it, and found it wonderfully fragrant and sweet. Only at dawn the next day did he see that the water had flowed out from a grave, and he could not help but vomit violently. Thereupon he awakened to the truth that all dharmas are mind-only, and returned to his own country to write his works. These are all direct perception, personally verifying that all dharmas are mind-only.

[Inference means taking up the various characteristics and contemplating their meaning, knowing by analogy. Among all analogies, the dream is the most apt. For example, the mountains, rivers, people, and things seen in a dream, however countless their differences, never depart from the mind that is able to dream them. Apart from the dreaming mind, not a single dharma is obtainable. By this one may know by analogy that all the ten thousand dharmas before us are only manifestations of mind.]

Inference means taking up the various characteristics and examining the principle within them, knowing by analogy. Among the many analogies, that of the dream is the most apt for showing that all dharmas are mind-only. For example, the mountains, rivers, people, and things seen in a dream, however countless their differences, never depart from the mind that is able to dream them. Apart from the dreaming mind, not a single dharma is obtainable. From this analogy one knows that all the ten thousand dharmas before us are only manifestations of mind.
[Scriptural authority means: the three realms are mind-only, the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness-only. A thousand sutras and ten thousand treatises all speak thus.]

Scriptural authority is the teaching of the sages. The single phrase “the three realms are mind-only, the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness-only” is spoken thus in a thousand sutras and ten thousand treatises.

[The three realms are mind-only] All phenomena of the three realms (the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the realm of formlessness) are manifested by the one mind alone. It is also called “the three realms are only one mind”, “the three realms are one mind”, and so forth. That is, the mind is the root of all things, and apart from it there is no other dharma. All dharmas such as birth and death in the three realms and the twelve links of conditioned arising are in truth produced by the deluded mind. The old translation of the Avatamsaka Sutra

chapter ten, says: “The mind is like a master painter, painting the various five aggregates; in all the worlds there is no dharma it does not create. As the mind is, so too is the Buddha; as the Buddha is, so too are living beings. Mind, Buddha, and living beings — these three are without difference. All Buddhas fully understand that everything turns from the mind... and the mind creates all Tathagatas.” The old translation of the Avatamsaka Sutra

chapter twenty-five, says: “The three realms are false and delusive, made by the mind alone. The twelve conditioned links (that is, the twelve links of conditioned arising) all depend upon the mind.” The Mahayana Sutra of the Entry into Lanka

chapter two, says: “Mahamati, how should one contemplate what is manifested by one’s own mind? It is to contemplate that the three realms are nothing but one’s own mind, apart from self and what belongs to self, without activity and without coming or going.” [The ten thousand dharmas are consciousness-only] The Consciousness-Only school (that is, the Dharma-Characteristics school) holds that all dharmas are manifested by consciousness alone, and considers that the seeds of all dharmas stored in the alaya-consciousness are the source of all dharmas. All dharmas are manifested by the three transformative consciousnesses (the alaya-consciousness, the manas, and the first six consciousnesses). That is to say, the three transformative consciousnesses produce the seeing aspect (the knowing subject) and the objective aspect (the images of the objects known), and it is with the appearing of the seeing aspect and the objective aspect that all things in the universe come to be.

[Having already used the three means of valid cognition, such as direct perception, to definitively establish mind-only, we now further distinguish inherent containment and actual creation by way of the two gates of principle and fact. That is to say, because there is inherent containment in principle, there can be actual creation in fact. If principle did not contain it, how could fact create it? Therefore inherent containment in principle is only the containment of what is actually created. Apart from actual creation, there is nothing else contained. Because there is actual creation, the inherent containment of principle is revealed. If fact did not create, how would one know that principle contains it? Therefore actual creation only creates what principle contains. Apart from inherent containment in principle, there is nothing else created. Within this single thought of the present mind, the ten realms and ten thousand dharmas are inherently contained. And this same single thought, following conditions, can create the ten realms and ten thousand dharmas. Inherent containment is like the principle within gold by which it can become a vase, a plate, a hairpin, or a bracelet; actual creation is like following the conditions of the craftsman and the furnace hammer to make vessels that are vases, plates, hairpins, and bracelets. Again, inherent containment is like the principle within flour by which it can become all kinds of food; actual creation is like following the conditions of water, fire, and human labor to make all kinds of food.]

Above we used direct perception, inference, and scriptural authority to definitively establish the principle that all dharmas are mind-only. Now we further distinguish inherent containment and actual creation by way of the two aspects of fact and principle. This is to say that because there is inherent containment in principle, there can be actual creation in fact. If principle did not contain it, how could fact create it? Therefore inherent containment in principle is only the containment of what is actually created; apart from actual creation, principle has nothing else contained. Because there is actual creation, the inherent containment of principle can be revealed. If fact did not create, how would one know that principle contains it? Therefore actual creation only creates what principle contains; apart from inherent containment in principle, fact has nothing else created. Within this single thought of the present mind, the ten realms and ten thousand dharmas are inherently contained (inherent containment in principle). And this same single thought, following conditions, can create the ten realms and ten thousand dharmas (actual creation in fact). Inherent containment is like the principle within gold by which it can become a vase, a plate, a hairpin, or a bracelet; actual creation is like following the conditions of the craftsman, the furnace, and the hammer to make vessels that are vases, plates, hairpins, and bracelets. Again, inherent containment is like the principle within flour by which it can become all kinds of food; actual creation is like following the conditions of water, fire, and human labor to make all kinds of food.

[Having distinguished principle and fact, we now further determine the true and the false by way of the sameness or difference of name and essence. In the Buddha-Dharma there are cases where the name is the same but the essence differs, and cases where the name differs but the essence is the same. As for the same name with a different essence: take the single name “mind”. There is the fleshy heart, the deliberating mind, the storehouse mind, and the solid mind. The fleshy heart is the same as the external four great elements, and has no knowing. The deliberating mind extends through the eight consciousnesses, because all eight consciousnesses can deliberate upon and take as object their own respective spheres — this is the false. The storehouse mind refers only to the eighth, because it can gather the seeds of all dharmas and can bring about the arising of all dharmas — this is the union of true and false. The solid mind is the solid and real nature, the numinous knowing free of thought, the essence of pure truth. What is meant here by mind-only is the solid and purely true mind. As for different names with the same essence: such terms as true suchness, Buddha-nature, true character, and dharma-realm spoken of in the various sutras — all these various names of the ultimate are this solid and purely true mind.]

Having distinguished fact and principle, we now determine the true and the false by way of the sameness or difference of name and essence. In the Buddha-Dharma there are cases where the name is the same but the essence differs, and cases where the name differs but the essence is the same. As for the same name with a different essence, take the name “mind”: there is the fleshy heart, the deliberating mind, the storehouse mind, and the solid mind. The fleshy heart (the heart organ) is the same as the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, and is incapable of knowing. The deliberating mind extends through the eight consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness, manas, and alaya-consciousness), because these eight consciousnesses can all deliberate upon and take as object their own respective spheres — this is the false. The storehouse mind refers to the eighth consciousness (the alaya-consciousness), because it can gather the seeds of all dharmas and can bring about the arising of all dharmas — this mind is the union of true and false. The solid mind is the solid and real nature, the numinous knowing free of thought, the essence of pure truth. What is meant here by mind-only is the solid and purely true mind. As for different names with the same essence: such terms as true suchness, Buddha-nature, true character, and dharma-realm spoken of in the various sutras — all these various names of the ultimate are this solid and purely true mind.

[Having now determined the true and the false, we return to the inherent and the presently manifest, and point them out in a balanced way. For all the sutras say that from beginningless time there is an inherently existing true mind. Now if it is said to be inherent, how could it be absent today? And what exists today is precisely what is inherent. If there were no beginningless past, there would be no present; and if one departed from the present, how could there be a beginningless past? Therefore one need not exalt the inherent and revere it, nor push it far off into the beginningless past: the self-nature of this single thought of the present mind is precisely the inherently existing true mind. For this single present thought is wholly true become false and wholly false is just true; all day long it follows conditions, all day long it does not change. Apart from this single present thought, would there be some other true mind and self-nature? The ancient worthies said: the yonder shore of King Majestic Sound is not apart from the gateways of the six senses in this very life; the active ignorance of living beings is itself the Buddha’s unmoving substance of wisdom. How near the mark this is!]

Having determined the true and the false, we now distinguish the inherent and the presently manifest, and point them out in a balanced way. For all the sutras speak of an inherently existing true mind from beginningless time. Since it is said to be inherent, how could it be absent today? And what now exists is precisely what is inherent. If there were no beginningless past, there would be no present; if one departed from the present, how could there be a beginningless past? Therefore one need not exalt the inherent and revere it, nor push it far off into the beginningless past: only this self-nature of the single thought of the present mind is the inherently existing true mind. For this single present thought is wholly true become false and wholly false is just true; all day long it follows conditions, all day long it does not change. Apart from this single present thought, would there be some other true mind and self-nature? The ancient worthies said: the yonder shore of King Majestic Sound is not apart from the six sense-gates of this very life; the active ignorance of living beings is itself the Buddha’s unmoving substance of wisdom. This is very near the mark!

[The yonder shore of King Majestic Sound] Before King Majestic Sound Buddha, that is, before the appearance in the world of King Majestic Sound Buddha. King Majestic Sound Buddha is a Buddha who appeared in an extremely distant past age, and the Chan forest borrows this Buddha’s name to indicate a time in the past so remote as to be beyond measure. “Yonder shore” means that far side. “The yonder shore of King Majestic Sound” is a phrase the Chan forest commonly uses to point students toward their own original face, and it means the same as “before one’s parents were born”. [The active ignorance of living beings is itself the Buddha’s unmoving substance of wisdom] This says: the substance of living beings’ active ignorance is the true mind, and the substance of the Buddhas’ unmoving wisdom is also the true mind; both are the true mind — only the former is deluded while the latter is awakened.
[From the four meanings above, mind-only is revealed; therefore the first tenet is mind-only.]

The four meanings above (the three means of valid cognition, principle and fact, name and essence, and the inherent and the presently manifest) all reveal that all dharmas are mind-only; therefore the single phrase “Amitābha Buddha” takes mind-only as its tenet.

Question: The sutras and treatises often say: “All dharmas are within the mind. All Buddhas and living beings are also within the mind; the Pure Land and the defiled land are also within the mind.” How should this be understood?

Answer: All dharmas, all Buddhas and living beings, the Pure Land and the defiled land, are all seen in a dream by the self-mind (the dream of ignorance), and so are within the mind; but living beings, not yet awake from the dream of delusion, take them to be outside. The Sutra of the Entry into Lanka says: “Contemplate that all dharmas are without self-nature, like clouds in the sky, like a fire-wheel whirled, like a gandharva city, like an illusion, like a mirage, like the moon in the water, like things seen in a dream — not apart from one’s own mind; because of beginningless false views, one takes them to be outside.” The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life says: “The ocean of the Buddhas’ perfect universal knowledge is born from the mind’s thought.”

[A fire-wheel whirled] Whirling a fire in a circle so that it appears as a wheel of fire; but this fire-wheel seems to have form while not being real, and it is used to illustrate that all dharmas are illusory appearances. The Surangama Sutra says: “Dying here and being born there, being born and dying, they are like a fire-wheel whirled, and never have rest.” The Great Calming and Contemplation says: “For the sake of these views one creates all manner of entangling karma, falls into the three evil paths, and sinks without end, like a fire-wheel whirled. If one wishes to stop it, one should stop the hand.” The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says: “Like a fire-wheel whirled, it only deludes people’s eyes.” [Gandharva city] Refers to towers, mountains and rivers, forests and plains that appear illusory in midair. Legend says it is a city conjured in the sky by the gandharva deities; hence “gandharva city”. Or it may refer to the mirage that appears over the sea, in deserts, and on tropical plains when differences in the density of the air cause light to refract; the sutras and treatises often use it to illustrate unreal dharmas. Legend also says that the gandharvas, musicians of the Western Regions, often conjured cities by magic, and these were called gandharva cities. [The simile of the mirage] This says that a person without wisdom, first seeing a mirage, mistakenly takes it for water. The dharmas of affliction are likewise. The unwise do not understand, and within affliction falsely reckon a self (the self of a person, the self of dharmas); the wise understand that it is deceptive and unreal, all of it deluded thought — hence it is said to be like a mirage. [Mirage] A kind of vapor produced under the blazing sun that from afar looks like water; the thirsty long to drink it but in the end cannot obtain it, and it is used to illustrate that deluded thoughts are unreal. It is one of the ten similes of the Mahayana.

[Again, the single phrase “Amitābha Buddha” takes Buddha-only as its tenet. Since all the ten thousand dharmas are manifested by mind alone, in their entirety they are mind. The mind has no this or that, the mind has no boundaries. Among the ten realms and ten thousand dharmas — whether dependent or direct, whether provisional name or real dharma — whichever single dharma one picks up, it is the whole substance of the mind and possesses the great function of the mind, pervading horizontally as the mind pervades and reaching vertically as the mind reaches. Because the meaning of mind-only is established, the meanings of color-only, sound-only, scent-only, flavor-only, touch-only, and dharma-only, and even dust-mote-only and mustard-seed-only, are all established. Only when all the meanings of “only” are established is the true meaning of mind-only accomplished. If all the meanings of “only” were not established, there would be only the empty name of mind-only and no true meaning of mind-only. Because all the meanings of “only” are established, it is said that dharmas have no fixed character, and whatever condition they meet becomes the tenet. If even dust-mote-only or mustard-seed-only can be a tenet, could Amitābha of the fruition ground, adorned with the eighty thousand marks of excellence, on the contrary not be a tenet? Therefore it takes Buddha-only as its tenet.]

Again, the single phrase “Amitābha Buddha” takes Buddha-only as its tenet. Since all the ten thousand dharmas are manifested by mind alone, in their entirety they are mind. The mind has no this or that, the mind has no boundaries. Among the ten realms and ten thousand dharmas — whether dependent retribution or direct retribution, whether provisional name or real dharma — whichever single dharma one picks up, it is the whole substance of the mind and possesses the great function of the mind, pervading horizontally as the mind pervades and reaching vertically as the mind reaches. Because the meaning of mind-only is established, the meanings of color-only, sound-only, scent-only, flavor-only, touch-only, and dharma-only, and even dust-mote-only and mustard-seed-only, are all established. Only when all the meanings of “only” are established is the true meaning of mind-only fully accomplished. If all the meanings of “only” were not established, there would be only the empty name of mind-only and no true meaning of mind-only. Because all the meanings of “only” are established, it is said that dharmas have no fixed character, and whatever condition they meet becomes the tenet. If even dust-mote-only or mustard-seed-only can be a tenet, could Amitābha Buddha of the fruition ground, adorned with the eighty thousand marks of excellence, on the contrary not be a tenet? Therefore it takes Buddha-only as its tenet.
[Provisional name] A false name. All dharmas originally have no name; it is people who arbitrarily assign them a name.

[Again, it takes the absolute and perfectly interfused as its tenet. Among the ten realms and ten thousand dharmas, whichever single dharma one picks up is nothing but the whole substance of the mind. It possesses the mind’s great function, pervading the ten directions horizontally and reaching through the three periods vertically; it is free of the four propositions and cut off from the hundred negations. Alone as a single substance it is wholly true, with nothing further outside it. Filling all, pure, it admits nothing else within. Since one dharma is thus, all dharmas are so. Each is spoken of with regard to the dharma itself, absolute and without anything outside — this is the absolute.]

Again, the single phrase “Amitābha Buddha” takes the absolute and perfectly interfused as its tenet. Among the ten realms and ten thousand dharmas, whichever single dharma one picks up is nothing but the whole substance of the mind. It possesses the mind’s great function, pervading the ten directions horizontally and reaching through the three periods vertically, free of the four propositions and cut off from the hundred negations. Alone as this single substance it is wholly true, with nothing further outside it. Filling all, pure, it admits nothing else within. Since one dharma is thus, all dharmas are so as well. Each is spoken of with regard to the dharma itself, absolute and without anything outside — this is the absolute.

[Free of the four propositions, cut off from the hundred negations] “The four propositions and the hundred negations” is the phrase commonly used to wipe out living beings’ deluded and erroneous views of such dualities as existence and nonexistence, and to explain the principle that true emptiness is signless and unobtainable; the Chan school often uses it to receive and guide students. “The four propositions” usually refers to the four: existent, nonexistent, both existent and nonexistent, and neither existent nor nonexistent. “The hundred negations” means a hundred kinds of negation, “hundred” being a word of enumeration.

[Again, since the ten realms and ten thousand dharmas each mutually pervade and each mutually contain, each interwoven with each and each penetrating all, they are mutually without obstruction and without hindrance, each without destruction and without admixture. They are like many ancient mirrors set on their stands, reflecting images upon images. They are like the thousand pearls of Indra’s net
(the net of jewels hung in the palace of Indra)

, circling and interreflecting. This is spoken with regard to the dharmas mutually regarding one another, and it is perfect interfusion. Now we join the absolute and the perfectly interfused into one tenet: precisely when it is absolute it is perfectly interfused, and precisely when it is perfectly interfused it is absolute; it is not that apart from the absolute there is a separate perfect interfusion. The absolute is the absolute of that perfect interfusion — it is not that apart from perfect interfusion there is a separate absolute; perfect interfusion is the perfect interfusion of that absolute. The absolute and perfect interfusion are each inconceivable. Now that they are joined together into one tenet, it is the inconceivable within the inconceivable.]

Again, because the ten realms and ten thousand dharmas each mutually pervade and each mutually contain, each interwoven with each and each wholly penetrating, they are mutually without obstruction and without hindrance, each without destruction and without admixture. They are like many ancient mirrors facing one another, reflecting images upon images. They are like the thousand pearls of Indra’s net (the net of jewels hung in the palace of Indra), circling and interreflecting and mutually absorbing. This is spoken with regard to the dharmas mutually regarding one another, and it is perfect interfusion. Now joining the absolute and the perfectly interfused into one tenet: precisely when it is absolute it is perfectly interfused, and precisely when it is perfectly interfused it is absolute; it is not that apart from the absolute there is a separate perfect interfusion. The absolute is the absolute of that perfect interfusion — it is not that apart from perfect interfusion there is a separate absolute; perfect interfusion is the perfect interfusion of that absolute — it is not that apart from the absolute there is a separate perfect interfusion. The absolute and the perfectly interfused are each inconceivable. Now that they are joined together into one tenet, it is the inconceivable within the inconceivable.

[Again, it takes transcending emotion and cutting off views as its tenet. For if one speaks only of the dharmas as absolute — free of faults and cut off from the erroneous — this already transcends the deluded emotional attachments of all living beings and the differences seen by the sages and worthies of the three vehicles. If one speaks of the dharmas as perfectly interfused, then they perfectly encompass the four propositions and melt together the hundred negations, which is still less within the reach of ordinary emotions or sage views; therefore on the whole it establishes transcending emotion and cutting off views as its tenet.]

Again, the single phrase “Amitābha Buddha” takes transcending emotion and cutting off views as its tenet. For if one speaks only of the dharmas as absolute — free of faults and cut off from the erroneous — this already transcends the deluded emotional attachments of all living beings and the differences seen by the sages and worthies of the three vehicles. If one speaks of the dharmas as perfectly interfused, then they perfectly encompass the four propositions and melt together the hundred negations, which is still less within the reach of ordinary emotions or sage views; therefore on the whole it establishes transcending emotion and cutting off views as its tenet.

[First it takes mind-only as its tenet, next it takes Buddha-only as its tenet, third it takes the absolute and perfectly interfused as its tenet, and last it takes transcending emotion and cutting off views as its tenet. Only the sum of these four layers of tenets is the authentic tenet of the single phrase Amitābha — how easily spoken of!]

In all that has been discussed above, first it takes mind-only as its tenet, next it takes Buddha-only as its tenet, third it takes the absolute and perfectly interfused as its tenet, and last it takes transcending emotion and cutting off views as its tenet. Only the sum of these four layers of tenets is the authentic tenet of the single phrase Amitābha — how could it be attained merely by speaking of it!
[How easily spoken of] How could it be easy (to attain)! The phrase comes from the Book of Rites

the Record of Examples: “Confucius said: The plainness of Yu and Xia and the refinement of Yin and Zhou reached the utmost. The refinement of Yu and Xia did not surpass their plainness; the plainness of Yin and Zhou did not surpass their refinement. To hit the mean between plainness and refinement — how easily spoken of?”
[This single-recitation Buddha-recitation dharma-gate covers all as the sky covers all and upholds all as the earth upholds
(holds up from below)

, so that there is not one person or one dharma that can go outside it or fail to be within it. In the whole Avatamsaka Sutra, though there is the difference of the five cycles and the four divisions, the two words “cause and effect” encompass all without remainder. Of the causal minds of the forty-one stages
(the mind of the causal ground)
, there is not one mind that does not tend toward the fruition-enlightenment
(the enlightenment of the fruition ground)

. The various practices cultivated through the forty-one stages — are they not all Buddha-recitation practices? And at the end Samantabhadra, with the Ten Great Vows, guides them back to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, which is the great concluding focus of the whole sutra — is it not so?]

This single-recitation Buddha-recitation dharma-gate covers the four directions as the sky covers all and upholds all things as the earth upholds (holds up from below), so that there is not one person or one dharma that can go outside it or fail to be within it. In the whole Avatamsaka Sutra, though there is the difference of the five cycles and the four divisions, the two words “cause and effect” encompass all without remainder. Of the causal minds of the forty-one bodhisattva stages (the mind of the causal ground), there is not one mind that does not tend toward the fruition-enlightenment (the enlightenment of the fruition ground). The various practices cultivated by the bodhisattvas of the forty-one stages — are they not all Buddha-recitation practices? And at the end Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, with the Ten Great Vows, guides them back to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, which is the great concluding focus of the whole sutra — is it not so?

[The five cycles] That is, the five cycles of cause and effect: 1. the cause and effect of what is believed, 2. the cause and effect of differentiation, 3. the cause and effect of equality, 4. the cause and effect of accomplishing the practices, 5. the cause and effect of entering realization. [The four divisions] That is, “the four divisions of the Avatamsaka”, which judges the nine assemblies of the Avatamsaka Sutra as four divisions: 1. the division of faith, 2. the division of understanding, 3. the division of practice, 4. the division of realization. [The forty-one stages] The stages of the bodhisattva: the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, and equal enlightenment. [The Ten Great Vows] The ten vows of practice of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, namely: to worship and respect all Buddhas, to praise the Tathagatas, to cultivate offerings extensively, to repent of karmic obstacles, to rejoice in merit and virtue, to request the turning of the Dharma-wheel, to request the Buddhas to remain in the world, to follow the Buddhas in study always, to accord with living beings constantly, and to dedicate all merit universally. [Concluding focus] The geomancers say that where the earth’s vein suddenly halts and the terrain dips or rises, there the earthly qi gathers and congeals, and this is called a “concluding focus”; here it is used to illustrate the culminating point of a text.
[Again, “Avatamsaka” means adorning the one-vehicle Buddha-fruit with the causal flower of ten thousand practices
(the flower of the causal ground)

; are these ten thousand practices not the practice of Buddha-recitation? The Avatamsaka contains such measureless gates as the maiden Vasumitra, King Never-Satiated, and the Brahmin Druma of Fierce Heat, yet all of them display the realm of Vairocana — are these measureless gates not precisely the gate of Buddha-recitation? The whole Lotus Sutra, from beginning to end, is nothing but opening, showing, awakening to, and entering the Buddha’s knowledge and the Buddha’s view — is this not the single Buddha-recitation dharma-gate from first to last? The Surangama first reveals the treasury-nature
(the Tathagata-treasury nature)

, clarifying the true cause of becoming a Buddha. Next it selects the perfect penetration, showing the wonderful practice of becoming a Buddha. Afterward it passes through the sixty sage-stages, perfects bodhi, returns to nothing obtained, and realizes the ultimate fruit of the Buddha-ground. Turning away from this, one falls into the sinking of the seven destinies; turning toward it, one understands the disturbance of the five maras. At the end it says: “Suppose a person’s body has committed the four grave offenses and the ten parajikas, and in a flash he passes through the Avici hells of this land and other lands, until he has exhausted the ten directions and passed through every one without exception. If he can, in a single thought, take this dharma-gate and in the final kalpa
(the kalpa of the Dharma’s end)

reveal it to those who come after, this person’s karmic obstacles will be extinguished in that very thought. The causes of suffering he would have undergone in hell will be transformed into a land of peace and bliss.” This then is, from first to last and through and through, nothing but the single Buddha-recitation dharma-gate. In sum, through the Buddha’s teaching of one whole age, the three baskets and twelve divisions, the half and the full, the provisional and the real, the partial and the perfect, the sudden and the gradual, all these various dharma-gates are nothing but the revelation of mind-only self-nature and the perfect accomplishment of supreme wonderful enlightenment — are they not all one great Buddha-recitation dharma-gate?]

Again, the two words “Avatamsaka” mean adorning the one-vehicle Buddha-fruit with the causal flower of ten thousand practices (the flower of the causal ground); are these ten thousand practices not the practice of Buddha-recitation? In the Avatamsaka Sutra, such measureless dharma-gates as the maiden Vasumitra, King Never-Satiated, and the Brahmin Druma of Fierce Heat all display the realm of Vairocana — are these measureless dharma-gates not precisely the gate of Buddha-recitation? The Lotus Sutra, from beginning to end, is nothing but opening, showing, awakening to, and entering the Buddha’s knowledge and the Buddha’s view — is this not the single Buddha-recitation dharma-gate spoken from first to last? The Surangama Sutra first reveals the Tathagata-treasury nature, clarifying the true cause of becoming a Buddha. Next it selects the perfect-penetration dharma-gate, showing the wonderful practice of becoming a Buddha. Afterward it passes through the sixty sage-stages, perfects bodhi, returns to nothing obtained, and realizes the ultimate fruit of the Buddha-ground. Turning away from this, one falls into the sinking of the seven destinies; turning toward it, one understands the disturbance of the five maras. And at the end it says: “Suppose a person’s body has committed the four grave offenses and the ten parajikas, and in a flash he passes through the Avici hells of this land and other lands, until he has exhausted the ten directions and passed through every one without exception. If he can, in a single thought, take this dharma-gate and in the kalpa of the Dharma’s end reveal it to those who come after, this person’s karmic obstacles will be extinguished in that very thought. The causes of suffering he would have undergone in hell will be transformed into a land of peace and bliss.” This then is, from first to last and through and through, nothing but the single Buddha-recitation dharma-gate. Taking the whole of the Buddha’s teaching of one age, the three baskets and twelve divisions, the half and the full, the provisional and the real, the partial and the perfect, the sudden and the gradual, all these various dharma-gates are nothing but the revelation of mind-only self-nature and the perfect accomplishment of supreme wonderful enlightenment (Buddhahood) — are they not all one great Buddha-recitation dharma-gate?

[Vairocana] An abbreviation of Vairocana, the general name for the dharmakāya Buddha. [Selecting the perfect penetration] In the Surangama Sutra twenty-five great ones each, in answer to the Buddha’s question, set forth a dharma-gate of perfect penetration; the Buddha then had Bodhisattva Manjusri choose which was the easiest to accomplish. [The sixty sage-stages] To the fifty-five stages are added the three progressive stages and the stage of dry wisdom before them, and the stage of wonderful enlightenment after them, making sixty in all. [The three progressive stages] In the Surangama Sutra, the Buddha, wishing to speak of the stages of practice, first spoke of these three progressive stages as the foundation, because all the stages, though differing in depth, take these three as the basis of progress. The three progressive stages are: 1. removing the contributing cause, that is, eradicating the causes that aid living beings in evil, such as the five pungent vegetables — scallion, leek, garlic, onion, and asafoetida — which, when eaten, easily provoke lust and anger, cause one to be possessed by evil spirits, and make the gods and humans keep their distance; therefore the practitioner must first cut off these contributing causes of evil. 2. Hollowing out the proper nature: all evils such as stealing and lying arise from lust and killing, so living beings take the nature of lust and killing as their proper nature; one who wishes to cultivate bodhi must break through the nature of lust and killing and not allow it to be transgressed. 3. Turning away from present karma: one who cultivates bodhi, having cut off the five pungent vegetables and not transgressing against lust and killing, then turns away from and no longer engages the objects of the six sense-fields before him. [The fifty-five stages] The Surangama Sutra says: “The fifty-five stages are the true road to bodhi.” The fifty-five stages are: the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, and equal enlightenment, together with warmth, summit, patience, and the first in the world. [The seven destinies] The destiny of hell, the destiny of hungry ghosts, the destiny of animals, the destiny of humans, the destiny of immortals, the destiny of gods, and the destiny of asuras. “Destiny” means the direction toward which one tends. [The five maras] The maras of the five aggregates. The five aggregates are form, feeling, conception, volition, and consciousness; because these five, together with the afflictions, all delude people, they are called “maras”. [The four grave offenses] The four grave offenses: transgressing the precept against lust, transgressing the precept against stealing, transgressing the precept against killing, and transgressing the precept against great false speech. [The ten parajikas] The ten grave precepts: the precept against killing, the precept against stealing, the precept against lust, the precept against false speech, the precept against selling alcohol, the precept against speaking of the faults of the four assemblies, the precept against praising oneself and disparaging others, the precept against stinginess and reviling, the precept against anger and refusing to accept apology, and the precept against slandering the Three Jewels.
[As for the Chan school: when Master Bodhidharma
(Damo)

came from the West, if it were only a matter of seeing the nature, he need only have said “directly pointing to the human mind, seeing the nature, and that is all”; but since he said “directly pointing to the human mind, seeing the nature, and becoming a Buddha”, is the Chan gate not also the gate of Buddha-recitation? Therefore, taking together the two schools, the five houses, and the seventeen hundred koans, they are nothing but pointing out the original mind-nature of the person before you and revealing the inherently existing pure dharmakāya. The dharmakāya pervades horizontally and reaches vertically, and there is nowhere it does not pervade; and for the one who practices Chan, the essential thing is that the dharmakāya be present at every moment and correspond at every turn — where is this not the Buddha-recitation dharma-gate?]

Above we have spoken of the teaching gate as the Buddha-recitation dharma-gate; now let us consider the Chan school. When the Patriarch Bodhidharma (Damo) came from the West, if it were merely a matter of seeing the nature, then saying “directly pointing to the human mind, seeing the nature” would have sufficed; but since he said “directly pointing to the human mind, seeing the nature, and becoming a Buddha”, is the Chan gate not also the gate of Buddha-recitation? Therefore, taking together the two schools, the five houses, and the seventeen hundred koans, they are nothing but pointing out the original mind-nature of the person before you and revealing the inherently existing pure dharmakāya. The dharmakāya pervades horizontally and reaches vertically, and there is nowhere it does not pervade; and for the one who practices Chan, the essential thing is that the dharmakāya be present at every moment and correspond at every turn — where is this not the Buddha-recitation dharma-gate?

[The two schools and five houses] From the First Patriarch Bodhidharma, five transmissions reached the Fifth Patriarch Hongren; under Hongren there divided the Northern school of Shenxiu and the Southern school of Huineng. The Northern school flourished in the north, and in later ages had no subdivisions; the Southern school flourished in the south, and had the distinction of five houses and seven houses. The five houses are the Weiyang, Linji, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan houses; the seven houses add the Huanglong and Yangqi houses to these. [The seventeen hundred koans] The original meaning of “koan” is a case decided by an official in a government office. The Chan school recorded the words and deeds of the eminent monks of successive generations as instructions for those who sit in meditation, and in time these also became an object of thought and a motto for those who practice sitting meditation. Such records of words and deeds are like the official proclamations of a government — dignified and not to be violated — and they can also inspire thought, be studied by others, and serve as models for later generations to rely upon; hence they are called koans. This custom began in the Tang dynasty and flourished greatly in the Song. The total number of koans is generally reckoned at about seventeen hundred, though in fact there may not truly be seventeen hundred, and those commonly used number only about five hundred; the rest are either repetitions or of comparatively little value for investigation.

[As for such sayings as “the single word Buddha, I am not fond of hearing” and “a single blow to kill it and give it to the dog to eat” — these all reveal the supremely wonderful skillful means of the ascent above the dharmakāya, and are true Buddha-recitation. Often ignorant people say that those in the Chan gate should not recite the Buddha’s name. Such people not only do not know Buddha-recitation — do they truly know the Chan
(the Chan school)

? Not only are the Chan and the teaching gates like this: even in all the world, among scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants, among the hundred schools of thought, those who do not wish to recite the Buddha’s name and do not know the Buddha cannot escape outside the Buddha-recitation dharma-gate. For in their coming and going, their movement and stillness, they all follow this way, and the common people use it daily without knowing it. As it is said: The one breath speaks not, yet holds all forms within; where shall ten thousand spirits thank the selfless one? Peach blossoms line the road when wind and rain are done — no place for horse-hooves to escape the fallen red.]

As for Zhaozhou’s “the single word Buddha, I am not fond of hearing” and Chan Master Yunmen Wenyan’s “a single blow to kill it and give it to the dog to eat” — these all reveal the supremely wonderful skillful means of the matter of the ascent above the dharmakāya, and this is true Buddha-recitation. Often ignorant people say that those in the Chan gate should not recite the Buddha’s name. Such people not only do not know Buddha-recitation; how could they truly know the Chan gate? Not only are the Chan and teaching gates the Buddha-recitation dharma-gate: even in all the world, scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants, and the hundred schools of thought — even those who do not wish to recite the Buddha’s name and do not know the Buddha cannot escape outside the Buddha-recitation dharma-gate. For in their coming and going, their movement and stillness, they are all reciting the Buddha, yet they use it daily without knowing it. As it is said: The one breath speaks not, yet holds all forms within; where shall ten thousand spirits thank the selfless one? Peach blossoms line the road when wind and rain are done — no place for horse-hooves to escape the fallen red.

[As for such sayings as “the single word Buddha, I am not fond of hearing” and “a single blow to kill it and give it to the dog to eat”, which all reveal the supremely wonderful skillful means of the ascent above the dharmakāya and are true Buddha-recitation] “The ascent above the dharmakāya” is the state of breaking through the last of the three barriers of the Chan gate, the fortress barrier, transcending the dharmakāya. At this point Buddha-recitation is the recitation of the Buddha of true character. In the Sutra of the Buddha-Treasury, in “The Chapter on Buddha-Recitation, the Second” and “The Chapter on Dharma-Recitation, the Third”, the World-Honored One sets forth this principle in detail. For example, in “The Chapter on Buddha-Recitation, the Second” of the Sutra of the Buddha-Treasury, the Buddha says: “Sariputra, what is called Buddha-recitation? To see nothing whatsoever is called Buddha-recitation. Sariputra, the Buddhas are measureless, inconceivable, and immeasurable; for this reason, to see nothing whatsoever is called Buddha-recitation. The real is without discrimination, and the Buddhas are without discrimination; therefore it is said that to be mindful without discrimination is precisely Buddha-recitation.” [The one breath speaks not, yet holds all forms within; where shall ten thousand spirits thank the selfless one? Peach blossoms line the road when wind and rain are done — no place for horse-hooves to escape the fallen red] The one breath (referring to the primal qi, which the ancients held to be the origin constituting heaven, earth, and all things) speaks not, yet holds all forms (the myriad phenomena); where shall the ten thousand spirits (living beings) thank the selfless one (the Buddha)? Peach blossoms line the road when wind and rain are done — no place for horse-hooves to escape the fallen red (these last two lines say that the dharmakāya, in the case of every person, is inherently complete and present, not a hair’s breadth removed, and everywhere). This verse restates with poetic feeling and pictorial imagery: “This single-recitation Buddha-recitation dharma-gate covers all as the sky covers all and upholds all as the earth upholds, so that there is not one person or one dharma that can go outside it or fail to be within it.” And: “Not only are the Chan and teaching gates like this: even in all the world, scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants, and the hundred schools of thought — even those who do not wish to recite the Buddha’s name and do not know the Buddha cannot escape outside the Buddha-recitation dharma-gate.”
