Note: “The one breath speaks not, yet holds all forms within; where shall ten thousand spirits thank the selfless one?” is quoted rather often in the recorded sayings of the Chan school. It comes from “Reflections in Mid-Spring” by the poet-monk Qiji of the late Five Dynasties in the Tang. The whole poem reads: “Spring wind each day, rain hour by hour; the cold’s force secretly yields as warmth gains power. The one breath speaks not, yet holds all forms within; where shall ten thousand spirits thank the selfless one? When poetry reaches the nature of things, its practice may be gathered up; when the Way accords with heaven’s mechanism, one may glimpse it in sitting. Truly it must be a right man who holds creation’s power, driving every hidden subtlety into the forge and hammer.”

[1. Taking true deliverance from birth and death as the aim and arousing the bodhi-mind is the common road of those who learn the Way. 2. Holding the Buddha’s name with deep faith and vows is the authentic practice of the Pure Land. 3. Reciting with a collected and focused mind is the point of entry. 4. Subduing the afflictions presently active is the essential task of cultivating the mind. 5. Firmly upholding the four grave precepts is the root of entering the Way. 6. Various ascetic practices are the contributing conditions of cultivating the Way. 7. Single-mindedness without distraction is the final home of the purified mind. 8. Various auspicious signs are the verification of rebirth. These eight matters should each be expounded earnestly; those who cultivate the pure karma must not fail to know them.]

[Authentic practice] The teaching that is authentically transmitted. [The four grave precepts] The precept against lust, the precept against stealing, the precept against killing, and the precept against great false speech.

blocks.text: 26. A Single Thought of True Faith

inline.s: [The reason living beings revolve in samsara is the six paths. Living beings of the other destinies are obstructed by fear and anger, by suffering and by pleasure, and have no leisure to turn toward the Way; to be able to order the mind and its concerns and tend toward bodhi — this only the human path can do. But those who lose the human body are as numerous as the soil of the great earth, and those who gain the human body are as few as the soil beneath a fingernail — is the human body easy to obtain? For living beings of the human path, from birth to maturity and on to old age and death, what the eyes see and the ears hear is nothing but the world’s dust and toil, the karmic conditions of birth and death — is the Buddha-Dharma easy to hear? It is already hard to gain the human body, and harder still to gain a man’s body with the six senses complete. It is already hard to hear the Buddha-Dharma, and harder still to hear the name of Amitābha and the Pure Land dharma-gate. How fortunate to have gained the human body that is hard to gain, how fortunate to hear the Buddha-Dharma that is hard to hear! And having heard it, still to refuse to believe — is this not deeply to be regretted?]

The place where living beings revolve in samsara is within the six paths. Of the five paths of living beings other than the human path, the animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings are obstructed by fear and suffering, the asuras by anger, and the gods by pleasure, and none of them has leisure to turn toward the Way. To be able to order the mind and its concerns and tend toward bodhi — only the human path can do this. But as the Buddha said: “Those who lose the human body are as numerous as the soil of the great earth; those who gain the human body are as few as the soil beneath a fingernail.” Is the human body so easily obtained? For living beings of the human path, from birth to maturity and on to old age and death, what the eyes see and the ears hear is nothing but the world’s dust and toil, the karmic conditions of birth and death — is the Buddha-Dharma so easily heard? It is already hard to gain the human body, and harder still to gain a man’s body with the six senses complete. It is already hard to hear the Buddha-Dharma, and still harder to hear the name of Amitābha and the Pure Land dharma-gate. How fortunate to have gained the human body that is hard to gain, how fortunate to hear the Buddha-Dharma that is hard to hear, how fortunate to hear the Pure Land dharma-gate that is especially hard to hear! And having heard it, still to refuse to believe — this is truly too much to be regretted!

[As for those who do not believe, let that be set aside. Even among those who believe: to believe but not to vow is still not to believe. To vow but not to practice is still not to vow. To practice but not vigorously is still not to practice. The reason practice is not vigorous is that the vow is not earnest. The reason the vow is not earnest is that the faith is not true. In short, to give rise to true faith is hard. If faith is truly there, the vow will of itself be earnest. If the vow is truly earnest, the practice will of itself be vigorous. With true and earnest faith and vows, together with brave and vigorous practice, one will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land, certainly see Amitābha, certainly attain the three non-retrogressions, and certainly reach the stage of being one lifetime from Buddhahood.]

Those who do not believe in the Pure Land dharma-gate, let us for the moment set aside and not speak of them. Even among those who do believe in the Pure Land dharma-gate: to believe but not to vow is as if not to believe. To vow but not to practice is as if not to vow. To practice but not vigorously is as if not to practice. The reason practice is not vigorous is that the vow is not earnest. The reason the vow is not earnest is that the faith is not true. In short, to give rise to true faith is hard. If faith is truly there, the vow will of itself be earnest. If the vow is truly earnest, the practice will of itself be vigorous. With true and earnest faith and vows, together with brave and vigorous practice, one will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land, certainly see Amitābha, certainly attain the three non-retrogressions, and certainly reach the stage of being one lifetime from Buddhahood.

[Once reborn in the Pure Land, the root of the karma of birth and death from vast kalpas past is forever cut off. Once one lifetime from Buddhahood, the utmost honored and supreme wonderful enlightenment is fully accomplished. What a single thought of true faith brings about — is it slight? If one’s obstructive conditions were not thin, one’s karma of birth and death not light, one’s good roots not long planted, one’s past causes not deep and thick, how could one be like this? Yet the weight of our karma and the depth of our good roots over measureless kalpas are all things we cannot know. But karma is transformed by the mind, and good roots are cultivated by the person. Therefore those who propagate the Dharma cannot but use skillful means and earnestly instruct; and those who learn the Way cannot but strive with all their might and press bravely forward. If but a single word enters the ear and a single thought stirs the mind, one can transform karma and cultivate good roots. Though one hears all kinds of urgent instruction and not a single word enters, though one meets all kinds of adverse and favorable conditions and not a single thought is roused — that is truly one whose karma is heavy and whose good roots are slight and few, and there is nothing to be done for such a person.]

Once reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, the root of the karma of birth and death from beginningless kalpas is forever cut off. Once one lifetime from Buddhahood, the utmost honored and supreme wonderful enlightenment is fully accomplished. What a single thought of true faith brings about — how great it is! If one’s obstructive conditions were not thin, one’s karma of birth and death not light, one’s good roots not long planted, one’s past causes not deep and thick, how could one be like this? Yet the weight of our karma and the depth of our good roots over measureless kalpas are all things we cannot know. But karma is transformed by the mind, and good roots are cultivated by the person. Therefore those who propagate the Dharma cannot but use skillful means and earnestly instruct; and those who learn the Way cannot but strive with all their might and press bravely forward. If but a single word is taken in and a single thought stirs one’s own mind, one can transform karma and cultivate good roots. Though one hears all kinds of urgent instruction and not one word is taken in, though one meets all kinds of adverse and favorable conditions and never once rouses a thought — that is truly one whose karma is heavy and whose good roots are slight and few, and there is nothing I can do for such a person.
[Vast kalpas] A very distant past is called “vast kalpas”; a very distant future is called “eternal kalpas”.

[The single thought of the present mind-nature is originally of one substance with the Buddha. The Buddha awakened long ago, while I am still deluded. Though the Buddha is already awakened, there is nothing added. Though I am still deluded, there is nothing subtracted. Though nothing is added to the Buddha, because he accords with the nature he enjoys great Dharma-bliss. Though nothing is subtracted from me, because I turn my back on the nature I undergo extreme suffering. Within the mind-nature of one substance, the Buddha, though he enjoys Dharma-bliss, with the great compassion of one body and the unconditioned great loving-kindness, remembers me in every thought and gathers and transforms me in every thought. Within the mind-nature of one substance, I, though I undergo all suffering, do not know to look up and seek the Buddha, do not know to remember the Buddha, but only pursue objects and give rise to thoughts, following my feelings and creating karma. Through vast kalpas, the five deadly sins and the ten evil deeds, all kinds of heavy karma — what have I not created? The three evil paths and the eight difficulties, all kinds of great suffering — what have I not undergone? To speak of it brings shame; to think of it brings terror. If from now on I still do not recite the Buddha’s name, but as before bury my head and create all kinds of karma, and as before undergo all kinds of suffering from the beginning — should I not be ashamed? Should I not be afraid?]

The substance of the single thought of the present mind is originally the same as the Buddha’s mind-substance. The Buddha awakened long ago, while I am still deluded. Though the Buddha is already awakened, this mind-substance has nothing added. Though I am still deluded, this mind-substance has nothing subtracted. Though nothing is added to the Buddha’s mind-substance, because he follows the nature he enjoys great Dharma-bliss. Though nothing is subtracted from my mind-substance, because I turn my back on the nature I undergo extreme suffering. Within the mind-substance that is the same, the Buddha, though he enjoys Dharma-bliss, with the great compassion of one body and the unconditioned great loving-kindness, remembers me in every thought and gathers and transforms me in every thought. Within the mind-substance that is the same, I, though I undergo all suffering, do not know to look up and seek the Buddha, do not know to remember the Buddha, but only pursue objects and give rise to thoughts, following my feelings and creating karma. From beginningless kalpas, the five deadly sins and the ten evil deeds, all kinds of heavy karma — what have I not created? The three evil paths (hell, hungry ghosts, and animals) and the eight difficulties, all kinds of great suffering — what have I not undergone? To speak of it brings shame; to think of it brings terror. If from now on I still do not recite the Buddha’s name, but as before bury my head and create all kinds of karma, and as before undergo all kinds of suffering from the beginning — should I not be ashamed? Should I not be afraid?

[Mind-nature] The eternally unchanging mind-substance, that is, the Tathagata-treasury. [The eight difficulties] Eight places and circumstances in which one is hindered from seeing and hearing the Buddha-Dharma, namely: hell, hungry ghosts, animals, the northern continent of Uttarakuru, the heaven of no thought, being blind, deaf, or mute, being clever in worldly wisdom and eloquent in debate, and being before the Buddha or after the Buddha.

[Now that we know the Buddha, with great loving-kindness and great compassion, remembers and gathers and transforms us in every thought, then I, deeply moved by the Buddha’s kindness, should recite the Buddha’s name. Having all along through long kalpas suffered all kinds of suffering to no purpose, and wishing to be free of suffering, I should recite the Buddha’s name. The karma already created cannot be helped, but can future karma be created again? Giving rise to a mind of shame, I should recite the Buddha’s name. The mind-nature of one body, since it is said to be inherent, how could it be absent today? It is only that awakening and realization are still lacking. Seeking to awaken to the mind-nature, I should recite the Buddha’s name.]

Now that we know the Buddha, with great loving-kindness and great compassion, remembers and gathers and transforms us in every thought, then I, deeply moved by the Buddha’s kindness, should therefore recite the Buddha’s name. Having all along through long kalpas suffered all kinds of suffering to no purpose, and now wishing to be free of suffering, I should therefore recite the Buddha’s name. The karma already created cannot be helped, but can future karma be created again? Giving rise to a mind of shame, I should therefore recite the Buddha’s name. The mind-nature of one body, since it is said to be inherent, how could it be absent today? It is only that awakening and realization are still lacking. Seeking to awaken to the mind-nature, I should therefore recite the Buddha’s name.

[Reciting the Buddha’s name with a mind seeking awakening, one’s recitation will surely be earnest. Reciting with a mind of shame, one’s recitation will surely be earnest. Reciting with a mind that fears suffering, one’s recitation will surely be earnest. Reciting with a mind of gratitude, one’s recitation will surely be earnest. I do not recite the Buddha’s name, yet the Buddha still remembers me; now that I recite earnestly, the Buddha will surely remember me all the more. Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta says: “The Buddhas of the ten directions pity and remember living beings as a mother remembers her child. If the child runs away, what use is her remembering? But if the child remembers the mother as the mother remembers the child, then mother and child through life after life will not be far apart. If the minds of living beings remember the Buddha and recite the Buddha’s name, then now or in the future they will certainly see the Buddha and not be far from the Buddha. Without resort to other means, the mind will of itself open.” This is the state personally realized and actually attained by the Great One, told out with heart and entrails laid bare.]

Reciting the Buddha’s name with a mind seeking awakening, one’s recitation will surely be earnest. Reciting with a mind of shame, one’s recitation will surely be earnest. Reciting with a mind that fears suffering, one’s recitation will surely be earnest. Reciting with a mind of gratitude, one’s recitation will surely be earnest. I do not recite the Buddha’s name, yet the Buddha still remembers me; now that I recite earnestly, the Buddha will surely remember me all the more. Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta says: “The Buddhas of the ten directions pity and remember living beings as a mother remembers her child. If the child runs away, what use is her remembering? But if the child remembers the mother as the mother remembers the child, then mother and child through life after life will not be far apart. If the minds of living beings remember the Buddha and recite the Buddha’s name, then now or in the future they will certainly see the Buddha and not be far from the Buddha. Without resort to other means, the mind will of itself open.” This is the state personally realized and actually attained by the Great One, the words with which he told it out with heart and entrails laid bare.

[Now I recite the Buddha’s name, and I will certainly see the Buddha. Once I see the Buddha, I will be free of all suffering, and awakening will be within reach. If I truly awaken, I can in one stroke wash away all my past shame. Can the Buddha then go unrecited?]

Now I recite the Buddha’s name, and I will certainly see the Buddha. Once I see the Buddha, I will be free of all suffering, and awakening will be within reach. If I truly attain awakening, I can at once thoroughly wash away all my past shame. Can the Buddha then still go unrecited?

[All living beings are originally Buddhas. The true mind is inherently existent; the false nature is originally empty. All wholesome dharmas are inherently complete in the nature. It is only because for so long one has followed the conditions of delusion and defilement that one has not cut off the originally empty false and has not realized the inherently existent true. The good is inherently complete but not cultivated; the Buddha is originally so but not accomplished. Now, wishing to cut off the originally empty false, realize the inherently existent true, cultivate the inherently complete good, and accomplish the originally so Buddha — and following the conditions of awakening and purity — if one seeks what is most direct and delightful, utterly sudden and utterly perfect, there is nothing like the single practice of reciting the name.]

All living beings are originally Buddhas. The true mind is inherently existent, and the false nature is originally empty. All wholesome dharmas are inherently complete in the self-nature. It is only because for so long one has followed the conditions of delusion and defilement that one has not cut off the originally empty false and has not realized the inherently existent true. The good is inherently complete but not cultivated; the Buddha is originally so but not accomplished. Now, wishing to cut off the originally empty false, realize the inherently existent true, cultivate the inherently complete good, and accomplish the originally so Buddha — and following the conditions of awakening and purity — if one seeks what is most direct and delightful, utterly sudden and utterly perfect, there is nothing beyond the single practice of reciting the name.

[Because the mind that recites is originally wholly true become false and wholly false is just true. The Buddha recited is likewise originally the whole virtue establishing the name, and the whole name is the virtue. Outside the reciting mind there is no separate Buddha recited; outside the Buddha recited there is no separate reciting mind. Reciting and recited both forgotten, mind and Buddha are one suchness. In every thought one perfectly subdues and perfectly cuts off the five abiding afflictions, perfectly turns and perfectly extinguishes the three defiled obstructions, perfectly breaks the five aggregates, perfectly transcends the five turbidities, perfectly purifies the four lands, perfectly recites the three bodies, perfectly cultivates the ten thousand practices, perfectly realizes the original truth, and perfectly accomplishes supreme wonderful enlightenment.]

Because the mind that recites is originally wholly true become false and wholly false is just true. The Buddha recited is likewise originally the whole virtue establishing the name, and the whole name is the virtue. Outside the reciting mind there is no separate Buddha recited; outside the Buddha recited there is no separate reciting mind. Reciting and recited both forgotten, mind and Buddha are one suchness. In every thought one perfectly subdues and perfectly cuts off the five abiding afflictions, perfectly turns and perfectly extinguishes the three defiled obstructions, perfectly breaks the five aggregates (form, feeling, conception, volition, and consciousness), perfectly transcends the five turbidities, perfectly purifies the four lands (the land of common residence of ordinary beings and sages, the land of expedient remainder, the land of true reward adornment, and the land of eternal quiet light), perfectly recites the three bodies (dharmakāya, reward body, and response body), perfectly cultivates the ten thousand practices, perfectly realizes the original truth, and perfectly accomplishes supreme wonderful enlightenment (Buddhahood).

[The whole virtue establishes the name, the whole name is the virtue] The Buddha’s name is established by the whole of the Buddha’s virtue; therefore the entire Buddha’s name is the Buddha’s virtue, and so in reciting the Buddha’s name one possesses the Buddha’s virtue — “Therefore, when you and others think of the Buddha, that mind is itself the thirty-two marks and the eighty secondary characteristics. This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha.” (The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life) [The five abiding afflictions] Also called “the five abiding delusions”: the view-delusion of the three realms is one abiding; the thought-delusion of the three realms is divided into three abidings (the abiding delusion of desire-craving, the abiding delusion of form-craving, and the abiding delusion of existence-craving); fundamental ignorance is one abiding. Because of these five delusions living beings abide attached to birth and death, hence they are called “abiding places”. The three realms are the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the realm of formlessness. Fundamental ignorance can give rise to the two delusions of view and thought, hence it is called fundamental. [The three defilements] Delusion, karma, and suffering. Living beings create karma through delusion, suffer because of karma, and because of suffering become deluded and create karma again — an unceasing vicious circle. This is the cause and effect of the continuation of birth and death. [The five turbidities] The Buddhas use the five turbidities to explain the turbidity and evil of the world: 1. the turbidity of the kalpa — the age meets with evil fortune and disasters arise repeatedly; 2. the turbidity of afflictions — people’s minds are filled with such afflictions as greed, anger, and delusion; 3. the turbidity of living beings — living beings are of inferior capacity, with much suffering and little joy; 4. the turbidity of views — false views prevail and thought is confused; 5. the turbidity of lifespan — living beings, receiving retribution for evil karma, are worn out in body and mind and their lifespan is short.
[One thought is thus, and every thought is so.
But so long as thought succeeds thought without interruption

, the subduing, the severing, the cultivating, and the realizing that result cannot be conceived or spoken of. With the mind of the whole Buddha one recites the Buddha of the whole mind, and truly there is the entire awesome virtue and spiritual power of the fruition-Buddha of one’s own mind, secretly perfuming and blessing one.
A single recitation of the Buddha’s name, free of all other conditions; when the ten recitations are perfected, one instantly transcends many kalpas.
To disbelieve this is truly to be wood and stone. To abandon this and cultivate something else is either madness or folly. What more is there to say! What more is there to say!]

One thought is thus, and every thought is so. So long as one can recite in this way, with thought succeeding thought without interruption, then the subduing of affliction, the cutting off of affliction, the cultivating, and the realizing will bring about an inconceivable efficacy. With the mind of the whole Buddha one recites the Buddha of the whole mind, and there is the entire awesome virtue and spiritual power of the fruition-Buddha of one’s own mind, secretly perfuming and blessing one. A single recitation of the Buddha’s name, unmixed with deluded thoughts; when the ten recitations at the end of life are perfected and continuous, one instantly transcends the birth and death and bitter cultivation of many kalpas. If one still does not believe even this, one is truly as dull as wood and stone. To abandon this Buddha-recitation and cultivate something else is either madness or folly. To such a person, what more is there to say! What more is there to say!

[Other conditions] The mind roving after other matters — idle thinking. [When the ten recitations are perfected] The ten thoughts at the end of life succeeding one another and being accomplished. This is the condition for rebirth — ten thoughts succeeding one another at the end of life. That is to say, if only at the moment of death the thoughts of Buddha-recitation continue for ten thoughts without interruption by deluded thoughts, then one is in mutual interchange of stimulus and response with Amitābha Buddha, and is received and guided by the Buddha and reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. (See in full
“The Conditions for Rebirth”

) [Successive] The thoughts of Buddha-recitation linked one to the next, not interrupted by deluded thoughts. [Mutual interchange of stimulus and response] The stimulus of living beings and the response of Amitābha Buddha mutually communicating.
[Question: All directions have their Pure Lands; why do you praise the West alone and seek rebirth there?]
Question: The worlds of the ten directions all have Pure Lands; why does one praise the Western Pure Land alone and vow to be reborn there?

[Answer: This is not the intention of the human teachers. It is because the golden-mouthed, truthful words clearly point it out; because the Mahayana sutras, exoteric and esoteric, all alike direct their return there; because it lets the beginner focus on a single object and thus easily accomplish samādhi; because the forty-eight vows are the condition, and the condition is strong; because the ten thoughts are the cause, and the cause is supreme; because the Buddha and living beings have a special connection.]

Answer: The reason one praises the Western Pure Land and vows to be reborn there is that this is not the patriarchs’ and great masters’ own idea, but because it is the truthful word of Śākyamuni Buddha’s golden mouth, clearly pointing the way; because the Mahayana sutras, exoteric and esoteric, all alike direct their return there; because it lets the beginner focus on a single object and thus easily accomplish samādhi; because the forty-eight great vows are the condition, and the condition is strong; because the ten thoughts continuous at the end of life are the cause, and the cause is supreme; because Amitābha Buddha and living beings have a special connection.

[The ten thoughts as cause] The “ten thoughts” here are the ten thoughts at the end of life “unmixed with other conditions” spoken of above, that is, the ten thoughts at the end of life that are continuous (unmixed with deluded thoughts).
Ten thoughts continuous at the end of life can bring an end to birth and death.
See in full
“The Conditions for Rebirth”

[Living beings of this land, whether monastic or lay, man or woman, old or young, good or evil — when they are in circumstances of extreme favor or adversity, of extreme suffering or extreme joy, most often it rises up from within and bursts from the mouth as a single recitation of the Buddha’s name. And if they do not recite, well and good; but whenever they do recite, they always recite Amitābha Buddha. Who makes it so? It is because living beings have long been transformed by the Buddha and have long received the Buddha’s kindness, and so their connection with the Buddha is deep.]

Living beings of this land (the Sahā world), whether monastic or lay, man or woman, old or young, good or evil — when they are in circumstances of extreme favor, extreme adversity, extreme suffering, or extreme joy, most often it rises up from the mind and bursts from the mouth as a single recitation of the Buddha’s name. And if they do not recite, well and good; but whenever they do recite, they always recite Amitābha Buddha. Who makes them do so? It is because living beings have long been transformed by Amitābha Buddha’s teaching and have long received Amitābha Buddha’s kindness, and so their connection with Amitābha Buddha is especially deep.

[Moreover, this Amitābha Sutra was first translated by Kumarajiva. The founding patriarch of the East Forest, Huiyuan, at once formed a society with one hundred and twenty-three people to recite the Buddha’s name. These one hundred and twenty-three people passed away one after another, and all left auspicious signs at the end of life. Even the parrot Baba’er recited the Buddha’s name, and at its passing there were auspicious signs. If this is not a deep connection between living beings and the Buddha, what is it? Again, the Sutra of Immeasurable Life says: When in the future the scriptures and the Way are utterly extinguished, by the power of my vow I will specially preserve this sutra to remain a further hundred years, to deliver living beings far and wide. Now to preserve not other sutras but this sutra alone — is it not because this dharma-gate is easy to take up and gathers all capacities, and because entering the Way is secure and the benefit gained is swift? From this we know that the later the age, the more this dharma fits the capacities of beings.]

Moreover, this Sutra of Amitābha Buddha was only just translated by the Great Master Kumarajiva when the founding patriarch Huiyuan of the East Forest Temple at once formed a society with one hundred and twenty-three people to recite the Buddha’s name. These one hundred and twenty-three people passed away one after another, and all left auspicious signs at the end of life. Even the parrot Baba’er, though an animal, recited the Buddha’s name, and at its passing there were also auspicious signs. If this is not a deep connection between living beings and Amitābha Buddha, what else could it be? Again, the Sutra of Immeasurable Life says: “When in the future the scriptures and the Way are utterly extinguished, by the power of my vow I will specially preserve this sutra to remain a further hundred years, to deliver living beings far and wide.” Why preserve not other sutras but this sutra alone? Is it not because the Buddha-recitation dharma-gate is easy to take up and gathers all capacities, and because entering the Way is secure and the benefit gained is swift? From this we know that the further the ages go, the more this Buddha-recitation dharma-gate fits the capacities of beings.

[Even the parrot Baba’er recited the Buddha’s name, and at its passing there were auspicious signs] Someone kept a parrot named Baba’er. It saw monks reciting the Buddha’s name and recited along with them, and so this person gave it to a monk. The monk often taught it to recite Amitābha Buddha. Later Baba’er died, and the monk made a small coffin and buried it. A lotus flower grew on the grave, and so the coffin was opened to look, and it was found that the root of the lotus grew out of Baba’er’s beak.

blocks.text: 29. Holding Firm to a Single Thought

inline.s: [Living beings in the world, when they are in the midst of urgent danger and suffering, howl for their parents and cry out to heaven and earth. They do not know that parents, other people, and heavenly kings cannot save me from birth and death or end my samsara, because they too are together in birth and death and samsara. The sages of the two vehicles, though they have escaped birth and death, have no great compassionate mind and are of no benefit to me. The bodhisattvas, though they have a mind of great loving-kindness and compassion, have each their own limit to what they have realized, and cannot universally benefit living beings and fulfill every vow. The Buddhas of the ten directions, though they have all perfectly realized the dharma-realm, are not easily stirred by me; and even if stirred to the utmost and seen, it is no more than a temporary escape from suffering, and in the end not ultimate. Only Amitābha Buddha: once seen, one instantly escapes birth and death and forever cuts off the root of suffering. It is this single phrase, Amitābha Buddha, that we should recite with all our hearts and all our strength.]

Living beings in the world, whenever they are in the midst of urgent danger and suffering, howl for their parents and cry out to heaven and earth. They do not know that parents, other people, and heavenly kings cannot save me from birth and death or deliver me from samsara, because they too are together in birth and death and samsara. The sages of the two vehicles, though they have escaped birth and death, have no great compassionate mind of universal deliverance, and so are of no benefit to me. The bodhisattvas, though they have a mind of great loving-kindness and compassion, have each their own limit to what they have realized, and cannot universally benefit all living beings and fulfill all their vows. The Buddhas of the ten directions, though they have all perfectly realized the dharma-realm without limit, are not easily stirred by me; and even if stirred to the utmost and seen, it is no more than a temporary escape from suffering, and in the end not ultimate. Only Amitābha Buddha: once seen, one instantly escapes birth and death and forever cuts off the root of suffering. From this we know that it is this single phrase, Amitābha Buddha, that we should remember with all our hearts and all our strength!

[I once had a verse that ran: “In all the world and beyond the world my thoughts have wandered through, and if I do not call Amitābha to mind, whose name should I call instead?” Yet Buddha-recitation is not difficult; what is difficult is to keep it up long and firm. If one can truly hold to this one thought, like raw iron cast, like wrought steel forged, like a single man withstanding ten thousand foes — then a thousand sages cannot hold one back, and ten thousand oxen cannot drag one around. Persevere in this way for long, and one will surely reach a sympathetic response. But if one cannot apply the mind in this way, and then declares that the Buddha's words do not come true and that the Buddha's mind is hard to move — how could that possibly be right? Only gain a response in a single thought, and one at once escapes birth and death, ascends straight to the stage of non-retrogression, and steadily accomplishes the fruit of Buddhahood. How could that be called an easy thing!]

I once had a verse that ran: “In all the world and beyond the world my thoughts have wandered through, and if I do not call Amitābha to mind, whose name should I call instead?” Yet Buddha-recitation is not difficult; what is difficult is to keep it up long and firm. If one can truly hold to this one thought, like raw iron cast, like wrought steel forged, like a single man withstanding ten thousand foes — then a thousand sages cannot hold one back, and ten thousand oxen cannot drag one around. Persevere in this way for long, and one will surely reach a sympathetic response. But if one cannot apply the mind in this way, and then declares that the Buddha's words do not come true and that the Buddha's mind is hard to move — how could that possibly be right? Only gain a response in a single thought, and one at once escapes birth and death, ascends straight to the stage of non-retrogression, and steadily accomplishes the fruit of Buddhahood. How could that be called an easy thing! — Therefore Buddha-recitation absolutely requires bitter effort, held without remission.

[Knowing what is small but not what is great, seeing what is near but not what is far — this is the common lot of sentient beings. Thus Amitābha Buddha has shown great grace and virtue toward all sentient beings, yet sentient beings do not know it. Countless kalpas ago, in the presence of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, the Buddha made forty-eight great vows on behalf of all the suffering beings of evil worlds. In accord with those vows he practiced the Bodhisattva path through long kalpas. He gave away the position of a golden wheel-turning king, his kingdom and cities, his wife and children, his head, his eyes, his marrow — countless thousands of millions of billions of times. Yet this was but one practice among the myriad practices: the giving of inner and outer wealth. In this way he endured what others cannot endure and did what others cannot do, perfecting the myriad practices. When his power was complete and his merit pure, he adorned and accomplished the Pure Land and attained Buddhahood of himself. Then he manifested countless transformation bodies to receive and guide sentient beings, drawing them in with skillful means and causing them to be born in that land.]

Knowing what is small but not what is great, seeing what is near but not what is far — this is the common condition of sentient beings. Amitābha Buddha, for example, has shown great grace and virtue toward all sentient beings, yet sentient beings do not know it. Countless kalpas ago, in the presence of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, Amitābha Buddha made forty-eight great vows on behalf of all the suffering beings of evil worlds. Then, in accord with those vows, he practiced the Bodhisattva path through long kalpas. He gave away the position of a golden wheel-turning king, his kingdom and cities, his wife and children, his head, his eyes, his marrow — countless thousands of millions of billions of times. Yet this was but one practice among the myriad practices: the giving of inner and outer wealth. In this way he endured what others cannot endure and did what others cannot do, perfecting the myriad practices. When his power was complete and his merit pure, he adorned and accomplished the Pure Land and realized the fruit of Buddhahood himself. Thereupon he manifested countless transformation bodies to receive and guide sentient beings, drawing them in with skillful means and causing them to be born in that land.

[Yet if it is thus for one person, it is thus for many; if it is thus for many, it is thus for one. Viewed in terms of the many, the Buddha works universally for all sentient beings. Viewed in terms of the one, the Buddha works solely for me alone. The vow that accords with the nature was made for me; the long kalpas of great practice were cultivated for me; the four lands were adorned and purified for me; the three bodies were perfected for me; and so too, wherever he appears to receive and guide beings, and wherever auspicious signs appear — all of it is for me.]

Now, if it is thus for one person, it is thus for many; if it is thus for many, it is thus for one. Viewed in terms of the many, the Buddha works universally for all sentient beings. Viewed in terms of the one, the Buddha works solely for me alone. The vow that accords with the nature was made for me; the long kalpas of great practice were cultivated for me; the four lands were adorned and purified for me; the three bodies were perfected for me; and so too, wherever he appears to receive and guide beings, and wherever auspicious signs appear — all of it is for me.

[When I create karma, the Buddha alerts me. When I suffer, the Buddha rescues me. When I take refuge, the Buddha receives me. When I cultivate, the Buddha empowers me. Everything the Buddha does for me in all these ways is only that I may recite his name, that I may be reborn in the Pure Land, that I may escape all suffering forever and receive the Dharma's bliss in full, that I may transform and save all beings everywhere, until I reach the stage of one lifetime from Buddhahood — and only then rest. Ah! The Buddha's profound grace and weighty virtue cannot be compared to that of parents; even heaven and earth cannot represent its height and breadth. Without hearing the teaching unfolded, how could one know this meaning? Without reading the Buddhist scriptures, how could one understand this principle? From this day forward, I know it. There is nothing else to do but strive with all my might, cultivate with utmost diligence, repay his grace with wholehearted devotion, and recite the Buddha's name with all my strength. What more is there to say!]

When I create karma, the Buddha alerts me. When I suffer, the Buddha rescues me. When I take refuge, the Buddha receives me. When I cultivate, the Buddha empowers me. Everything the Buddha does for me in all these ways is only that I may recite his name, that I may be reborn in the Pure Land, that I may escape all suffering forever and receive the Dharma's bliss in full! It is that I may transform and save all beings everywhere, until I reach the stage of one lifetime from Buddhahood! Ah! The Buddha's profound grace and weighty virtue cannot be compared to that of parents; even heaven and earth cannot represent its height and breadth! Without hearing the teaching unfolded, how could one know these things? Without reading the Buddhist scriptures, how could one understand this principle? From this day forward, I know them all. There is nothing else to do but strive with all my might, cultivate with utmost diligence, repay his grace with wholehearted devotion, and recite the Buddha's name with all my strength — only thus can I repay Amitābha Buddha's profound grace and weighty virtue!

[All sentient beings are driven by the ten fetters, sharp and dull, and through long kalpas revolve in birth and death, enduring great suffering and unable to escape. How pitiable! What are the ten fetters? They are self-view, extreme view, wrong view, attachment to views, and attachment to precepts — these five are the sharp fetters, because they are light and quick to stir; and greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt — these five are the dull fetters, arising from the sharp fetters, and called dull in contrast to the sharp. Of these ten fetters, every sentient being has more or less, each with his own particular emphasis. If one carries them along while cultivating the Way, one only increases wrong views and afflictions, and there is absolutely no response to be had. To try to cut them off is truly difficult, for these ten fetters, ranged under the Four Noble Truths, extend through the three realms and nine levels, yielding eighty-eight kinds of delusion of view and eighty-one kinds of delusion of thought. To cut off the delusion of view alone is like cutting across a torrent forty li wide — how much more the delusion of thought! If the two delusions of view and thought are not exhausted to the last hair, one cannot escape fragmentary birth and death. This is what is meant by transcending the three realms vertically. How hard! How hard!]

All sentient beings are driven by the ten fetters, sharp and dull, and through long kalpas revolve in birth and death, enduring great suffering and unable to escape. How truly pitiable! What are the ten fetters? Self-view, extreme view, wrong view, attachment to views, and attachment to precepts — these five are called the sharp fetters, because they are light and quick to stir; greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt — these five are called the dull fetters, because they arise from the sharp fetters and are called dull in contrast to them. Of these ten fetters, every sentient being has more or less, each with his own particular emphasis. If one carries them along while cultivating the Way, one only increases wrong views and afflictions, and there is absolutely no share in response. To try to cut them off is truly difficult, for these ten fetters, ranged under the Four Noble Truths, extend through the three realms and nine levels, yielding eighty-eight kinds of delusion of view and eighty-one kinds of delusion of thought. To cut off the delusion of view alone is like cutting across a torrent forty li wide — how much more difficult the delusion of thought, which is even harder to sever! But if the two delusions of view and thought are not exhausted to the last hair, one cannot escape fragmentary birth and death. Cutting off view and thought and so ending birth and death is what is meant by transcending the three realms vertically. How hard! How hard!

[The ten fetters] Also called the ten delusions, or the ten fundamental afflictions: 1. Greed — craving the five desires; 2. Hatred — anger without forbearance; 3. Delusion — folly and ignorance; 4. Pride — arrogance and self-conceit; 5. Doubt — suspicion and disbelief; 6. Self-view — grasping the body as the five aggregates; 7. Extreme view — grasping the two extremes of permanence and annihilation; 8. Wrong view — denying cause and effect and destroying all good works; 9. Attachment to views — holding to fixed opinions, taking the non-fruit for the fruit; 10. Attachment to precepts — holding to improper precepts, taking the non-cause for the cause. The first five are the five dull fetters (delusion of thought); the latter five are the five sharp fetters (delusion of view). “Fetter” is another name for affliction, because afflictions can drive sentient beings to revolve in birth and death. [The Four Noble Truths] That is, the four truths of the noble ones: the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin of suffering, the truth of the cessation of suffering, and the truth of the path. The truth of suffering states the truth that human life is full of suffering; human life has three sufferings, eight sufferings, and immeasurable sufferings, and suffering is the reality of the universe and human life as it is. In the truth of origin, “origin” means the arising or accumulation; it states the truth of how the suffering of human life comes about: the suffering of human life arises because ordinary beings, moved by their own folly and ignorance and by afflictions such as greed and hatred, commit all kinds of unwholesome karma, and only as a result do they accumulate all kinds of suffering. The truth of cessation states the truth that the state of nirvāṇa is the most ideal and ultimate home of this suffering-filled life, because nirvāṇa is the state of permanence, bliss, and stillness. The truth of the path states the truth that one must cultivate the Way in order to realize nirvāṇa. These Four Noble Truths encompass the two levels of cause and effect, within the world and beyond it: origin is the cause and suffering the effect — the cause and effect of the deluded realm; the path is the cause and cessation the effect — the cause and effect of the awakened realm. [The three realms and nine levels] The three realms comprise nine levels in all. Of these, the desire realm occupies one level (the level where the five destinies are intermixed); the form realm occupies four levels (the level of joy and delight born of separation, the level of joy and delight born of concentration, the level of wondrous bliss beyond joy, and the level of equanimity and purity of mindfulness); and the formless realm occupies four levels (the level of infinite space, the level of infinite consciousness, the level of nothingness, and the level of neither perception nor non-perception).

[Delusion of view and delusion of thought] The delusion of view and the delusion of thought. The delusion of view is the confusion and error of ordinary beings in their views, such as the five wrong views of self-view, extreme view, wrong view, attachment to views, and attachment to precepts. The delusion of thought is the confusion and error of ordinary beings in their thinking, such as the afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root by which sentient beings drift through the three realms and suffer birth and death to no purpose; cut them off, and one can end birth and death and escape the three realms. [The eighty-eight kinds of delusion of view] That is, the eighty-eight kinds of delusion of view; within the three realms the kinds of delusion of view number eighty-eight in all. [The eighty-one kinds of delusion of thought] Within the three realms the kinds of delusion of thought number eighty-one in all.

[Yet these ten fetters are collectively called the sentient being's knowledge and views. The ancient virtuous ones said: the knowledge and views of sentient beings must be treated by the Buddha's knowledge and views. The Buddha's knowledge and views are precisely the present numinous knowing that is free of thought. Yet this numinous knowing cannot stand alone in isolation; it must arise in dependence on conditions. If it does not arise in dependence on the conditions of the Buddha realm, it arises in dependence on the conditions of the nine realms. For apart from the ten realms there are no other conditions for arising. If one wishes to arise in dependence on the conditions of the Buddha realm, there is nothing better than to hold the Buddha's name with a mind of faith and vow.]

Yet these ten fetters are collectively called the sentient being's knowledge and views. The ancient virtuous ones said: the knowledge and views of sentient beings must be treated by the Buddha's knowledge and views. The Buddha's knowledge and views are precisely the present numinous knowing that is free of thought. Yet this numinous knowing cannot stand alone in isolation; it must arise in dependence on conditions. If it does not arise in dependence on the conditions of the Buddha realm, it arises in dependence on the conditions of the nine realms. This is because apart from the ten realms there are no other conditions for arising. If one wishes to arise in dependence on the conditions of the Buddha realm, the best way is to hold the Buddha's name with a mind of faith and vow.

[But faith is valued for its depth, vow for its earnestness, and holding the name for its single-mindedness. If with a mind deep, earnest, single-minded, and diligent one holds the name in faith and vow, then one is taking the Buddha's knowledge and views as one's own knowledge and views; that is, in every thought one uses the Buddha's knowledge and views to treat the knowledge and views of sentient beings. Though the ten fetters blaze in the mind, one need only set within it the single thought of holding the name in faith and vow, and one turns the conditions arising in the realm of sentient beings into conditions arising in the realm of the Buddha. In the gate of cultivating the Way, this is the most wondrous method of turning iron into gold. One need only shoulder it bare-bodied, and never let it lapse through long ages; then one may be assured of waiting at ease for the golden terrace and of the precious lotus coming to welcome one before many days. Thus from this Land of Shared Residence one is born in that Land of Shared Residence — transcending the three realms sideways. Compared with transcending them vertically, is it not far less laborious!]

But faith is valued for its depth, vow for its earnestness, and holding the name for its single-mindedness. If with a mind deep, earnest, single-minded, and diligent one holds the name in faith and vow, then one is taking the Buddha's knowledge and views as one's own knowledge and views; that is, in every thought one uses the Buddha's knowledge and views to treat the knowledge and views of sentient beings. When the ten fetters blaze in the mind, one need only apply the single thought of holding the name in faith and vow, and one turns the conditions arising in the realm of sentient beings into conditions arising in the realm of the Buddha. In the gate of cultivating the Way, this is the most wondrous method of turning iron into gold. One need only shoulder it with all one's strength, never letting the thought of holding the name in faith and vow be replaced by deluded thoughts through long ages; then one may be assured of taking the golden terrace, and the precious lotus will come to welcome one before many days. Thus from the Land of Shared Residence of Sages and Ordinary Beings in this Sahā world one is born in the Land of Shared Residence of Sages and Ordinary Beings in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is what is meant by transcending the three realms sideways; compared with transcending them vertically, is it not far less laborious!
[The single phrase Amitābha Buddha is the agada medicine
(the medicine of deathlessness)

, curing every disease. It is the king of wish-fulfilling pearls, satisfying every wish. It is the compassionate ship on the sea of the suffering of birth and death, ferrying all across. It is the lamp of wisdom in the long night of ignorance, dispelling every darkness. One need only let it pass once through the ear to have a connection with it. One need only have a single thought of faith to be in accord with it. If faith is genuine, the vow arises of itself without being sought. Simply keep these two dharmas of faith and vow ever present in the mind, as a loyal minister receives his wise sovereign's secret decree, as a filial son receives his loving father's stern command, remembering them without forgetting, and make this the first and most essential matter. No matter what circumstances one is in — still or noisy, at leisure or busy — whether one recites much or little, all of it is a true cause of rebirth; the only fear is that one takes it as something merely approximate and intermittent
(or: the only fear is that one stands between diligence and indolence)

The single phrase Amitābha Buddha is the medicine of deathlessness, curing every disease. It is the king of wish-fulfilling pearls, satisfying every wish. It is the compassionate ship on the sea of the suffering of birth and death, ferrying all across. It is the lamp of wisdom in the long night of ignorance, dispelling every darkness. One need only let it pass once through the ear to have a connection with it. One need only have a single thought of faith to be in accord with it. If faith is genuine, the vow arises of itself without being sought. Simply keep these two dharmas of faith and vow ever present in the mind, as a loyal minister receives his wise sovereign's secret decree, as a filial son receives his loving father's stern command, remembering them without forgetting, and make this the first and most essential matter. If one truly succeeds in “keeping these two dharmas of faith and vow ever present in the mind and remembering them without forgetting,” then no matter what circumstances one is in — still or noisy, at leisure or busy — whether one recites much or little, all of it is a true cause of rebirth; the only fear is that one does not truly succeed in it.

[The agada medicine] Also called the medicine of deathlessness. This medicine is wondrous and beyond price; taken, it removes all diseases at once. It is the most supreme of wish-fulfilling pearls. [The compassionate ship] The ship that ferries people across and delivers them from the sea of suffering. The Collection of the Common Return of All Good Works says: “Drive the compassionate ship of great prajñā, and cross the bitter ford of the three realms.”

[From time without beginning we have long dwelt in the cycle of rebirth — could it be that we have never once brought forth the mind of renunciation and cultivated the practices that lead to the Way? No; all has been ruined by procrastination
(putting things off; slackness)

, and undone by indolence. That is why we remain in birth and death, enduring great suffering. Now that we have heard the essential and concise Dharma-gate of holding the name, if we still follow the old rut and rest content in defeat
(being overthrown and ruined)
, we may be called the most spineless of men!]

From time without beginning we have long dwelt in the cycle of rebirth — could it be that we have never once brought forth the mind of renunciation and cultivated the practices that lead out of the cycle? No; all has been because we drift with the current and give way to laziness and slackness, and so we go on being born and dying, enduring great suffering. Now that we have heard this most simple and most essential Dharma-gate of holding the name and reciting the Buddha, if we still rest content in birth and death as before without diligent practice, we may be called the most spineless of men!
[What is meant by holding the name is what is called clasping it to the bosom
(engraving it firmly in the heart)

: holding it firmly in the mind without a moment's forgetting. If even a single thought is interrupted, it is not holding. If even a single thought is mixed with other things, it is not holding. When thought follows thought without interruption, without mixture and without gap, that is true diligence. With diligence unceasing, one gradually enters single-minded concentration and perfectly accomplishes the pure karma. If one reaches single-minded concentration and still continues diligently without stopping, one will open wisdom, bring forth eloquence, gain spiritual powers, accomplish the samādhi of Buddha-recitation, and even all manner of wondrous and auspicious signs will appear before one. It is like a wax figure held to the fire: the thin places are pierced first. But one must not harbor beforehand the thought of expecting results; one should only devote oneself to single-minded concentration. Single-minded concentration is the home of the pure karma and the great gate of the Pure Land. If one has not entered this gate, one is never truly secure. Can the student fail to strive!]

What is meant by holding the name is that the Buddha's name is to be engraved firmly in the heart: holding it firmly in the mind without a moment's forgetting. If even a single thought is interrupted and the Buddha's name is not remembered, it is not holding. If even a single thought is mixed with other things, it is not holding. When thought follows thought without interruption, without deluded thoughts mixed in and without gaps, that is true diligence. With diligence unceasing, one gradually enters single-minded concentration and perfectly accomplishes the pure karma. If one reaches single-minded concentration and still continues diligently without stopping, one will open wisdom, bring forth eloquence, gain spiritual powers, accomplish the samādhi of Buddha-recitation, and even all manner of wondrous and auspicious signs will appear before one. It is like a wax figure held to the fire: the thin places are pierced first. But one must not harbor beforehand the thought of expecting results; one should only devote oneself to single-minded concentration. Single-minded concentration is the home of the pure karma and the great gate of the Pure Land. If one has not entered this gate, one is never truly secure. Can the student fail to strive!

[Clasping it to the bosom] Engraving it firmly in the heart. [Like a wax figure held to the fire, the thin places are pierced first] This quotes a Chan case: “A monk asked: ‘Where the stages are not fallen into, please, Master, say a word.’ The master (Baoyan) said: ‘A wax figure held to the fire.’ ‘After all, how is it?’ The master said: ‘The thin places are pierced first.’” (The Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp). Master Chewu quotes this simile to mean: once holding the name in Buddha-recitation has reached single-minded concentration, one need not set up another stove to further open wisdom, attain samādhi, and enter the patient acceptance of non-arising; one need only continue holding the name with diligence. From this one knows that the single method of holding the name reaches through heaven and earth. [The patient acceptance of non-arising] That is, the patient acceptance of the non-arising of all dharmas: true wisdom rests securely in the principle that “all dharmas were never born, and therefore are not extinguished,” and never again retrogresses. The Buddha said: “All dharmas are false and illusory.” (Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Forty,
Chapter on Kaundinya)

[In cultivating all Dharma-gates, what matters is to understand the teaching and grasp its essential meaning. People today know only that the myriad dharmas are mind-only, and do not know that the mind is the myriad dharmas. They know only that outside the mind there is no Buddha, and do not know that outside the Buddha there is no mind. They know only that the immeasurable is the one, and do not know that the one is the immeasurable. They know only that one may turn the mountains, rivers, and great earth and return them to oneself, and do not know that one may turn oneself and return to the mountains, rivers, and great earth. But if one does not know that the mind is the myriad dharmas, how can one truly know that the myriad dharmas are mind-only? If one does not know that outside the Buddha there is no mind, how can one truly know that outside the mind there is no Buddha? This is what is called taking one round ball and cleaving it in two: separated, both are spoiled; joined, both are beautiful.]

In cultivating all Dharma-gates, what matters most is to understand the teaching and grasp its essential meaning. People today know only that the myriad dharmas arise from the mind (the myriad dharmas are mind-only), and do not know that the myriad dharmas are the mind itself (the mind is the myriad dharmas). They know only that outside the mind there is no Buddha, and do not know that outside the Buddha there is likewise no mind. They know only that the immeasurable is the one, and do not know that the one is the immeasurable. They know only that one may turn the mountains, rivers, and great earth and return them to oneself, and do not know that one may turn oneself and return to the mountains, rivers, and great earth. But if one does not know that the myriad dharmas are the mind, how can one truly know that the mind creates the myriad dharmas? If one does not know that outside the Buddha there is no mind, how can one truly know that outside the mind there is no Buddha? It is as has been said: taking one round ball and cleaving it in two — separated, neither half is a ball (both are spoiled); joined together, it is a ball (both are beautiful).

[Therefore, one who recites the Buddha's name must take “only Buddha, only land” as the teaching. If the teaching of “only Buddha, only land” is not clear, then the true meaning of mind-only is not established. If one truly penetrates the true meaning of mind-only, then the teaching of “only Buddha, only land” establishes itself. Once this teaching is established, then the Buddha recited in a single phrase and the land in which one is born are, in their whole essence and great function, pervading horizontally and exhausting vertically, a single substance wholly true, embracing all and excluding nothing.]

Therefore, one who recites the Buddha's name must take “Amitābha of one's own nature, the Pure Land of mind-only” (only Buddha, only land) as the teaching. If the teaching of “Amitābha of one's own nature, the Pure Land of mind-only” is not clear, then the true meaning of mind-only is not established. If one truly penetrates the true meaning of mind-only, then the teaching of “Amitābha of one's own nature, the Pure Land of mind-only” (only Buddha, only land) establishes itself. Once this teaching is established, then the Buddha recited in a single phrase and the land in which one is born are, in their whole essence and great function, pervading horizontally and exhausting vertically, a single substance wholly true, embracing all and excluding nothing.

[Only Buddha, only land] The nature alone is the Buddha; the mind alone is the land. That is: Amitābha of one's own nature, the Pure Land of mind-only. Master Lianchi said: “Reciting the Buddha's name is reciting the mind; being born there does not depart from being born here. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are one substance, and one dwells neither in the midstream nor on either shore. Hence it is called Amitābha of one's own nature, the Pure Land of mind-only.”

On “Amitābha of one's own nature, the Pure Land of mind-only,” Master Lianchi said: “Moreover, since the gate of vow is vast and wide, what matters is to know what comes first; since the contemplation of dharmas is deep and profound, one should above all keep to what is essential. To know what comes first is to devote oneself to being born in that land; to keep to what is essential is to attend to nothing but holding the name. Raise the name, and all virtues are complete within it; devote yourself to holding it, and all practices are gathered up without omission. From this, ten thousand concerns all come to rest, and one reaches the utmost of single-minded concentration. Then one knows that without stirring a half step, the precious pool wells up with flowers of four colors; without going out the door, the golden ground is ringed with trees of seven rows. Everywhere Amitābha preaches the Dharma; at every moment one is transformed and born within a lotus calyx. Rare birds and common birds share one voice; jeweled courts and thatched halls share one splendor. This is because, when thought is emptied, one truly thinks, and birth enters the unborn. Reciting the Buddha's name is reciting the mind; being born there does not depart from being born here. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are one substance, and one dwells neither in the midstream nor on either shore. Hence it is called Amitābha of one's own nature, the Pure Land of mind-only. This is the one mind of principle, wholly the domain of the highest wisdom; yet it also accords with matters and forms, bending to suit the duller faculties. Why is it, then, that the dull-witted who cling to their folly are attached to matters and never hear of principle, while those of small cleverness grasp principle and so let practice fall into disuse? To be attached to matters and deluded about principle is like a child reciting the books of the ancient sages; to grasp principle and neglect matters is like a poor man who has obtained a rich man's bond. Yet if one is attached to matters and one's recitation can continue without interruption, the merit of entering the grades is not in vain; while if one grasps principle but the mind is not truly clear, one instead suffers the calamity of falling into emptiness. So it is that one's outstretched hand toils in vain and one gazes empty-eyed from the gate. Above, one betrays the Buddha's teaching; below, one fails one's own spirit. In this life and in many lives to come, one error becomes a hundred errors; one willingly heads for the bitter destinies, hands bound at the door of death, with no rescue and no refuge. How sad, how painful!” (Commentary and Subcommentary on the Amitābha Sūtra)

[Like a poor man who has obtained a rich man's bond] This is like a poor man who finds on the road a list belonging to a wealthy house, and reads the various figures recorded there of fields, gardens, palaces, rooms, gold, silk, grain, and millet. He is overjoyed beyond measure and says that he is a man of great wealth. But he does not know that he is counting another man's treasure, and what has it to do with him? So too is one who, not yet having attained single-minded concentration in practice, would cultivate the practice of Buddha-recitation by way of the principle of the Middle Way: though he knows the principle that “the Buddha is the mind,” he can make no use of it at all. [Instead suffers the calamity of falling into emptiness] One who grasps principle and neglects matters says with his lips “Amitābha of one's own nature, the Pure Land of mind-only,” yet talks lightly of the Pure Land and scorns rebirth there. Reciting the Buddha's name in this way, even if one reaches single-minded concentration, even if one awakens to the mind and sees the nature, even if one is greatly and thoroughly enlightened — so long as the afflictions of view and thought are not cut off in the least, one still remains within the cycle of birth and death.
In this passage of instruction there are the following three essential points:

1. First, one must hold the name in faith and vow, reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and seeking birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, until one reaches a state of perfect clarity, neither dulled nor scattered. This is called single-minded concentration in practice.

2. After reaching single-minded concentration in practice, one should continue to hold the name diligently, cultivating the practice of Buddha-recitation by way of the principle of the Middle Way: from holding the name, penetrating deeply into true reality and realizing in awakening “Amitābha of one's own nature, the Pure Land of mind-only.” This is single-minded concentration in principle. Though one has realized “Amitābha of one's own nature, the Pure Land of mind-only” in principle, in practice one should still seek birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss — what is called being born yet unborn, unborn yet born. Only thus are principle and practice perfectly fused, and one both escapes the calamity of falling into emptiness and enjoys the incomparable supreme benefit of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Hence: “At the final assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Sudhana traveled everywhere to visit the wise, and came to the place of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, where, empowered by Samantabhadra's awesome spiritual power, what he realized was equal to Samantabhadra and equal to all Buddhas, so that he was a Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment. Samantabhadra then, in order to praise the Tathāgata's supreme and wondrous virtues, urged Sudhana and the whole ocean-wide assembly of the Flower Treasury to dedicate the merit of the Ten Great Vows alike toward rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, so as to bring the fruit of Buddhahood to perfection.” (Master Yinguang's Collected Writings, Continued Series,
Preface to the Ode to the Immeasurable Life Sūtra)

3. Having already reached single-minded concentration in practice and no longer pressing on further is to be attached to matters and deluded about principle. Not yet having reached single-minded concentration in practice, yet saying with one's lips “Amitābha of one's own nature, the Pure Land of mind-only,” talking lightly of the Pure Land and scorning rebirth there, is to grasp principle and neglect matters. One must neither be attached to matters and deluded about principle, nor still less grasp principle and neglect matters. For “if one is attached to matters and one's recitation can continue without interruption, the merit of entering the grades is not in vain; while if one grasps principle but the mind is not truly clear, one instead suffers the calamity of falling into emptiness.”
The meaning of these three essential points is discussed in detail by Master Lianchi in his Commentary and Subcommentary on the Amitābha Sūtra.

As for the question “Since there is the Pure Land of mind-only and Amitābha of one's own nature, are these and the Western Pure Land and its Buddha one and yet two, two and yet one?”, Master Yinguang answered: “It is because there is a Pure Land of mind-only that one is born in the Western Pure Land. If one's own mind is not pure, how could one attain rebirth at once? Even the sinful and perverse, who attain rebirth through ten recitations, are born in the Western Pure Land through the pure mind of Buddha-recitation. The world mostly holds that if all is mind-only there is no land — that is the knowledge and views of demons and outsiders. Such specious and false views account for the greater half of them, so that those who recite the Buddha's name fail to obtain real benefit. They still consider themselves lofty and brilliant, not knowing that this is the false view of grasping principle and abolishing practice, which ruins oneself and ruins others. Because of Amitābha of one's own nature, one must recite the name of the Western Amitābha and seek rebirth, and by gradual progress one may personally realize Amitābha of one's own nature. If one clings only to Amitābha of one's own nature and does not recite the Western Amitābha, then even if one has truly awakened, one still cannot at once end birth and death — let alone that those who speak such words are all a bunch of pole-carrying men and empty-talkers! ‘One and yet two’ pertains to the time before Buddhahood is attained. ‘Two and yet one’ pertains to the time after Buddhahood has been attained.” (Master Yinguang's Collected Writings,
Continued Series,
Answers to Twenty-Seven Questions from Layman Qu Tianxiang)

[Pole-carrying man] Originally meaning a laborer who carries a plank on his back; because he can see only what is in front of him, it is used to describe one whose views are biased and one-sided and who cannot comprehend the whole. A common saying goes: “A pole-carrying man sees but one side.”

[What is recited being thus, what recites is likewise so. This is called using the mind of true reality to recite the Buddha of true reality; using the mind of the Dharma-realm to recite the Buddha of the Dharma-realm; thought after thought absolute, thought after thought perfectly fused. Because it is absolute, it wholly surpasses all Dharma-gates, and none can equal it. Because it is perfectly fused, it wholly gathers in all Dharma-gates, and none falls outside it. This is what is meant by: dharmas have no fixed form, and whatever condition they meet becomes the teaching; in the flourishing of great function, whatever is raised is wholly true. The single phrase Amitābha Buddha must be believed in this way and recited in this way — only then is it the inconceivable within the inconceivable.]

The Buddha that is recited being thus, the mind that recites is likewise so. This is what is called using the mind of true reality to recite the Buddha of true reality; using the mind of the Dharma-realm to recite the Buddha of the Dharma-realm; thought after thought absolute, thought after thought perfectly fused. Because it is absolute, holding the name in Buddha-recitation wholly surpasses all Dharma-gates, and none can equal it. Because it is perfectly fused, holding the name in Buddha-recitation wholly gathers in all Dharma-gates, and none falls outside it. This is what is meant by: dharmas have no fixed form, and whatever condition they meet becomes the teaching; in the flourishing of great function, whatever is raised is wholly true. The single phrase Amitābha Buddha must be believed in this way and recited in this way — only then is it the inconceivable within the inconceivable.

[Dharmas have no fixed form, and whatever condition they meet becomes the teaching] The Buddhadharma has no fixed form; meeting conditions and responding to capacities, it causes all to return to the teaching (the cultivation of the Pure Land Dharma-gate). Master Yinguang said: “Dharmas have no fixed form; what suits the capacity is wondrous. The Tathāgata takes the one-flavored Dharma and makes all kinds of statements. It is like a great officer's fine delicacies: if he meets an adult, he serves the whole tray and lets him eat his fill; if he meets an infant who cannot chew, he must chew it for him and feed it from his own mouth. Only thus can it benefit body and mind and quickly bring him to maturity.” (Master Yinguang's Collected Writings, Third Series,

Preface to the Broad Tongue) He also said: “The three realms were always a single theater; all of you, go home early. Do not wait until drums and gongs have all fallen silent — then, not knowing the road home, you will have busied yourself in vain. Dharmas have no fixed form; whatever condition they meet becomes the teaching. This mountain monk carries his staff with him and may as well play his part as the play demands. Responding to the capacities that come, he sends them home along the road they came.” (Master Yinguang's Collected Writings,

Address to the Head of the Theatrical Troupe at the Dharma Hall) [In the flourishing of great function, whatever is raised is wholly true] The single method of holding the name has all manner of great functions, shallow and deep, but whether shallow or deep, all accord with the ultimate truth. “Flourishing” means abundant and manifold in arising.

blocks.text: 35. The Four Gates of Cultivating the Way

inline.s: [What is not two as between sentient beings and Buddhas, and is equally shared by all, is only this present numinous knowing that is free of thought. Because the Buddhas follow the conditions of awakening and purity, awakening again and again, purifying again and again, until awakening and purity reach their utmost, their numinous knowing pervades horizontally and exhausts vertically, vast and all-embracing. Because sentient beings follow the conditions of delusion and defilement, deluded again and again, defiled again and again, their numinous knowing is confined and cramped, tiny and inferior.]

What is not two as between sentient beings and Buddhas, and is equally shared by all, is only this present numinous knowing that is free of thought. Because the Buddhas follow the conditions of awakening and purity, awakening again and again, purifying again and again, until awakening and purity reach their utmost, their numinous knowing pervades horizontally and exhausts vertically, vast and all-embracing. Because sentient beings follow the conditions of delusion and defilement, deluded again and again, defiled again and again, their numinous knowing is confined and cramped, utterly tiny and inferior.
[Tiny] Describing what is utterly small and minute.

[Yet this tiny numinous knowing is, in its very substance, not two with the vast numinous knowing of all Buddhas, not different by a hair. If it could follow the conditions of awakening and purity, so that karma is exhausted and defilement emptied, then this tiny knowing would at that very moment turn into the vast and all-embracing numinous knowing. It is like a single spark of fire that can burn ten thousand acres of wild field.]

Yet this utterly tiny and minute numinous knowing is, in its very substance, not two with the vast and all-embracing numinous knowing of all Buddhas, not different by a hair. If it could follow the conditions of awakening and purity, so that karma is exhausted and defilement emptied, then this utterly tiny and minute numinous knowing would at that very moment turn into the vast and all-embracing numinous knowing. It is like a single spark of fire that can burn ten thousand acres of wild field.
[Dí
dí
] To see, to face.

[Yet this present single thought of numinous knowing, if considered in terms of the objects known, does indeed differ in breadth and narrowness, superiority and inferiority. If considered in terms of the knowing that knows, then it is wholly without difference. It is like the same fire: burning sandalwood it is fragrant, burning dung it stinks. Though what is burned differs, the fire that burns is not two. Again, it is like the same water: clear and turbid differ. The same mirror: dull and bright are not the same. Though clear and turbid differ, the nature of wetness is not two. Though dull and bright are not the same, the substance of light is the same. The water shares one wetness, and the turbid can be settled until it is clear. The mirror shares one light, and the dull can be polished until it is bright. The dullness of the light is owing to the grime it carries, but grime is not the light; the light is the mirror's own substance. The turbidity of the water is owing to the dust it carries, but dust is not the wetness; the wetness is the water's own nature.]

Yet this present single thought of numinous knowing, if considered in terms of the objects known, does indeed differ in breadth and narrowness, superiority and inferiority.
