If considered in terms of the knowing that knows, then it is wholly without difference from the Buddhas. It is like the same fire: burning sandalwood it is fragrant, burning dung it stinks. Though what is burned differs, the fire that burns is not two. Again, it is like the same water, which may be clear or turbid. The same mirror, whose dullness and brightness are not the same. Though clear and turbid differ, the nature of wetness is not two. Though dull and bright are not the same, the substance that gives out light is the same. The water shares one wetness, and the turbid can be settled until it is clear. The mirror (in ancient times a bronze mirror) shares one light, and the dull can be polished until it is bright. The reason the mirror's light is dim is that it carries grime, but grime is not what gives out light. What gives out light is the mirror's own substance. The reason the water is turbid is that it carries dust, but dust is not what has the nature of wetness; what has the nature of wetness is the water's own nature.

[This single thought of numinous knowing is like the wetness of water, like the light of a mirror, like the burning of fire — in its whole substance it is without difference. Precisely because it is without difference in its whole substance, there are many gates among the skillful means of cultivating the Way: some only revere the sages, some only respect their own spirit, some revere the sages outwardly and respect their own spirit inwardly, and some neither revere the sages nor respect their own spirit.]

This single thought of numinous knowing is like the wetness of water, like the light of a mirror, like the burning of fire — their essential substance is the same. Precisely because their essential substance is the same, there are many gates among the skillful means of cultivating the Way: some only revere the Buddhas, some only respect their own spirit, some revere the Buddhas outwardly and respect their own spirit inwardly, and some neither revere the Buddhas nor respect their own spirit.

[Spirit] That is, the Tathāgatagarbha. The Tathāgatagarbha of sentient beings is not two with that of all Buddhas. [Tathāgatagarbha] When true suchness is within affliction and holds within it all the virtues of the Tathāgata on the ground of fruition, it is called the “Tathāgatagarbha”; once it emerges from affliction, it is called the “dharmakāya.”

[As for those who only revere the sages: such are people who recite the Buddha's name according to their original lot. Because they know that all the sages have already realized my own spirit before me, and that in speech and silence, in movement and stillness, they are all worthy models, if we did not revere the sages, we would have no road for advancing in cultivation. So they may single-mindedly hold the name, or contemplate the sound and countenance, with the three karmas devout, bowing in reverence six times a day, pouring out their hearts in refuge, and following and upholding to the end of their lives. When the time comes and conditions ripen, response meets response, the ground of the mind opens wide, and the numinous light stands alone revealed; then they know that their own spirit was originally equal to and no different from all the sages, and that one cannot but respect oneself as well.]

Those who only revere the Buddhas: such are people who recite the Buddha's name according to their original lot. Because they know that all the Buddhas realized their own mind-nature in full before me, and that in speech and silence, in movement and stillness, they are all models, if we did not revere the Buddhas, we would have no road for advancing in cultivation. So they may single-mindedly hold the name, or contemplate the sound and countenance, with the three karmas (body, speech, and mind) devout, bowing in reverence six times a day, pouring out their hearts in refuge, and following and upholding throughout their lives. When the time comes and conditions ripen, response meets response, the ground of the mind opens wide, and the numinous light stands alone revealed; only then do they know that their own spirit was originally equal to and no different from all the Buddhas, and that one cannot but respect oneself as well.
[We] Us. [To the end of their lives] To the end of one's whole life.
[Again, those who only respect their own spirit
(who respect only their own mind-nature)

. Such are those who practice Chan in the Chan school, which points directly at the human mind and sees the nature to become Buddha. So they wish only that through the twelve hours of the day, within the four dignities of walking, standing, sitting, and lying, the true face of the person should stand alone revealed, and that they enjoy the scenery of their native place
(their original face)

; apart from the mind-nature, they grasp at nothing at all. This is what is meant by: let a thousand sages appear before me, I have my own innate Buddha. When their attainment runs deep and their awakening and realization reach the utmost, they then know that all the sages long ago realized my own spirit before me, and that one cannot but revere them.]

Again, those who only respect their own mind-nature. Such are those who practice Chan in the Chan school, which points directly at the human mind and sees the nature to become Buddha. Therefore they wish only that through the twelve hours of the day, within the four dignities, the true face of the person should stand alone revealed, and that they enjoy the scenery of their native place; apart from the mind-nature, they grasp at nothing at all. This is what is meant by: let a thousand sages appear before me, I have my own innate Buddha. When their attainment runs deep and their awakening and realization reach the utmost, only then do they know that all the Buddhas long ago realized their own spirit before them, and that one cannot but revere them.

[Again, those who revere the sages outwardly and respect their own spirit inwardly. Now, to wish to respect one's own spirit, one must revere the sages. It is precisely because one reveres the sages that one is respecting one's own spirit. And to revere the sages, one must respect one's own spirit. If one did not respect one's own spirit, how could one revere the sages? Thus inner and outer are cultivated together, and mind and Buddha are held in equal weight. Since there is no one-sided attachment, one advances on the Way all the more swiftly. When power reaches its utmost and merit is pure, and the whole substance responds, then one knows that the sages did no more than realize my own spirit before me, and there is no need to revere them. And my own spirit does no more than stand equal with all the sages, so what toil is there in respecting it?]

Again, those who revere the sages outwardly and respect their own spirit inwardly. To wish to respect one's own spirit, one must revere the Buddhas. It is precisely because one reveres the sages that one is respecting one's own spirit. Moreover, to wish to revere the Buddhas, one must respect one's own spirit. If one did not respect one's own spirit, how could one revere the Buddhas? Thus inner and outer are cultivated together, and mind and Buddha are held in equal weight. Since there is no one-sided attachment, one advances on the Way all the more swiftly. When power reaches its utmost and merit is pure, and the whole substance responds, only then does one know that the Buddhas did no more than realize their own spirit before me, and there is no need to revere them. And my own spirit does no more than stand equal with all the Buddhas, so what toil is there in respecting it?

[Again, those who neither revere the sages nor respect their own spirit. This is called not hanging on by a single thread, forgetting both mind and Buddha, utterly let go, with nowhere to lean. Outwardly one abandons the world, inwardly one sheds body and mind. Not a single thought arises, and ten thousand conditions are cut off at once. When after long practice the work is ripe and one enters perfect realization, the original spirit stands alone revealed, and one is at once equal to all the sages. Though one does not revere the sages, one reveres them well. Though one does not respect one's own spirit, one truly respects it.]

Again, those who neither revere the Buddhas nor respect their own spirit. This is called not hanging on by a single thread, forgetting both mind and Buddha, utterly let go, with nowhere to lean. Outwardly one abandons the world, inwardly one sheds body and mind. Not a single thought arises, and ten thousand conditions are cut off at once. When after long practice the work is ripe and one enters perfect realization, the original spirit stands alone revealed, and one is wholly equal to all the Buddhas. Though one does not revere the sages, one reveres them well. Though one does not respect one's own spirit, one truly respects it.
[In these four roads, the student judges his own faculties
(students judge according to their own faculties; “judge,” that is, to consider)

, and each follows what he delights in. But one should penetrate deeply through one gate, and in time all will surely be gained. One must never rashly give rise to attachment or lightly voice opinions, treating one's own as master and others' as servants
(clinging to the prejudices of one's own sect)
, affirming one and denying the rest. That not only turns one away from the wondrous Way and creates obstacles, but I fear one will slander the great Dharma and bring down guilt upon oneself.]

In these four roads, students judge according to their own faculties, and each follows what he delights in. But one should penetrate deeply through one gate, and in time all will surely be gained. One must never rashly give rise to attachment or lightly voice opinions, clinging to the prejudices of one's own sect, holding to one gate and denying and opposing all the rest. That not only turns one away from the wondrous Way and makes an obstacle of oneself; I fear one will bring down calamity upon oneself by slandering the great Dharma!

[Judge] To consider. [Treating one's own as master and others' as servants] Clinging to the prejudices of one's own sect. [Affirming one and denying the rest] Holding to one gate and denying and opposing all the rest. [I fear one will slander the great Dharma and bring down guilt upon oneself] The Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: “To accept one and deny the rest is to be held in the grasp of demons.” [Guilt] Blame and fault.

[The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says: “What all the sages know, they transmit one to another in teaching: deluded thinking has no nature of its own.” The Second Patriarch said: “Seeking the mind, it is utterly unobtainable.” The Awakening of Faith says: “If there is one who can contemplate no-thought, that one is tending toward the Buddha's wisdom.” The Comprehensive Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: “Sudden awakening to the single thought arising from conditions and unborn surpasses the views of those who study the three vehicles by expedient means.”]

The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says: this is what the Buddhas of the past knew, and now they transmit it one to another in teaching: deluded thinking has no substantial nature; it is an illusion. The Second Patriarch of Chan, Huike, said: I sought the mind and could not find it at all. The Awakening of Faith says: if there is one who can contemplate no-thought, that one is tending toward the Buddha's wisdom. The Comprehensive Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: sudden awakening to the truth that “a single thought arises from conditions and is an illusion that was never born” already surpasses the views of those who study the three vehicles by expedient means.

[No nature] Nature means substance; all dharmas have no substantial nature but are illusions, and this is called having no nature. The Lotus Sūtra says: “Know that all dharmas are always without nature.” The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: “All illusions are without nature.” [Seeking the mind, it is utterly unobtainable] Bodhidharma said: What have you come here to seek after all? Huike (the Second Patriarch of Chan) replied: “My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to pacify it for me.” Bodhidharma said: “Bring me your mind, and I will pacify it for you.” He replied: “Seeking the mind, it is utterly unobtainable.” Bodhidharma said: “I have pacified your mind for you.” [The three vehicles] The vehicle of the hearers, the vehicle of the solitary realizers, and the Bodhisattva vehicle. [Expedient study] Study by expedient means.

[These words of the Buddhas and patriarchs, and the treatises composed by Bodhisattvas and good teachers, all point directly at the present single thought and reveal that the nature of delusion is originally empty. Now, if delusion is originally empty and the true is originally present, what is this but Buddha? It is only that sentient beings have long followed the conditions of defilement and have not been able at once to restore their original emptiness. One must therefore use pure conditions to turn it gradually. With the causal mind that is itself Buddha, one recites the fruition Buddha that is one's own mind. Cause and effect have always interpenetrated; mind and Buddha are naturally
(spontaneously)

one suchness. And the fruition Buddha that is my own mind, with its unconditional great loving-kindness and its great compassion of one substance, is originally inconceivable. Moreover, the causal mind that is itself Buddha, with deep faith, earnest vow, and single-minded devoted holding of the name, is likewise inconceivable. It can, in every thought, wholly settle all defilements, perfectly reveal the original emptiness, at once attune to the numinous source, and go straight to the ocean of fruition. Thus
(therefore)
no pure condition surpasses this one.]

These words of the Buddhas and patriarchs, and the treatises composed by Bodhisattvas and great good teachers, all point directly at the present single thought and reveal that thought is delusion and its nature is originally empty. Since delusion is originally empty and the true is originally present, is this not precisely Buddha? It is only that sentient beings have long followed the conditions of defilement and have not been able at once to restore their original emptiness. One must use pure conditions to turn it gradually and restore its original emptiness. With the causal mind that is originally Buddha, one recites the fruition Buddha within one's own mind (Amitābha Buddha). Cause and effect have always interpenetrated; mind and Buddha are naturally one and not two. And the fruition Buddha within my mind, with its unconditional great loving-kindness and its great compassion of one substance, is originally inconceivable. Moreover, the causal mind that is originally Buddha, with deep faith, earnest vow, and single-minded devoted holding of the name, is also inconceivable. It can, in every thought, remove all defilements and perfectly reveal that its nature is originally empty; then one at once attunes to the source and goes straight to the ocean of fruition. Therefore no pure condition surpasses this one.

[Naturally] Spontaneous. [The causal ground] From the stage of ordinary being, when one first brings forth the mind to study Buddhism, until the perfection of Buddhahood, this whole process is called the “causal ground.” [The fruition ground] As opposed to the “causal ground,” that is, the supreme stage of perfect wondrous enlightenment attained through cultivation on the causal ground. [One suchness] “One” means equal and not two; “such” means unchanging as it is. [Inconceivable] What cannot be thought with the mind and cannot be spoken of in words.
[But when reciting, one should let go of ten thousand conditions and raise the single thought alone. It is like saving one's head from fire
(burning)

, like mourning a parent, like a hen brooding on her eggs, like a dragon guarding its pearl. Do not expect small results, do not seek quick success; only recite with one mind constantly in this way, and it is called the supreme and profound gate of Chan. Then the body of faculties and the world secretly follow the mind and are transformed thought after thought. This is not something the ordinary mind and fleshly eye can know or see. And when the retribution ends and life is exhausted, Amitābha and the host of sages suddenly appear before one, or there appear rare fragrances and heavenly music and all manner of auspicious signs, and only then does the world say that the pure karma is accomplished. But when was the pure karma accomplished? Was it at that moment?]

However, when reciting the Buddha's name, one should let go of ten thousand conditions and raise the single thought alone (the thought of Buddha-recitation). It is like saving one's head from fire, like mourning a parent, like a hen brooding on her eggs, like a dragon guarding its pearl; do not expect small results, do not seek quick success, but only recite with one mind constantly in this way — this is the supreme and profound gate of Chan. In this way the future body of faculties and the world secretly follow the mind and are all transformed thought after thought. This is not something the ordinary mind and fleshly eye can know or see. And when the retribution ends and life is exhausted, Amitābha Buddha and the host of sages suddenly appear before one, or there appear rare fragrances and heavenly music and all manner of auspicious signs, and only then does the world say that the pure karma is accomplished. But when was the pure karma accomplished? Was it at that very moment?
[The body of faculties] The body composed of the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind).

blocks.text: 37. The Four Minds to Be Aroused

inline.s: [In reciting the Buddha's name one should arouse four kinds of mind. What are the four? First, from time without beginning until now one has created karma, and one should arouse a mind of shame. Second, having heard this Dharma-gate, one should arouse a mind of rejoicing. Third, since beginningless karma-obstacles make this method hard to encounter and hard to meet, one should arouse a mind of grief. Fourth, since the Buddha is so compassionate, one should arouse a mind of gratitude. If among these four minds there is even one, the pure karma can be accomplished.]

In reciting the Buddha's name one should arouse four kinds of mind. What are the four? First, from time without beginning until now one has created karma, and one should arouse a mind of shame. Second, having heard this Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation, one should arouse a mind of rejoicing. Third, since beginningless karma-obstacles make this Pure Land Dharma-gate hard to encounter and hard to meet, one should arouse a mind of grief. Fourth, since the Buddha is so compassionate, one should arouse a mind of gratitude. If among these four minds there is even one, the pure karma can be accomplished.

[In reciting the Buddha's name one should keep at it long, and must not interrupt it. If one interrupts it, the pure karma cannot be accomplished either. Keeping at it long, one should be brave and fierce, and must not grow weary. If one grows weary, the pure karma cannot be accomplished either. If one keeps at it long but is not brave and fierce, one retreats. If one is brave and fierce but does not keep at it long, one does not advance.]

In reciting the Buddha's name one should keep at it long, and must not interrupt it. If one interrupts it, the pure karma cannot be accomplished either. Keeping at it long, one should be brave and fierce, and must not grow weary. If one grows weary, the pure karma cannot be accomplished either. If one keeps at it long but is not brave and fierce, one retreats. If one is brave and fierce but does not keep at it long, one does not advance.

[When reciting the Buddha's name, one must not have other thoughts. To have no other thoughts is calm abiding. When reciting the Buddha's name, one must be perfectly clear. To be able to be perfectly clear is clear seeing. Within the single thought, calm abiding and clear seeing are complete; there is no separate calm abiding and clear seeing. Calm abiding is the cause of concentration, and concentration is the fruit of calm abiding. Clear seeing is the cause of wisdom, and wisdom is the fruit of clear seeing.]

When reciting the Buddha's name, one must not have other thoughts. To have no other thoughts is calm abiding. When reciting the Buddha's name, one must be perfectly clear. To be able to be perfectly clear is clear seeing. Within this single thought of Buddha-recitation, calm abiding and clear seeing are complete; there is no separate calm abiding and clear seeing. Calm abiding is the cause of concentration, and concentration is the fruit of calm abiding. Clear seeing is the cause of wisdom, and wisdom is the fruit of clear seeing.

[Not a single thought arising, yet perfectly clear — this is stillness while illumining. Perfectly clear, yet not a single thought arising — this is illumining while still. One who can be thus will surely accomplish the pure karma. Those who accomplish it in this way all attain the upper grades. Whether one person or a hundred thousand million billion people, if they cultivate in this way, all will accomplish it in this way. Can those who recite the Buddha's name fail to be careful?]

When reciting the Buddha's name, deluded thoughts do not arise and one is perfectly clear — this is stillness while illumining. Perfectly clear, yet deluded thoughts do not arise — this is illumining while still. One who can be thus will surely accomplish the pure karma. Those who accomplish it in this way all attain the upper grades. Whether one person or a hundred thousand million billion people, if they cultivate in this way, all will accomplish it in this way. Can those who recite the Buddha's name fail to be careful when they recite (the implication being: when reciting, one must surely have no other thoughts)?
(Excerpted from Master Chewu's Remainder Collection,
Letter in Reply to Layman Xiangyan)

[One must simply believe deeply and understand truly that outside the mind there is no Buddha and outside the Buddha there is no mind; that the whole mind is Buddha and the whole Buddha is mind. When a single thought appears before one, one responds in a single thought; when thought after thought appears before one, one responds thought after thought.]

One should believe deeply and understand truly this state: “outside the mind there is no Buddha, outside the Buddha there is no mind; the whole mind is Buddha, the whole Buddha is mind” — only the single thought of Buddha-recitation remains, with no other thought besides. When one's practice reaches this state, then: when a single thought (a pure, undefiled thought of Buddha-recitation) appears before one, one responds in that single thought; when thought after thought appears before one, one responds thought after thought.

Here “mind” means the thought; “Buddha” means the name of the Buddha that is recited; “response” means “this mind becomes Buddha, this mind is Buddha” — as is said, one thought in response, one thought a Buddha; thought after thought in response, thought after thought a Buddha.

[Outside the mind there is no Buddha, outside the Buddha there is no mind; the whole mind is Buddha, the whole Buddha is mind] Outside the thought there is no thought of Buddha (the thought of Buddha-recitation), and outside the thought of Buddha there is no thought; the whole thought is the thought of Buddha, and the whole thought of Buddha is the thought. This describes the state in which the thought and the thought of Buddha wholly coincide, and the thought of Buddha-recitation is pure and undefiled.

Concerning this passage of Master Chewu's instruction, Master Yinguang says in his Answer to a Lay Buddhist's Questions on Buddha-Recitation (that is, Zhou Mengyou): “Question: In ‘a single thought appears before one’ and ‘thought after thought appears before one,’ is the word ‘thought’ the same in meaning as the word ‘mind’ in ‘mind and Buddha’? Answer: Mind and thought are one and the same. It is only that with respect to what is constantly present, one calls it mind, and with respect to what arises in the present, one calls it thought. Question: Do the four lines ‘outside the mind there is no Buddha, outside the Buddha there is no mind’ refer to the virtue of nature? And do the four lines ‘a single thought appears before one, one responds in a single thought’ refer to the virtue of cultivation? Answer: Both are the virtue of cultivation. For ‘outside the mind there is no Buddha, outside the Buddha there is no mind’ is brought about by one's practice. Question: As for the four lines ‘a single thought appears before one, one responds in a single thought,’ can a beginner be capable of this? Can a long-time cultivator be capable of this? Answer: The beginner has the beginner's response, and the long-time cultivator has the long-time cultivator's response. How could one hold rigidly to one view?”

[But if one can keep this thought ever present before one, that is the true test. To seek a test apart from this thought is to be interrupted, to be out of touch, to have entered a forked road! The scripture says: “This mind becomes Buddha; this mind is Buddha.” This is exactly what it means.]

So long as one can keep this thought (the pure, undefiled thought of Buddha-recitation) ever present before one, that is the true test. To seek a test apart from this thought is to be interrupted, to be out of touch, to have entered a forked road! The scripture says: “This mind becomes Buddha; this mind is Buddha.” This is exactly the state it speaks of!

blocks.text: Appendix: Preface to the Reconstruction of the Life-Release Pond at Jile Temple in Nanxun

inline.s: Master Yinguang

The practice of abstaining from killing and releasing living beings is shallow and easy to see. The principle of abstaining from killing and releasing living beings is deep and hard to understand. If one does not understand the principle, then even though one may carry out the practice, one's mind can never be truly sincere and compassionate; and the blessings of the field of merit will likewise become slight and shallow in proportion to the narrowness of one's mind. If one meets with the obstruction and slander of those who do not understand, one may well be turned around by them, and there are those whose whole heart of goodness is thereupon extinguished. Therefore, not shrinking from prolixity, I set forth its meaning, so that creatures may alike bathe in compassionate grace and human beings each cultivate their own welfare. With earnest and profound benevolence, may we extinguish the retribution of killing for self and others, together reach the realm of long life, and together enjoy our natural span. I further pray that this merit be dedicated toward the West. Then one will forever escape the cycle of rebirth, rise above the three realms, become a disciple of Amitābha, and be a good friend to the ocean-wide assembly. May the reader kindly take note.

Originally, the mind-nature of beings in water and on land is, directly and immediately, no different from that of the Buddhas of the three times. It is only that the power of past evil karma obscures their wondrous clarity so that it cannot appear, and they sink into other kinds of beings. Thus their knowledge is mean and inferior, and apart from seeking food and avoiding death they know nothing at all. It is like a great precious bronze mirror covered with dust through many kalpas. Not only does it have no light at all; even its bronze substance does not appear, and it is just like a piece of junk. Suddenly it meets a wise man who knows it is a precious mirror possessing boundless light that illumines heaven and earth. So he polishes it day after day: at first the mirror's substance is slightly revealed, then its light gradually comes forth. And when the polishing reaches its utmost, the light that illumines heaven and earth appears in full. Only then do the unwise consider it precious and regard it as a treasure beyond price. One should know that this light is inherent in the mirror itself; it is not obtained from the polishing. Yet though it is inherent, if there were no condition of polishing, then kalpa after kalpa there would be no day on which its light came forth.

The mind-nature of all sentient beings in the human and heavenly realms and the six destinies is entirely like this. From time without beginning, delusion and karma have obscured it, so that the inherent wondrous clarity cannot appear; they turn their backs on the true nature and create the karma of birth and death. The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One knew that the single thought, the mind-nature, of all sentient beings is of the same kind as the Buddha's. Therefore, by all manner of skillful means, he taught the Dharma according to capacity. He universally caused them to cultivate the path of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, hoping that they might cut off delusion and karma and recover their original possession, perfect their merit and wisdom, and realize the dharmakāya. He further caused people of the world to bring forth a compassionate mind, to abstain from killing and to release living beings. This is because I and all sentient beings are alike within the cycle of rebirth. From time without beginning we have given birth to one another in turn and killed one another in turn. They have each and all been my father and mother, my brothers, my sisters, my sons and daughters, and I have each and all been their father and mother, their brothers, their sisters, their sons and daughters. They have again and again, through the power of evil karma, whether among humans or among other kinds of beings, suffered my slaughter; and I too, through the power of evil karma, whether among humans or among other kinds of beings, have suffered their slaughter. Through long kalpas we give birth to one another and kill one another, with no end at all. Ordinary beings do not know this; the Tathāgata sees it clearly. If one does not think of it, well enough; but when one thinks of it, one cannot but feel overwhelming shame and compassion!

I am now fortunate to have inherited the blessings and goodness of past lives and to be born in the human realm. I ought certainly to dissolve resentment and untie knots, to abstain from killing and release living beings, so that all who have life may each find their place. And I should recite the Buddha's name and dedicate the merit toward the Pure Land on their behalf, so that they may attain deliverance. Even if their karma is heavy and they cannot be born there at once, I shall rely on this merit of kindness and compassion and resolve to be reborn in the Western Land at the end of my life. Once reborn there, one at once transcends the ordinary and enters the sage, ends birth and death, forever escapes the cycle of rebirth, and gradually realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.

Moreover, loving creatures and releasing living beings is something all the ancient sages and worthies practiced. Thus the Book of Documents has the passage “birds, beasts, fish, and turtles all follow their nature,” and King Wen's grace extended even to dry bones — how much more to creatures that have awareness! As for Jianzi releasing the turtledove, Zichan keeping fish, the Marquis of Sui rescuing the snake, and Yang Bao saving the sparrow — these were indeed the hearts of sages and worthies who viewed all with equal kindness, yet they still did not know such principles as that the humblest crawling creature with consciousness all possesses Buddha-nature, that humans and animals rise and sink in turn and are one another's foes and kin, and that in the future they will surely become Buddhas. Only when the great teaching came east did the three periods of cause and effect, and the principle that the mind-nature of sentient beings and Buddhas is equal and not two, become greatly clear to the world. Every great sage and great worthy has taken abstaining from killing and releasing living beings as the foundation for turning back the kalpa of killing and cultivating the fruit of blessing, for ending war and enjoying one's natural span.

The ancients said: “If you would know the kalpa of swords and soldiers in the world, listen to the sounds at midnight in the slaughterhouse.” They also said: “If you would have the world free of the kalpa of war, only let sentient beings not eat meat.” From this one knows that abstaining from killing and releasing living beings is the good counsel that pulls up the root and stops the source in aiding the world. Thus Master Zhiyi of the Chen dynasty bought more than sixty places along the rivers, inlets, streams, and bridges of Linhai, stretching over four hundred li, as life-release ponds. He requested an imperial edict and set up steles forbidding fishing and netting. Those who secretly fished often met with misfortune. This was still so down to the Zhenguan era of the Tang. In the second year of Qianyuan under Emperor Suzong of the Tang, an edict was issued for every prefecture in the empire to establish life-release ponds, and Yan Zhenqing was commanded to compose the stele text and write it in red. It says: “Our sovereign takes the whole empire as a pond, and the whole realm receives blessing, inheriting the power of the dhāraṇī's empowerment, and exhausting the ocean of affliction and the ford of birth and death. Compared with antiquity, how can it be matched?” In the first year of Tianxi under Emperor Zhenzong of the Song, an edict was issued for the empire to establish life-release ponds, and West Lake in Hangzhou was also a life-release pond of the Song. Master Lianchi of the Ming established life-release ponds at Shangfang and Changshou. His “Essay on Abstaining from Killing and Releasing Living Beings” circulated throughout the world. For more than three hundred years since, monks and laypeople of broad understanding who admire his lofty spirit and compassionately aid creatures — how could they be counted!

Someone may say: Widowers, widows, orphans, and the childless, the poor and the afflicted, are found everywhere — why not relieve them, instead of hurrying after creatures that have no connection with us? Is this not to reverse what is urgent and what is slight, what is weighty and what is light?

The answer: You do not know the reason the Tathāgata taught people to abstain from killing and release living beings. Humans and creatures differ, yet the Buddha-nature is originally the same. They, through evil karma, have sunk into other kinds of beings; I, through good karma, am fortunate to have obtained a human body. If I show them no compassion and pity, but give free rein to my feelings and eat them, then once my blessings are exhausted or their offenses are finished, I can hardly avoid repaying from the beginning, filling their mouths and bellies. One should know that the great kalpa of swords and soldiers is all evoked by the killing karma of past lives. If there were no killing karma, then even meeting bandits and robbers, they would bring forth a good mind and not put one to the sword. How much less would one meet with plagues, floods, fires, and other calamities and misfortunes — those who abstain from killing and release living beings rarely encounter them. From this one knows that protecting life is originally protecting oneself. Abstaining from killing can avoid being killed by heaven, killed by ghosts and spirits, killed by thieves, and killed in the future by the mutual repayment of resentment upon resentment. Widowers, widows, orphans, and the childless, the poor and the afflicted, should likewise be relieved according to one's means and strength. Would one who abstains from killing and releases living beings never perform such meritorious deeds at all? Yet widows and orphans, though deeply deserving of pity, have not yet reached the point of death. Creatures, if not rescued and redeemed, will at once be seen upon the chopping block and cauldron, filling someone's mouth and belly.
Again it is said: Creatures are without end; how many can one release?

The answer: One should know that the practice of releasing living beings is in truth the most supreme good mind that inspires all people to protect life universally. One hopes that they will enter into the meaning of releasing living beings, and that their hearts will be moved with compassion so that they cannot bear to eat them. And if they do not eat them, then the catchers will stop. Then all creatures of water, land, and air may freely fly, run, and swim within their own domains — and this becomes a universal release that is no release at all. Is this not what is meant by taking the whole world as a pond? Even if not everyone can be like this, if one person cannot bear to eat meat, then immeasurable lives in water and on land escape slaughter. How much more if it is more than one person! Moreover, for all people present and future, one cuts off the causes of being a widower, a widow, an orphan, or childless, of poverty and affliction, and creates the conditions for long life without sickness, for wealth and honor and peace, for fathers and sons reunited, and for husband and wife growing old together. This is precisely to relieve them in advance, so that in life after life to come they may never again meet with the suffering of widowhood and the like, and long enjoy the joys of long life and wealth. Is this not what is meant by the whole realm receiving blessing? How can one set it aside with indifference? Consider it carefully: is abstaining from killing and releasing living beings, after all, a hurried concern for people, or is it only a hurried concern for creatures, and are the urgent and the slight, the weighty and the light, reversed?

Outside Jile Temple in Nanxun there was formerly a life-release pond. Because the embankment was not fully built up, it collapsed. Moreover, it had not been dredged for many years and was full of silt. Whenever good people released living beings into the river, though they brought forth a good mind, the creatures found it hard to benefit. Of those that were released in the morning and caught again by evening, more than half were such cases. If it were near a great river, then indeed one should release them into the river, but a small river is by no means suitable. Master Yuanlin could not bear it in his heart, and proposed to dredge the pond deeply and to build a wall around it as a protection, so that there would be a place for releasing living beings and no way for thieving catchers to take them. His intention was generous indeed. Before work had begun, it happened that Master Juesan of Putuo arrived, and at the first meeting they found their aspirations in accord. Soon after, he entrusted the temple affairs to him, and himself put down ten thousand conditions to devote himself solely to the pure karma. Master Jue carried on the old undertaking and wished to complete the work quickly. But because the project was vast, it was hard to accomplish alone. He proposed to solicit the faithful of the whole town to join in the excellent deed. He asked me to write a preface.

I have often grieved deeply over the misery of the kalpa of killing in recent times, and wished to turn it back but had no strength to do so. Their request touched my heart. So I have set forth in brief the original true mind shared by us and by creatures, how they rise and sink according to karma, and the present and future retributions of killing and of protecting life. I hope that all you benefactors will alike bring forth a good mind, alike donate pure wealth, and bring this undertaking swiftly to success, so that all creatures may find their place, and its merit and benefit be boundless and unlimited. Not only will ten thousand calamities melt like ice in this life and a thousand auspicious signs gather like clouds; those in future lives who remember the grace and repay the virtue will be beyond knowing — thousands of millions of billions of them!

The practice of abstaining from killing and releasing living beings is shallow and easy to see, while the principle of abstaining from killing and releasing living beings is deep and hard to understand. If one does not understand the principle, then even though one may carry out the practice, one will by no means have a truly sincere and compassionate heart; and the blessings of the field of merit will likewise become slight and shallow in proportion to the narrowness of one's mind. If one meets with the obstruction and slander of those who do not understand the principle, it is quite likely that one will change one's original intention, and one's whole heart of goodness will thereupon be extinguished. Therefore I do not shrink from prolixity here, but set forth the principle of abstaining from killing and releasing living beings, so that animals may alike bathe in compassionate grace and human beings each cultivate their own welfare. With earnest and profound benevolence, may we extinguish the retribution of killing for self and others, together enjoy long life, and together delight in our natural span. And I pray that this merit be dedicated toward rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Then one will forever escape the cycle of rebirth, rise above the three realms, become a disciple of Amitābha Buddha, and be a good friend to the Bodhisattvas of the pure ocean-wide assembly. May the reader read carefully.

Originally, the mind-nature of animals in water and on land is wholly the same as that of the Buddhas of the three times. It is only that past evil karma has obscured the wondrous true mind so that it cannot appear, and they have fallen and become other kinds of beings. Thus their knowledge is mean and inferior, and apart from seeking food and avoiding death they know nothing at all. It is like a great precious bronze mirror covered with dust through countless kalpas. Not only does it have no light at all; even its substance does not appear, and it is simply like a piece of junk. Suddenly it meets a wise man who knows it is a precious mirror possessing boundless light that illumines heaven and earth. So he polishes it day after day: at first the mirror's substance is slightly revealed, then its light gradually comes forth. When the polishing reaches its utmost, the light that illumines heaven and earth appears in full. Only then do the unwise know to prize it and regard it as a treasure beyond price. One should know that this light is inherent in the precious mirror; it is not obtained from the polishing. Yet though this light is inherent in the mirror, if there were no condition of polishing, then kalpa after kalpa there would be no day on which its light came forth.

The mind-nature of all beings in the human realm, the heavenly realm, and the six destinies is entirely like this. From time without beginning, delusion and karma have obscured it, so that the inherent wondrous clarity cannot appear; they turn their backs on the true nature and create the karma of birth and death. The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha, knew that the mind-nature of all sentient beings is the same as the Buddha's. Therefore, by all manner of skillful means, he taught the Dharma according to capacity. He universally caused sentient beings to cultivate the path of enlightenment of precepts, concentration, and wisdom, so as to cut off delusion and karma and recover their original possession, perfect their merit and wisdom, and realize the dharmakāya. He further caused people of the world to bring forth a compassionate mind, to abstain from killing and to release living beings. This is because I and all sentient beings are alike within the cycle of rebirth. From time without beginning we have given birth to one another in turn and killed one another in turn. They have each and all been my father and mother, my brothers, my sisters, my sons and daughters, and I have each and all been their father and mother, their brothers, their sisters, their sons and daughters. They have again and again, through the power of evil karma, whether as humans or as other kinds of beings, suffered my slaughter; and I too, through the power of evil karma, whether as a human or as another kind of being, have suffered their slaughter. Through long kalpas we give birth to one another and kill one another, without end. Ordinary beings do not know this, but the Tathāgata sees it clearly. Now, having received the Buddha's instruction, I know these circumstances of giving birth to and killing one another. If I do not think of it, well enough; but when I think of it, I cannot but feel overwhelming shame and compassion!

I am now fortunate to have inherited the blessings and good karma of past lives and to be born in the human realm. I ought certainly to dissolve enmity and untie knots, to abstain from killing and release living beings, and let all who have life each find their place. And I should recite the Buddha's name and dedicate the merit toward the Pure Land on their behalf, so that they may attain deliverance. Even if their karma is heavy and they cannot be reborn there at once, I shall rely on this merit of kindness and compassion and resolve to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at the end of my life. Once reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one at once transcends the ordinary and enters the sage, ends birth and death, forever escapes the cycle of rebirth, and gradually realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.

Moreover, loving creatures and releasing living beings is something all the ancient sages and worthies practiced. Thus the Book of Documents has the passage “birds, beasts, fish, and turtles all follow their nature (birds, beasts, fish, and turtles should all follow their own nature, so that they do not suffer the misery of being killed or the terror of being startled and fleeing),” and King Wen's grace extended even to dry bones — how much more to animals that have awareness! As for Jianzi releasing the turtledove, Zichan keeping fish, the Marquis of Sui rescuing the snake, and Yang Bao saving the sparrow — these were indeed the hearts of sages and worthies who viewed all with equal kindness, yet they still did not know such principles as that the humblest crawling creature with consciousness all possesses Buddha-nature, that humans and animals rise and sink in turn and are one another's foes and kin, and that abstaining from killing and releasing living beings will in the future surely lead to Buddhahood. Only when the Buddhadharma came to China did the three periods of cause and effect, and the principle that the mind-nature of sentient beings and Buddhas is equal and not two, become greatly clear to the world. Every great sage and great worthy has taken abstaining from killing and releasing living beings as the foundation for turning back the kalpa of killing and cultivating the fruit of blessing, for ending war and enjoying one's natural span.

[Jianzi releasing the turtledove] This is the story of the feudal lord Zhao Jianzi releasing a turtledove during the Spring and Autumn period: On New Year's Day (the first day of the first month), a man of Handan presented a turtledove to Zhao Jianzi. Zhao Jianzi was delighted and rewarded him generously. A guest asked him why he was so pleased. Zhao Jianzi answered: “I shall release it, to show my kindness and generosity.” The guest said: “When people learn that you release living beings, they will all cater to your taste and compete to catch them for you to release. In this catching and releasing, many will die or be injured. If you truly do not wish to harm them, the best way is to forbid catching them. If they are caught and then released, your kindness cannot outweigh your fault.” Zhao Jianzi gladly accepted the advice and issued a strict order forbidding the catching of turtledoves. [Zichan keeping fish] Someone gave fish to Zichan (a disciple of Confucius). He could not bear that they should be killed, and put them all into a pond. [The Marquis of Sui rescuing the snake] The Marquis of Sui was traveling to the state of Qi when on the road he saw a snake trapped in the sand, its head bleeding. So he lifted it up with his staff and put it into the water. On his return he passed this place again, and the snake held a precious pearl in its mouth and presented it to him. [Yang Bao saving the sparrow] When Yang Bao was young, he saw a yellow sparrow struck by an owl and fallen to the ground, and then surrounded by ants. So he picked up the yellow bird and took it home, put it in a box, and fed it with yellow flowers. When its wound healed, he let it fly away. At night he dreamed of a boy in yellow robes who bowed in thanks and gave him four jade rings, saying: “I am a messenger of the Queen Mother of the West, and I received your gift of life. Your descendants will all be of lofty character and integrity, wealthy and honored, ranked among the Three Excellencies, just like these four jade rings.” Later, for four generations the descendants of Yang Bao were eminent and honored.

The ancients said, "If you would know the calamity of war in the world, you must listen to the sound of the butcher's knife at midnight." And again: "If you wish the world to be free from the calamity of war, none but living beings must cease to eat flesh." From this we know that abstaining from killing and releasing life is the fundamental way to rescue the people of the world. Therefore Great Master Zhiyi bought more than sixty places along the sea and river at Linhai, stretching for over four hundred li, to serve as ponds for releasing life. He also petitioned the court to issue a decree and erect a stele forbidding fishing and poaching; those who secretly fished were severely punished. This continued even into the Zhenguan reign of the Tang dynasty. In the second year of Qianyuan during Emperor Suzong of the Tang, an edict was issued to the whole empire, ordering every prefecture to establish ponds for releasing life. The emperor commanded Yan Zhenqing, the great calligrapher who rose to be Minister of Personnel and Grand Mentor to the Crown Prince and was enfeoffed as Duke of Lu, to compose the inscription, which was then engraved upon stone. The inscription read: "Our enlightened sovereign takes the whole world as a pond for releasing life, blessing every place. Relying upon the sustaining power of the divine mantra, he severs the stream of birth and death within the sea of afflictions. Examining the ages past, where has there ever been such a glorious deed?"

In the first year of Tianxi during Emperor Zhenzong of the Song, an edict was issued to the whole empire to establish ponds for releasing life. West Lake of Hangzhou was likewise a pond for releasing life in the Song dynasty. In the Ming, the Great Master Lianchi (Zhuhong) established ponds for releasing life at the two places Shangfang and Changshou. His treatise on abstaining from killing and releasing life circulated throughout the world. For more than three hundred years since, monks and laypeople who have admired the master's noble conduct and extended compassion to living creatures have been beyond counting.

Someone asked: The widowed, the bereaved, the orphaned, the childless, the poor and those in distress are everywhere. Why not go to their aid, and instead rush about to rescue creatures not at all related to us? Are not the urgent and the trivial set upside down here?

I replied: You do not understand the reason why the Tathagata teaches people to abstain from killing and to release life. Humans and animals, though different in form, share the same buddha-nature. They have fallen into other species because of evil karma; we have been fortunate to gain a human body because of wholesome karma. If we do not pity them but indulge ourselves in eating them, then once our blessings are spent and their retribution is exhausted, we shall have to repay it all from the beginning, and we ourselves shall be eaten by them. You should know that the great calamities of war arise entirely from the karmic effects of killing in past lives. If there were no karma of killing, even if one met with bandits, they would give rise to good thoughts and would not do him harm. How much less so with disasters such as epidemics, floods, and fires; those who abstain from killing and release life rarely encounter them. From this we know that protecting creatures is, in truth, protecting ourselves. Abstaining from killing frees one from death by heaven's hand, death at the hands of ghosts and spirits, death by robbers, and death from the mutual reprisal of enmity in the future. As for the widowed, the bereaved, the orphaned, the childless, the poor and those in distress, one should likewise aid them according to one's station and strength. Does one who abstains from killing and releases life not perform this virtue as well? Moreover, people such as the widowed, the orphaned, the poor and the distressed, though deeply to be pitied, have not yet reached the point of death. But the creatures that are destined to be eaten, if not rescued immediately, are instantly slaughtered and cooked to fill the belly.
Again he asked: The animals that are to be eaten are beyond counting. How many can you release?

I replied: You should know that the act of releasing life is in truth the supremely excellent good thought of arousing all people to protect the lives of living creatures. We hope that they will grasp the meaning of releasing life and, pitying the creatures in their hearts, be unable to bear eating them. If everyone refrains from eating them, then no one will go to catch them. Then all creatures in the air, on the land, and in the water will freely fly, walk, and swim within their own realms, so that although no one is deliberately releasing life, yet life is universally released. Is this not taking the whole world as a pond for releasing life? Even if not everyone can do this, if a single person cannot bear to eat flesh, then countless creatures of water and land are spared from slaughter, how much more when there are far more than one such person! Moreover, this cuts off, for all who now and in the future abstain from killing and release life, the evil causes of widowhood, bereavement, orphanhood, childlessness, poverty and distress, and serves as the good conditions for long life free from illness, wealth and honor, peace and happiness, the reunion of father and son, and the growing old together of husband and wife. It is also precisely to aid in advance those who would otherwise become the widowed, the orphaned, the poor and the distressed, so that in life after life they will never suffer the miseries of widowhood, orphanhood, poverty, or distress, but will long enjoy longevity, wealth, and honor. Is this not making all places blessed? How can one be indifferent to it? Consider carefully: in abstaining from killing and releasing life, is one truly rushing about for the sake of people, or for the sake of animals? And have the urgent and the trivial been turned upside down?

Outside the Jile Temple at Nanxun there had long been a pond for releasing life. Because the embankment had not been fully built, it had collapsed. Moreover, having not been dredged or deepened for many years, it was filled with silt, and good-hearted people often released life in the river. Though they meant well, the released creatures gained little benefit. Of those released in the morning, most were caught again by evening. If one is near a great river, the creatures should be released into the river; a small river is quite unsuitable for releasing life. Master Yuanlin, grieved at heart by this situation of releasing in the morning and catching at evening, planned to dredge and deepen this pond for releasing life and to build an enclosing wall around it for protection, so that people would have a place to release the creatures without their being stolen or caught, an idea most compassionate. Before the work began, Master Juesan of Putuo Mountain happened to arrive, and at a glance the two found themselves of like mind. So Master Yuanlin entrusted the affairs of the temple to him, while he himself cast aside all conditions and single-mindedly practiced the pure karma of recitation. Master Juesan, succeeding to the task of restoring the pond for releasing life, wished to complete it as quickly as possible. But because the undertaking was vast, it could not be accomplished by one person alone. Therefore he planned to raise funds from the good and faithful people of the whole town and, together with them, to complete this fine work, and so he asked me to write a preface.

I have often grieved over the cruelty of the slaughter-karma of recent times, and wished to rescue people from it but had not the strength to act. His invitation stirred my heart. I have therefore set forth in brief the true mind originally possessed alike by humans and animals, their rise and fall in accordance with karma, and the present and future retributions of killing and of protecting life. I hope that all the benefactors will together give rise to good thoughts and together contribute pure funds, so that this work may speedily be accomplished and the fish, turtles, and other released creatures may each find their proper place. The merit and benefit will be boundless and measureless. Not only will ten thousand calamities melt away like ice in this present life and a thousand auspicious omens gather like clouds; among those in ages to come who repay their debt of gratitude, who knows how many millions of millions there will be.
